title: AI Lead Desk
pitch: Structured WebMCP actions turn one sales objective into a visible, human-controlled lead pipeline.
about_excerpt:
Structured WebMCP actions turn one sales objective into a visible, human-controlled lead pipeline.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sales prospecting is fragmented across search, company websites, spreadsheets, scoring tools, outreach editors, and CRM systems. Browser agents that rely on guessing which visual control to click can be brittle, while sensitive final actions still require human judgment. 

 AI Lead Desk was built to show a different model: give an AI agent a small set of structured WebMCP actions, keep every transition visible in the interface, and preserve a real human approval boundary. 

 What it does 

 AI Lead Desk turns one sales objective into a visible five-stage workflow: 

 Find → Research → Qualify → Prepare Outreach → Human Approval → Pipeline 

 ChatGPT can: 

 
 find five matching companies, 
 research the strongest candidate, 
 qualify the lead against a defined target profile, 
 prepare a personalized outreach draft, 
 and move the lead into Pipeline only after explicit human approval. 
 

 The outreach remains Draft / Not sent . The challenge version does not send email or WhatsApp messages. 

 The current demo uses synthetic logistics and freight-forwarding companies in Dubai. They are demonstration data, not verified real prospects. 

 How we built it 

 AI Lead Desk is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. 

 The application registers exactly five native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_leads 
 research_company 
 qualify_lead 
 prepare_outreach 
 add_to_pipeline 
 

 The WebMCP tools and the visible UI use the same validated domain actions and application state. That means tool execution, lead stages, qualification results, approval state, and the Activity Log remain synchronized. 

 For live execution, the application sends validated tool requests to a server-side Next.js endpoint. A secure n8n router handles the five known actions. The webhook URL and credential remain server-side and never enter the browser bundle. 

 A deterministic DEMO_MODE fallback is also available for network-independent testing. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent handles the repetitive work: lead discovery, company research, qualification, and draft preparation. 

 The human retains control where judgment and accountability matter. 

 add_to_pipeline cannot be authorized by the agent itself. Approval must first be recorded through the visible Approve for pipeline interaction in the application. 

 Clicking approval does not send outreach. It only authorizes the final Pipeline transition. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenges were: 

 
 verifying native WebMCP discovery and execution in a real supported browser client, 
 keeping agent actions and visible UI state on one shared workflow, 
 enforcing a genuine human-controlled approval boundary, 
 normalizing five typed actions through one secure n8n router, 
 and making the draft-only outreach behavior unmistakable. 
 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Exactly five native WebMCP tools are exposed. 
 A complete production workflow works from lead search through approved Pipeline transition. 
 Atlas Freight Network scores 91/100, Grade A in the canonical demo. 
 Human approval is enforced before the final transition. 
 Outreach remains Draft / Not sent . 
 Live n8n routing works in production. 
 42 automated tests across 10 files pass. 
 Lint, TypeScript validation, and production build all pass. 
 The full production E2E flow was verified successfully. 
 

 What we learned 

 Structured browser tools are more useful when they do more than expose actions. They also need strict contracts, shared application state, lifecycle cleanup, visible feedback, safe error handling, and clear authority boundaries. 

 WebMCP lets the agent perform predictable actions without guessing how the interface works, while the human can still see and control the workflow. 

 What's next 

 The commercial direction is to connect verified company-data providers, customer-specific qualification criteria, and integrations with existing CRM or sales systems. 

 Any future outreach-sending capability would require its own explicit review and authorization design. 

 The challenge version intentionally remains focused on lead research, qualification, draft preparation, and human-controlled pipeline management. 

 Data disclosure 

 All company records and evidence shown in the current challenge demo are synthetic test data. No claim is made that the demo generated verified real leads or sent real outreach.

title: Pursuit Permit
pitch: New facts need new authority.
about_excerpt: New facts need new authority. Like Comment Story Updates New evidence makes the £900k bid qualify, but the active permit survives: active_permit_conflict, 0h moved. The first permit call returns approval_required. No WebMCP tool can approve, and the page checkpoint still commits 0h. The flight recorder shows seven native WebMCP calls ending in a failed-closed capacity conflict. Pursuit Permit: recommendations can change without yesterday's approval drifting to a different bid. People approve snapshots; agents keep recomputing. Pursuit Permit lets recommendations update without letting permission drift. The £900k bid now qualifies. The active £750k / 32-hour permit does not change. active_permit_conflict . Zero hours moved. Inspiration A browser agent can discover new evidence in the same page where it can propose spending a scarce bid-team slot. The dangerous ambiguity is not ranking. It appears later: does yesterday's approval follow today's newly correct recommendation? Most approval demos end when approval is granted. Pursuit Permit starts where that becomes dangerous: after the facts change. It is a fixed, synthetic procurement replay of one narrow protocol—recommend, approve an exact revision, issue a bounded permit, and later re-prove the decision without inheriting yesterday's authority. What it does The demo gives every judge the same reproducible two-act decision: Five page-owned WebMCP tools search, compare, shortlist, issue, and retest. The apparent £900,000 winner fails two mandatory gates, so the eligible £750,000 alternative is proposed for the team's only 32-hour bid slot. issue_pursuit_permit returns structured approval_required . It creates no permit and commits no capacity. The registered tool surface intentionally exposes no approval endpoint. A visibly separate page checkpoint, labeled NOT AN AGENT TOOL , records an unverified reviewer label against the exact bid, allocation, evidence revision, and decision revision. Approval still commits zero hours. Only a matching WebMCP retry issues one idempotent, revision-bound permit and changes 32 hours from proposed to committed. A second page-only demo action revises the synthetic bidder evidence. Both reopening conditions stored in the historical receipt now pass, so the £900,000 bid becomes the better recommendation. retest_pursuit_permit(receiptId) re-proves the old receipt against the new facts and names the still-active permit the candidate would displace. It creates no new authority. A forced shortlist fails closed with active_permit_conflict . The original £750,000 permit survives. Zero hours move. The values, opportunities, evidence, and staffing hours are deterministic demo fixtures—not live procurement data, measured savings, staffing advice, verified identity, or production authorization. Why WebMCP This proof cannot live only in chat. The five imperative WebMCP tools and the React interface share one client-side controller. Every call changes the same opportunity rows, evidence panel, shortlist, capacity rail, checkpoint, receipt, and chain-of-custody ledger the reviewer sees. The built-in proof console exposes all five registered tools, the chronological invocation count, and selected request/response evidence. WebMCP therefore makes the state machine inspectable: an agent can re-evaluate and propose, encounter a machine-readable stop, retry after a visible checkpoint, and later discover that a better recommendation still lacks authority to displace an active permit. How we built it Pursuit Permit uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, strict Zod schemas, and the official webmcp-types package. Motion provides causal rank transitions and checkpoint-to-receipt continuity; NumberFlow handles the changing leader value; Rough Notation marks the defeated pursuit and failed clauses. Locally bundled IBM Plex fonts keep the interface self-contained. The controller validates every tool boundary and produces immutable state shared by UI and WebMCP. Approval binds the shortlist, allocation, exact evidence content, opportunity details, bidder profile, evidence revision, and decision revision. Idempotency keys cannot replay across revisions, one approval fingerprint can create only one receipt, and relevant state changes invalidate approval. The active permit is stored separately from the new working proposal, so reopened evidence cannot erase or silently replace it. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was separating planned , proposed , approved , and committed . Comparison may calculate a 32-hour move; shortlist may propose it; the page checkpoint may record approval. Only permit issuance can change committed capacity. The second was making retest useful without making it dangerous. New evidence must be allowed to prove that the recommendation changed, but it must not rewrite history or let a reopened tender steal an already committed slot. The third was visual: the safety property had to be visible in seconds. We used an evidence thread, physical rank reversal, NO-BID stamp, capacity rail, distinct reviewer checkpoint, permit seal, green reopening thread, and a proof-mode flight recorder so the product demonstrates the boundary instead of merely claiming it. Accomplishments that we're proud of Five discoverable, page-owned WebMCP tools operating on the same state the judge sees. A structured approval_required stop with 0h committed and no exposed approval tool. One exact approved retry that issues a proof-carrying permit and commits 32 demo hours. A historical-receipt retest followed by active_permit_conflict , preserving the active permit and moving 0h . Keyboard-only operation, reduced motion, forced-colors support, focus-managed modal inspection, and 320px reflow. A verified release gate: 129 unit/integration checks, 42 applicable browser checks, 87.55% statement coverage, 80.56% branch coverage, production build, lint, typecheck, and zero dependency-audit vulnerabilities. What we learned An agent becomes more useful when its state transitions are narrower than its recommendations. ‘Approved’ and ‘committed’ are not synonyms, and a receipt is most valuable when it can be re-tested without becoming a blank cheque. What's next A production version would ingest licensed procurement data, use a permissioned company evidence library, attach source-level provenance, authenticate reviewers, integrate with real staffing systems, and define explicit revocation and supersession rules. Those are roadmap items, not capabilities claimed by this challenge build. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace
video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: Locus
pitch: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together.
about_excerpt: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage trips-home trip-planner-hoem Inspiration Life is scattered across apps. An article waits in YouTube Watch Later. A restaurant is buried in Instagram Saved. A useful thread disappears into X Bookmarks. A recipe, a place to visit, and an idea for a future trip may all belong to the same plan, but the platforms where we found them keep them in separate feeds. We save because something feels useful. Most of those saves never become useful. Locus began as an attempt to change that: one private desk for the things you have already chosen to remember. It captures saves from the places where they live and brings them into a personal Library. The same Item can become something to read, a dish to cook, a Place, or part of a Trip Document without losing its source. WebMCP made the next step possible. Instead of copying personal context into a chatbot and hoping it understands the application, a browser agent can work through tools defined by the page currently open. The person and agent share the same visible artifact. What it does Locus turns your saved social content into practical, reviewable outcomes: Desk as the central hub that collects Items from X, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, or a URL added manually. Reading preserves available writing and helps the user choose what to read. Kitchen turns saved food posts into recipes if needed and presents them in a unique way, helps decide tonight's menu if you want. Atlas organises saved material that is there for travel. Trips can use your saved places to plan the trip you want, with ability to share them. Each relevant surface registers its own WebMCP tools. On Reading, an agent can inspect the current reading context, search saved writing, open stored text, and present recommendations. In Kitchen, it can search the Recipe Box or compose Tonight. In Trips, it can read the exact itinerary, search bounded Library sources, create Draft stops, apply an exact requested change, validate the schedule, or present three alternatives for a decision. The distinction between an instruction and a preference is central to the product. If the user says, “Add these three saved places to Saturday,” the agent can make that exact revision-checked change. If the user asks, “Where should I have dinner?”, the agent presents alternatives inside Locus and waits for the person to choose. Agent-created trip stops and recipes begin as Drafts. Publishing, deletion, review, capture setup, and other consequential actions stay with the person. How we built it We started with a simple belief: people should not have to change how they save things before those saves can become useful. Locus therefore meets people where they already are. A Chrome extension visits the saved pages they are already signed into on X, Instagram, YouTube, and Reddit, reads the posts they chose to keep, and brings them into one private Library. From there, we built the product around the ways those saves might become useful. React and TypeScript power one shared interface for Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, and Trips. Locus can run locally with Node.js and SQLite, and we also built a hosted edition on Cloudflare Workers and D1 so anyone judging the project can open it without installing a server. WebMCP became the bridge between that private Library and the browser agent. Instead of giving the agent one large, all-powerful connection, each Locus page offers only the tools that make sense there. On Reading, the agent can search saved articles and suggest what to read. In Kitchen, it can help compose Tonight's dinner/food recipes. In Trips, it can read the itinerary, find saved places, add Draft stops, or present three options for a decision. The most important part was making the agent's work visible. When it changes a trip, the stop appears in the trip the person is already looking at. When the question is subjective, such as choosing dinner, the agent places alternatives inside Locus and waits. The person can inspect the reasons, follow the original saves, choose an option, change the result, or dismiss everything. We built the tools around that relationship: the agent helps move the work forward, while the person remains responsible for the final artifact. We tested the experience in real browsers, not only as isolated code. Google Chrome and Puppeteer helped us verify capture, navigation, and visible updates. The ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser acted as a real WebMCP agent: it discovered the tools on the current page, called them, and lost access to them when we navigated elsewhere. OpenAI Codex helped us throughout development with implementation, debugging, testing, and documentation, while image generation helped us explore the final Locus Point identity. Locus existed before the challenge as a local personal-saves desk. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP experiences across Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips, and built the authenticated Cloudflare edition used for this submission. Our dated commit history clearly separates that challenge work from the earlier project. Challenges we ran into The hardest design challenge was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. Generic CRUD tools would have been easy to expose, but they would not create a good collaboration model. We had to separate exact user instructions from open-ended taste decisions, temporary recommendations from durable state, and agent-authored Drafts from human-reviewed artifacts. Browser lifecycle behavior was another challenge. Our first live interoperability test found that the target browser used the current document.modelContext registration model with AbortSignal cleanup, while an early implementation expected an older interface. Fixing that taught us to treat tool discovery, navigation, re-registration, and visible UI updates as one end-to-end protocol rather than isolated functions. Capture exposed a different class of browser problem. X uses a virtualised list, and Chrome extension service workers can stop while a long capture is running. Early runs saved several batches and then appeared frozen or ended too soon. We changed the scan behavior, progress reporting, retry model, and job handling so partial work remains useful and later capture continues instead of starting over. Hosting the complete application also required moving from one trusted local SQLite database to tenant-scoped D1 storage. Authentication alone was not enough: every item, tag, reading document, recipe, place, trip, capture job, and intake operation needed a Library boundary, including cross-user tests that return 404 for guessed identifiers. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Locus became a complete hosted product rather than remaining a local prototype. The deployed application includes Google authentication, one private Library per user, capture and manual intake, and working Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, Trips, and sharing experiences. Tenant isolation is enforced throughout the data model and covered by cross-user tests. We are especially proud that WebMCP is part of the product model rather than a thin demo layer. Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips each expose tools shaped around their own domain. Those tools update the visible application, respect route lifecycle, and share the same validation and persistence modules as human actions. The Trips workflow brings those decisions together. An agent can turn named saved sources into revision-checked Draft stops, identify deterministic itinerary problems, or present three reasoned choices inside Locus. The user can inspect the original source, choose an option, adjust the plan, and keep control of the durable result. We also completed live browser interoperability testing and deployed the whole application to Cloudflare Workers and D1 within the challenge period. The Chrome extension can capture from the user's existing social sessions without requiring the hosted service to hold social account credentials. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser page is more than a place to launch a tool. It should be the shared workspace where context, action, and review meet. A strong tool result changes something the person can see, inspect, undo, or reject. We also learned that narrower tools create better behaviour. A tool that searches saved trip sources is safer and more useful than a general Library export. A recommendation tool that can only present three bounded options makes the human decision visible. Registering tools only for the current page gives the agent less irrelevant capability and makes the interface easier to understand. Most of all, we learned that organising a digital life is not just a classification problem. The real goal

title: Mysynote
pitch: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Default startup interface Click on play and see the synth in action. Message sent to live AI agent. WebMCP tools verified. Confirmation of agent not changing things manually locked by hand. One single source of truth. Self-testing. Inspiration Every AI-powered creative tool right now works the same way: you describe what you want in a chat box, and the model either generates a static result or silently mutates state you can't see happening. Sound design tools especially suffer from this — either the agent is a chatbot bolted onto the side of a DAW, guessing its way through a UI it wasn't built to understand, or it just spits out a finished audio file with no room for you to steer it mid-process. WebMCP flips that. Instead of an agent scraping a UI, the app itself declares exactly what it can do — real, typed, callable tools. That felt like the right foundation for something more interesting than "agent generates a sound": a studio where a human and an agent operate the same live instrument at the same time, each able to see and change what the other just did. What it does Mysynote is a browser-based modular synthesizer built on the Web Audio API. You patch together oscillators, filters, distortion, delay, reverb, and a sequencer on a live canvas, exactly like a hardware modular rig. An AI agent (Gemini or Claude, bring your own API key) sits alongside you with access to the same graph through WebMCP tools — it can inspect the current state, spawn and remove modules, patch and unpatch cables, tweak parameters, and read the live spectrum, all through structured tool calls rather than by describing changes in text. The part I care about most: you can lock any parameter by hand. Once locked, that boundary isn't a suggestion sitting in a system prompt the model could talk itself around — it's enforced in the tool implementation itself. If the agent (or a WebMCP-enabled browser calling the tools directly) tries to write to a locked parameter, or even tries to call unlock_parameter on a lock you set, the call is rejected with a structured error before it ever reaches the audio graph. You define the boundaries; the agent works freely inside them. How I built it The frontend is Next.js/React/TypeScript, styled with Tailwind. The audio engine is hand-written against the raw Web Audio API — no framework wrapping it — with a reconciler that diffs a plain-object graph state against the live AudioNode graph and patches only what changed, so the agent's tool calls and your own dragging/clicking stay in sync against one authoritative source of truth instead of two. WebMCP tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool : get_audio_graph_state , spawn_module , remove_module , patch_cable , remove_cable , set_module_param , lock_parameter , unlock_parameter , get_spectrum_analysis , get_sequencer_state , set_sequencer_step , and clear_graph . The in-app agent console (Gemini/Claude, BYOK) drives these exact same tools, so what you see the agent do in-app is identical to what any WebMCP-aware browser or agent could do against the live site. Challenges I ran into The hardest bug wasn't a crash — it was a bug that looked like everything worked. Early on, a locked parameter really did block direct writes, but the agent could still call unlock_parameter on itself with no restriction, defeat the lock, and then set the value anyway. Nothing crashed; it just quietly broke the entire premise of the project. Fixing it meant tracking who set a lock (human vs. tool) and rejecting a tool-sourced unlock of a human-set lock at the enforcement layer — plus adding it as a permanent regression check in the app's own self-test, so it can't silently reappear. I also hit a nasty reconciler bug where removing a module threw an uncaught exception mid-cleanup (a plain string field was being treated like an AudioNode ), which left orphaned nodes that kept crashing every subsequent state change. Chasing a bug that hides behind unrelated symptoms — a stuck test button, a sequencer step failing — down to one bad property check was the toughest debugging of the project. What I learned Building the "hard boundary" wasn't a UI problem, it was an authorization problem — the interesting design work in an agent-native app isn't the tools you expose, it's deciding which of your own tools the agent is allowed to call on itself. And that a feature can look completely correct in every manual test and still have a real security-shaped hole in it until something actually tries to defeat it on purpose. What's next Multiplayer patching (multiple humans + one agent on the same graph), saved/shareable patches, and exposing the sequencer's per-step modulation as its own lockable, agent-modifiable surface. title: CommandDeck
pitch: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my own work, I often ask AI for help, but I still have to move the result into the actual admin screen by hand. I built CommandDeck because I wanted the AI's plan to appear directly as a workspace that staff could review and use. Retail staff often use separate screens for products, prices, inventory, and storefront content. When old stock must be cleared, staff have to find products, check margins, prepare discounts, and review the customer view by hand. We wanted one simple request to prepare the right workspace for the job. What it does CommandDeck turns a business request into a task-ready workspace. In the demo, a staff member asks for a clearance plan. The agent finds slow-moving products and creates a workspace with product photos, prices, stock levels, and margin checks. The staff member can remove a product and ask to see what customers will see. The agent then changes the same workspace into a storefront preview. CommandDeck also supports price reviews, inventory replenishment, and storefront editing. Each task gets the tools and layout it needs. The agent prepares the work, while the staff member can edit, lock, review, and approve it. How we built it CommandDeck is built with React and TypeScript. It uses Zustand for state management, Zod for validation, and native document.modelContext.registerTool() calls for WebMCP. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the demo catalog, create a workspace, add trusted interface blocks, and change the layout when the task changes. The agent chooses from 11 trusted React blocks and five layouts. The visible controls and WebMCP tools use the same service layer. We also added English and Japanese interfaces and responsive layouts for desktop and mobile. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was allowing the workspace to change without losing human edits and approvals. We added revision checks, locks, and separate review groups. We also separated previews from applied results, so staff can see what is planned and what has actually changed. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single request can create a complete workspace and then reshape it when the job changes. The human and the agent work with the same information on the same page. Staff do not need to copy AI advice into several admin screens. CommandDeck keeps important actions under human control. Emergency rollback is human-only. The public demo uses browser-local sample data, so it does not place real orders or change a real store. What we learned WebMCP can do more than automate clicks. It allows an agent to prepare the right interface for the current job while the human keeps final control. This makes AI assistance easier to understand and more useful for everyday store operations. What's next for CommandDeck Next, we want to connect CommandDeck to real commerce systems with secure authentication and audit logs. We also want to add more operation templates, team roles, and saved work histories. title: OCHECK — Agent-Ready Official Guides
pitch: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source.
about_excerpt: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every experience already has an integrator. Today, that integrator is usually the customer. People reconstruct events from emails, chats, PDFs, maps, deadlines, providers, partner offers, and last-minute changes. Organizers may publish information across multiple channels, but participants must still assemble it into a usable path. OCHECK changes who performs that integration. It creates an organizer-governed official experience in which people and AI agents work from the same live, verifiable outcome state. It represents a new mindset and an INNOVATIVE approach to e-commerce: not simply getting things done, but doing them well—and making them OFFICIAL . What OCHECK does OCHECK transforms fragmented event information into one official, sequenced experience that integrates rules, timing, AI assistance, verified progress, optional partner value, and shareable achievements. The Challenge Edition presents three connected perspectives: Organizer + AI: An agent reads a fragmented creation brief, identifies sources, actors, services, and open loops, and stages an official guide. The guide is validated and cannot become official until the organizer separately confirms its publication. Participant: The participant receives an official path instead of having to reconstruct the event. An agent can create a personal plan without modifying the official source of truth. Verified completion brings readiness to 100% and unlocks a Ready Pass. Sponsor Impact: Sponsored utility reaches a genuinely interested, specialized audience. Sponsors gain actionable insight into the audience segments that viewed and purchased their products, while preserving participant privacy. Their offerings are not merely presented as items for sale; they are integrated as useful components of the official experience. The Ready Pass is not a reward purchased through commercial interaction. It is a verified, shareable achievement. Its clean referral link opens a new official guide for another participant without transferring any personal progress. Why WebMCP? OCHECK is a strong WebMCP use case because the challenge is not simply to generate an answer. The agent must understand and act on the authoritative state of a live web experience and its relationship with the event sponsors’ products. Without WebMCP, an AI assistant can discuss an event, but it cannot reliably inspect which guide is official, what remains incomplete, whether a participant is eligible for a Ready Pass, or which action a person has authorized. Through WebMCP, the browser page exposes 13 narrowly scoped Site Tools: Six read tools inspect the official outcome, creation brief, draft validation, participant progress, sponsorship opportunities, and commercial impact. Seven action tools stage a guide, publish the official source of truth, create a personal plan, verify completion, activate an optional benefit, claim a Ready Pass, and undo the last confirmed mutation. This gives the agent structured access to the same state visible to the person while keeping authority within OCHECK. What people and agents can do together The demonstrated workflow is: ChatGPT reads the organizer’s fragmented brief through OCHECK Site Tools. The agent identifies the intended outcome, sources, actors, and unresolved questions. The agent stages an integrated guide proposal. OCHECK validates governance, deadlines, evidence, source traceability, sponsorship disclosure, optionality, and Ready Pass logic. The organizer decides whether the validated proposal becomes official. The participant’s agent creates a personal execution plan without rewriting the official guide. Human-confirmed completion unlocks a Ready Pass, while the audit history and Undo function preserve human control. The agent provides interpretation and execution leverage. The organizer retains authority. The participant controls personal actions. OCHECK preserves one official source of truth. How we built it The Challenge Edition is a standalone, dependency-free web application built with HTML, CSS, and modern JavaScript and deployed on Vercel. The tools are registered directly through the browser-native API: const tools = buildSiteTools({ store, confirmAction }); for (const tool of tools) { await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool); } Read operations use narrowly defined schemas and readOnlyHint . Every state-changing operation opens an in-page confirmation showing the proposed action and its exact data before any state changes. A dedicated state layer separates: the official guide as the source of truth; staged AI proposals; participant progress; personal planning; sponsored interactions; Ready Pass eligibility; audit activity; and reversible mutations. The repository contains the complete source code, synthetic demonstration data, execution instructions, a BSD 3-Clause license, trademark boundaries, challenge provenance, and an automated test suite. Sixteen tests cover the complete human-agent experience, including validation, authority, privacy, Ready Pass rules, referral behavior, sponsorship separation, and Undo. No login, private service, production database, third-party runtime SDK, or real participant information is required. Challenges The hardest challenge was not registering the tools. It was defining trustworthy boundaries between agent capability and human authority. We had to ensure that: an AI-generated draft could not automatically become official; personal planning could not rewrite the organizer-controlled source of truth; commercial interaction could never purchase completion of, or satisfy, an official requirement; a Ready Pass could not be claimed before readiness had been verified; every consequential action required human confirmation; and the previous state could be restored through Undo. We also designed the tool schemas to remain narrow enough for reliable agent use while supporting a complete product experience rather than merely a technical proof of concept. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose meaningful product state instead of merely duplicating interface buttons. A strong agent-ready experience requires three elements working together: structured access to authoritative state; explicit authority and confirmation boundaries; and visible outcomes shared by both the person and the agent. We also learned that personalization does not require changing the official source of truth. The official guide can remain stable while the agent creates a contextual path for each participant. Challenge-period work OCHECK existed before the challenge as a product concept, brand, business model, and private MVP for official guides. The WebMCP Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a separate, standalone implementation. Work completed during the challenge period includes the 13 browser-native tools, AI Guide Forge, explicit outcome contracts, draft validation, human-confirmed publication, separate organizer, participant, and partner perspectives, Ready Pass verification, privacy-preserving sponsor signals, audit history, Undo, synthetic data, and automated testing. The public repository includes a timestamped commit history and HACKATHON.md , which clearly distinguishes OCHECK’s previous work from the new WebMCP implementation. Potential impact Events are the first use case, but the underlying problem arises wherever people must reconstruct an official process from fragmented information: events, education, travel, onboarding, public services, healthcare preparation, compliance, and professional workflows. OCHECK proposes a web in which agents do not replace authority. Instead, they help people understand and act upon a governed source of truth provided directly by the organizer. Founder OCHECK was founded and is led by Gustavo García Figueroa, a Colombian lawyer without a traditional background in software engineering. Gustavo contributed the original idea, product judgment, governance model, privacy boundaries, commercial logic, and testing decisions. ChatGPT and Codex accelerated execution by translating those decisions into workflows, source code, tests, and rapid iteration. The project uses generally available tools and does not claim endorsement, investment, or preferential support from OpenAI, Vercel, or any other challenge sponsor. One experience. One official truth. Human intent. Agent execution. Verified growth. This is OCHECK. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: ONCE
pitch: Teach an agent by working with it once.
about_excerpt: Teach an agent by working with it once. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent actions share one semantic collaboration trace. Replay pauses at the learned human approval boundary before recommendation. Taught routine separates variables, fixed policy, regenerated outputs, and example-only corrections. Inspiration ONCE explores how one human-agent collaboration can become reusable procedural memory. People repeatedly tell agents which inputs change, which rules remain fixed, which corrections are one-off, and when human judgment is mandatory. UI macros capture clicks and chat history captures prose, but neither creates a reliable shared procedure. What it does A human and an agent work together on the same live application state, with the human using the UI and the agent using WebMCP. ONCE records their work as one readable semantic trace, then the human selects Teach this routine . ONCE deterministically separates: changing inputs, such as budget and candidates; durable policies, such as ordered criteria and approval requirements; repeatable agent procedures; outputs that must be generated again; and example-only corrections that must not become general rules. The routine then runs with new inputs. It restores the learned policy, starts with fresh evidence, scores, uncertainty, and recommendations, and pauses at the learned human approval boundary before completion. The competition MVP uses deterministic Vendor Evaluation to demonstrate this interaction model. It does not claim arbitrary workflow learning or live vendor research. All four vendor dossiers contain fictional, first-party challenge fixtures. How it works Human UI actions and native WebMCP actions route through the same synchronous TypeScript semantic command bus. The bus validates each command, applies state changes, and records the actor, channel, phase, outcome, and a readable summary. A deterministic, domain-specific compiler turns candidate names and budget into variables, preserves criteria and approval policy, compiles observed procedures, and excludes literal evidence, scores, recommendation text, and one-off corrections from durable rules. The replay engine instantiates that routine with new inputs and fresh outputs. Only the human UI can Teach, start replay, approve, reject, or reset. Required criteria need a score of at least 3. An eligible recommendation before approval is rejected with APPROVAL_REQUIRED . How WebMCP is used ONCE uses native WebMCP directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) with no wrapper. Ten native WebMCP tools let an agent read and mutate the live application through named domain actions. Those handlers and the React human UI call the same semantic command bus, so agent and human work becomes one structured history. WebMCP gives the agent semantic application actions rather than click or DOM recordings. That shared semantic substrate is what makes the collaboration structured enough for ONCE to compile into a constrained routine. State, trace, the taught routine, and replay persist locally in the browser. ONCE has no login, database, backend service, embedded LLM, external research dependency, API keys, or paid service requirement. Challenges The hardest problem was deciding what ONCE should learn without overgeneralizing. Candidate names and budget are safe variables; criteria and approval are durable policy; evidence, scores, and recommendations are regenerated outputs; and a single human correction is recorded as Example only — not generalized . A second challenge was enforcing a genuine approval boundary while keeping the flow deterministic and easy to inspect. Bulk agent tools also had to stay atomic while retaining granular semantic events. Native WebMCP calls were verified against production in Codex's in-app browser. A separate ChatGPT Work invocation could not be independently verified because the client repeatedly blocked browser access with an admin-policy verification error. Accomplishments Completed the full Collaborate → Teach → Replay → Human approval → Complete loop. Registered ten native WebMCP tools and routed them through the same command system as the human UI. Verified native production calls, persistence, policy rejection codes, human approval and rejection, and two consecutive completion dry runs. Passed 215 deterministic tests across seven files, plus lint, type checking, and the production build. Shipped a publicly accessible HTTPS deployment with no login required and a public MIT-licensed repository with no required environment variables. What we learned Semantic domain actions are a stronger foundation for procedural memory than gesture recording. A credible learning system must show both what it retained and what it deliberately refused to generalize. Human approval is most meaningful when it is compiled as policy and enforced during replay, not added as a decorative confirmation at the end. What's next The next step is to explore other constrained domains where inputs, policies, generated outputs, and approval boundaries can be modeled explicitly. Future work could add human-reviewed routine editing and broader native-client verification while preserving the current claim boundary rather than pretending to infer arbitrary workflows. Testing instructions Open https://once-webmcp.vercel.app/ in a WebMCP-capable browser and select Reset demo . Ask the agent: “In ONCE, evaluate Aegis Cloud and BeaconStack for a $24,000 annual budget. Use Security, Integration, and Cost as criteria in that priority order. Read the ONCE vendor dossiers, attach evidence, and score each candidate for every criterion using 1=does not meet, 2=materially below, 3=meets, 4=strong, 5=excellent. Flag any meaningful uncertainty and set an initial recommendation.” Make Security Required , keep priority 1, enable Require human approval before final recommendation , and correct BeaconStack's security evidence to emphasize that SAML SSO requires the Enterprise add-on. Select Teach this routine and review the variables, fixed policies, repeated procedures, generated outputs, approval gate, and example-only corrections. Open Replay with new inputs with Northwind AI, Orchid Systems, and an $18,000 budget. Ask the agent: “Run the active ONCE routine with the new inputs. Use the replay plan and ONCE vendor dossiers. Complete the required evidence and scores, then follow the routine through its approval boundary.” Review the paused evaluation and select Approve . The agent can then set the final recommendation and complete the replay. Reject ends the run without a recommendation. The app should report Native WebMCP registered · 10 tools . Registration confirms browser capability; a successful tool call confirms agent invocation. For Chrome testing, use Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and restart the browser before opening ONCE. title: HumanKey
pitch: A WebMCP control plane where human approval dynamically unlocks consequential agent capabilities with verifiable evidence and receipts.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP control plane where human approval dynamically unlocks consequential agent capabilities with verifiable evidence and receipts. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents are powerful, but consequential workflows still force them to infer meaning from pixels, DOM labels, and prose. HumanKey explores a stronger model: the page itself declares exactly what an agent may do, and consequential authority appears only after a visible human decision. What it does HumanKey is a WebMCP control plane for proof-carrying delegation. A human defines a mission envelope with a goal, spending ceiling, required evidence, and an approval threshold. The agent can read the mission, inspect verified evidence, stage a reversible action, evaluate deterministic policy, request approval, verify a receipt, and export an audit bundle. The key interaction is dynamic capability exposure. The demo starts with seven discoverable WebMCP tools. A synthetic $1,840 supplier release passes evidence and policy checks but exceeds a $1,000 human-approval threshold, so the commit capability does not exist. When the human visibly clicks Approve, commit_approved_action is registered and Chrome discovers an eighth tool. After the agent commits the synthetic action, the capability unregisters itself and the surface returns to seven tools. The committed action emits a SHA-256 receipt over the canonical mission/action record. verify_action_receipt independently recomputes the hash and confirms the receipt. Every state transition is attributed to the human, the agent, or the deterministic policy engine. No real payment API is connected; all demo data is synthetic. How I built it HumanKey uses both declarative and imperative WebMCP. The reversible staging step is an annotated HTML form exposed as stage_release_action , while mission, evidence, policy, approval-request, receipt-verification, and audit-export operations are imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The approval-gated commit tool is registered only after human approval and removed using an AbortController after its in-flight execution resolves. The experience was validated against Chrome's native document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() APIs. Native QA produced the expected 7 -> 8 -> 7 lifecycle and an exact SHA-256 receipt verification result of valid: true . The app is a static HTTPS site hosted on GitHub Pages with a public MIT-licensed repository. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making authority a real browser capability boundary rather than a hidden boolean. The commit tool must not exist before approval, must become discoverable immediately after approval, and must unregister safely without cancelling its own in-flight execution. Native Chrome QA exposed that lifecycle edge case and the implementation was corrected accordingly. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The agent cannot self-approve because the consequential tool literally does not exist before the human decision. Human-visible UI and agent-visible capability state stay synchronized. The final synthetic action produces a verifiable SHA-256 receipt and an auditable provenance trail. The demo works against native Chrome WebMCP rather than only a mock implementation. What I learned WebMCP can do more than make forms easier for agents. It can make authorization itself part of the website's structured capability surface. That creates a reusable pattern for procurement, finance operations, deployment gates, compliance workflows, and any task where automation is valuable but final authority should remain human. What's next for HumanKey The next step is to generalize the mission/evidence/approval/receipt pattern into reusable components that sites can adopt for high-consequence agent workflows, with richer evidence adapters, signed receipts, and policy modules while preserving the same visible human checkpoint model. title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. video_transcript_excerpt: Photo editors expect you to know exactly what saturation, tint, and exposure curves mean. Most people do not. Estro completely changes this dynamic. It is a powerful photo editor that runs entirely in your browser and actually explains itself. You open a project and tell the agent exactly what you want to achieve. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. The agent immediately gets to work. It moves the sliders for you. Every single edit drops a visible card right on the screen. The card names the specific control, shows the exact numerical value, and explains what the term means in plain English. Here we ask the agent to simply point out the contrast slider without making any changes to the photo. The agent immediately highlights the exact slider in the right panel. You can also ask it to perform an audit of the image. We ask if any of our recent changes ruined the fine details in the photo. The agent reads the live histogram and tells you exactly what is happening with your pixels. You click the split view to see the final result in comparison. 56 tools, one unified command system, and zero servers. Everything happens locally on your machine. Your photos always stay yours.

title: Codex Ascend
pitch: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent.
about_excerpt: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent. Like Comment Story Updates Mission state becomes mountain geography: camps, routes, confidence, moving weather, and WebMCP activity share one living world. A real blocker fractures the route and changes the weather. Cosmetic progress stops until the obstacle is actually resolved. The agent asks; the human decides. Only the user can authorize repair or bypass at Camp III before the agent continues. Evidence before Summit. Completion activates only after every dependency, blocker, and success criterion passes deterministic verification. What Codex Ascend does Codex Ascend turns long-running agent work into a living mountain shared by a human and an AI agent. Camps are verified outcomes, fog is uncertainty, crevasses are blockers, route forks are consequential choices, and the Summit stays locked until every required proof passes deterministic verification. Codex Ascend is for developers and technical leads supervising long-running AI execution, where blockers, approvals, and proof should never disappear inside a chat log. Why WebMCP is essential Most agent interfaces split the model’s plan from the person’s understanding: the agent sees tool state while the human gets a chat log or decorative progress bar. Ascend gives both sides one execution model. The page registers 18 native WebMCP tools with closed JSON schemas and structured results. An agent can inspect mission state, discover topology, advance stages, report blockers, propose routes, request a human decision, attach evidence, verify completion, and finish the mission. These tools manipulate mission semantics—not pixels—and run through the same validated command engine as the human UI. The centerpiece is a genuinely bidirectional loop: The agent reports a persistence blocker and proposes repair or bypass routes. The mountain fractures at that exact geography and renders the choice. Only the human can authorize the consequential route inside the website. The agent reads the structured decision through WebMCP, resolves the blocker, and continues. New required work can reveal another ridge; evidence finally unlocks Verified Summit. There is intentionally no agent tool that can resolve the human decision. WebMCP makes collaboration safer and clearer because authority remains explicit while state stays machine-readable. How it works A neutral TypeScript Mission Engine validates commands and records a versioned event journal. React provides the accessible HUD and geography-bound scenario cards; PixiJS renders the living scene and elevation topology. An Ascend projection layer maps mission truth into camps, waypoints, weather, camera focus, narration, and generated imagery. A Cloudflare Worker uses Workflows and R2 for reviewed OpenAI GPT Image 2 generation. Provider credentials stay server-side, retries require explicit operator intent, and only accepted candidates enter the public world. Rendering can never mutate mission truth. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the website owns an action the agent should not silently take. Structured inspection matters, but the memorable moment is the round trip: the agent surfaces a real decision, the human answers it in context, and the agent continues from shared structured state. Built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React, Vite, PixiJS, Zod, OpenAI GPT Image 2, Cloudflare Workers, Workflows, R2, Vitest, and ESLint.
