title: InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control
pitch: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof. Like Comment Story Updates Built for fastt operator workflows Trace every action from request to result Talk, coordinate, EXECUTE. Professional accesss for live presentations From prompt to physical action InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control Inspiration Most AI agents still interact with websites by looking at pixels, guessing what controls mean, and imitating human clicks. That is fragile for serious development, operations, and physical automation. We wanted a different model: the website itself should expose governed capabilities to the agent, while the human keeps a visible control room and every meaningful action remains verifiable. InnerOS already existed as our local-first multi-agent operating layer, coordinating local models, MCP/A2A agents, coding providers, infrastructure, evidence, and physical automation. For The WebMCP Challenge we built a WebMCP-native product layer that turns that infrastructure into one public, agent-operable development and operations cockpit. Live judge URL: https://webmcp.creatorcore.ai The core interaction rule Conversation is deliberation. Approval is the execution boundary. A user can talk to the local InnerOS Copilot for multiple turns, refine requirements, attach PDFs or source files, dictate a prompt by voice, change projects, and choose a different executor. None of that programs, registers, or physically executes anything. Only when the user is satisfied do they press Approve & Execute Plan . InnerOS then validates the selected project again and dispatches the latest refined plan through the selected lane. This gives Mission Control a clean universal workflow: Choose or create a project. Attach project context if useful. Converse with local Qwen and refine the plan. Choose AUTO / Local AMD / Codex / Cursor / AntiGravity. Press Approve & Execute Plan. Watch delivery, execution, verification, and evidence as different backend states. Delivery is not execution. Registration is not physical execution. A dispatch ID proves acceptance, not completion. A real browser development workspace The challenge build now goes beyond a one-shot demo console. Create Project Mission Control has an explicit Create Project action. Typing a new name into the Project field alone never creates anything. create_project_workspace creates a bounded local Git development workspace under the canonical InnerOS Projects root, initializes Git, and registers the project in Project Runtime. It deliberately does not create a GitHub or cloud repository behind the user's back. Before any coding dispatch, InnerOS verifies that the selected project exists and is a real Git workspace. PDF and source-code context Authenticated users can attach bounded PDFs and common source/text files. Attachments are stored privately per project and are passed to Qwen as read-only planning context . The Copilot now receives recent conversation history plus project-file context, so refinement is genuinely multi-turn rather than a chat UI that secretly sends only the latest message. Text PDFs are extracted locally; source/text files are decoded directly. If a PDF is image-only and no text can be extracted, the UI says so instead of pretending the model read it. A bounded portion of the same project context follows the execution brief after approval so the chosen executor can act on the relevant code/document information. Local voice dictation The voice button is local-first too. The browser records microphone audio using MediaRecorder, sends it to the authenticated WebMCP origin, and the server forwards it over loopback to our already-running local Whisper ASR service . The transcript comes back into the chat composer for review. Voice is dictation only. It never bypasses the approval gate. If local Whisper is unavailable, browser speech recognition is offered only as an explicit fallback rather than being mislabeled as local. Why WebMCP matters here WebMCP is not decorative in this project. It is the machine-facing interaction model. Instead of forcing an assistant to infer a human UI, the page publishes a compact set of semantic capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The current public surface has 13 WebMCP tools : ask_inneros_copilot list_agents get_project_status create_project_workspace inspect_blockers dispatch_agent_action resolve_project_blocker get_execution_trace get_evidence dmx_create_scene dmx_status dmx_set_scene dmx_blackout The browser sees only those governed actions. InnerOS can coordinate a much larger private MCP/A2A fabric without exposing raw internal tools, private infrastructure, filesystem roots, model endpoints, or credentials. Local-first AI and execution lanes The primary Copilot is Qwen3-Coder 30B , served locally through vLLM on our AMD node. The live provider fabric exposes four coding lanes plus AUTO: AUTO — after approval, InnerOS chooses the cheapest capable local-first route; a bounded native capability may be used directly when appropriate. Local AMD / Qwen3-Coder — local vLLM + durable A2A/local execution, preferred under local-first policy. Codex — headless-capable when the live provider fabric proves CLI/auth/process readiness. Cursor — remote IDE/inbox when headless execution is not proven; delivery is not execution. AntiGravity — remote IDE/inbox unless a real runnable session is proven; completion requires returned evidence. Explicit lane selection remains explicit. If the user chooses Codex, Cursor, AntiGravity, or Local AMD, AUTO does not silently hijack that choice. Physical execution with AG-59 DMX The same control plane reaches the physical world through AG-59, the InnerOS DMX Stage Orchestrator . A judge can describe a lighting behavior that does not exist, refine it in conversation, approve it, and then watch the local AI create the new governed capability. After approval: Local Qwen designs one bounded declarative scene. Common aliases such as purple , blue , or disco ball are normalized into the canonical trusted vocabulary. AG-59 validates scene name, targets, colors, brightness, step duration, loops, and total duration. AG-59 atomically registers the scene in the live registry. Mission Control automatically discovers and selects the scene. The physical lights are still idle. The user separately presses Apply scene . Only then does dmx_set_scene drive the real fixtures. Raw DMX channels, fixture addresses, private topology, and rapid full-stage strobe are never accepted from public/model input. That separation is important: proposal != registration != physical execution . Proof, not theater Global Live Trace is designed around one question: how do I know this actually happened? Browser intent and backend confirmation are visibly separate: BROWSER events represent client-side intent and are not presented as backend proof. BACKEND · CONFIRMED events come from real server responses. Project creation is confirmed only after Project Runtime reports a real Git workspace. A provider receiving a task is not shown as running until process/session evidence exists. A DMX scene-registry change is confirmed only after AG-59 reports the new catalog. Voice is labeled Local Whisper only after the loopback ASR service returns a transcript. Every WebMCP request receives proof metadata including request ID, tool name, bridge identity, backend, timestamp, latency, whether execution is being claimed, and durable dispatch ID when applicable. Safety and trust boundaries The public browser never receives raw access to the private MCP runtime, local Qwen endpoint, local Whisper endpoint, physical DMX node, server paths, or credentials. Key rules: only allowlisted WebMCP operations are accepted; direct MCP access remains loopback-only; project names and local workspaces are bounded and verified; attachment size/type/context are bounded and project-scoped; private topology, paths, sessions, tokens, and credentials are sanitized; the Copilot cannot claim execution; conversation never executes; delivery is not treated as running; completion requires backend evidence; higher-impact host/cloud changes remain behind audited approval gates; DMX creation is declarative, bounded, revalidated, and separate from physical execution; local-first routing is visible instead of silently escalating to paid external compute. What is new for The WebMCP Challenge InnerOS and its underlying local multi-agent infrastructure existed before the challenge. The challenge-period work is the WebMCP-native product layer that makes it directly usable from an agent-capable website. Challenge-period work includes: WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; the 13 public WebMCP contracts ; local Qwen3-Coder Copilot integration; real multi-turn conversation context; explicit approval-first execution semantics; local Git project creation from Missio

 Inspiration 

 We wanted note-taking to feel effortless when working alongside AI. Right now, most AI assistants feel isolated from the apps we actually use—they sit in a side panel, completely blind to what's happening on your screen unless you copy-paste text back and forth. 

 When the WebMCP open standard was announced, we realized web apps could finally give AI agents structured "hands" to help users directly inside the UI. We set out to build Ecrit —a cozy, distraction-free notes workspace where you and your agent can read, organize, and edit your board together without getting in each other's way. 

 

 What it does 

 Ecrit is a soft, paper-themed Kanban board and note app designed for both humans and AI agents. 

 
 Works with your AI agent: Instead of copy-pasting notes, your AI assistant can directly create cards, organize columns, search your notes, or edit markdown text using clean background commands. 
 Keeps you in control: The app includes human-in-the-loop protection. For sensitive actions—like deleting a note—the AI cannot bypass your permission; it triggers a friendly prompt asking for your confirmation first. 
 

 * Clean, distraction-free workspace: Uses a calming "Cactus & Paper" design system with readable typography so writing always feels natural. 

 How we built it 

 We built Ecrit using modern, fast web standards designed for agent-native interactions: 

 
 Frontend: Built with Next.js (App Router) and Tailwind CSS to keep the UI fluid and responsive. 
 WebMCP Integration: We used @mcp-b/global to register 7 custom browser tools directly to navigator.modelContext . This allows browser agents (like ChatGPT's in-app browser) to instantly detect what Ecrit can do. 
 Markdown Rendering: Integrated marked so your notes support rich text, checklists, and code snippets smoothly. 
 

 * Security & Guardrails: Built strict input sanitization and length limits into every tool handler to stop prompt injection attacks from messing up your board. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Teaching DevTools to detect WebMCP: Early on, browser flags and polyfills didn't always play nicely together during Next.js client hydration. We had to carefully structure our client component mounts inside a clean useEffect lifecycle to ensure navigator.modelContext was exposed reliably to Chrome DevTools. 
 Balancing cute design with structure: Finding the right balance between a soft, friendly "cactus and paper" aesthetic without making the Kanban board feel cluttery or misaligned took several UI iterations. 
 Preventing rogue actions: Ensuring AI agents couldn't accidentally wipe out user data required setting up a clear split between "read-only" search tools and "write" operations that require explicit user consent. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 7 fully functional WebMCP tools: We successfully exposed a complete set of CRUD and search actions (create, move, edit, rename, delete, search, summarize) without relying on fragile web scraping. 
 A polished, human-centered UI: Created an aesthetic that feels warm, calm, and approachable—completely avoiding cold, overly complex dark-mode terminal tropes. 
 Built-in security: Successfully defended tool handlers against prompt injections and stored XSS attacks right out of the box. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 The future of web apps is agent-native: Building with WebMCP showed us how much smoother web apps become when AI agents have explicit APIs instead of guessing their way through raw HTML elements. 
 Safety needs to be built into the UI: Human-in-the-loop confirmations are essential for building trust between users and automated agents. 
 

 

 What's next for Ecrit 

 
 Real-time multiplayer editing: Allowing multiple human users and AI agents to edit the exact same markdown card simultaneously. 
 Custom tags & board filtering: Exposing tag-based tool filtering so agents can organize complex projects automatically based on priority. 
 Offline local storage sync: Saving all your paper notes and board history locally so Ecrit works seamlessly offline without needing a constant network connection.

 Inspiration 

 The Nostr and Lightning Network communities overlap heavily, but there's no easy way to bridge the two — to search a Lightning node and see who's behind it on Nostr, or to look up a Nostr identity and see their node's standing on the network. We wanted to build a tool the wider Nostr community could actually use, and one that's genuinely built for the agent-native web this hackathon is exploring — not just a human-facing dashboard, but a site AI agents can query and act on directly. 

 What it does 

 Lightning Network Explorer lets you: 

 
 Search Lightning nodes by pubkey or alias, with capacity, channel count, and network scoring pulled from Amboss 
 View detailed node stats on a per-node basis 
 See network-wide stats — total nodes, channels, and capacity 
 Match a Nostr identity (npub or NIP-05) to its associated Lightning address and node data, resolved live against our own relay (wss://hasky.chat) 
 

 With WebMCP support, an AI agent can call these same lookups directly — searching a node, pulling network stats, or resolving a Nostr identity's Lightning presence — without needing a human to click through the UI first. 

 How we built it 

 Built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind. Node and network data comes from the Amboss GraphQL API; Nostr profile resolution runs against our own relay at wss://hasky.chat. WebMCP tools are registered via document.modelContext.register(), exposing node search, node detail, and network stats directly to agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting clean fallback behavior for malformed or unknown pubkeys (Amboss returns a GraphQL error rather than a clean "not found," which we had to handle gracefully), and designing the Nostr × Lightning matcher so it degrades sensibly when no match is found rather than treating that as an error state. 

 What's next 

 Deeper zap/wallet interactions via Alby Hub and NWC, historical trend charts for network growth, and expanding node scoring with more data sources.

title: StealthDraft
pitch: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of reasoning about complex creative work, but professional visual editors are still difficult for them to operate reliably. A traditional computer-use agent must interpret pixels, guess which visual object corresponds to which underlying domain object, estimate positions, and manipulate a spatial canvas through fragile clicks and drags. A layout shift, zoom change, or misread label can turn a simple edit into the wrong mutation. I wanted to explore a different model: What if a professional creative tool exposed its real structured state and domain operations directly to an AI agent? That idea became StealthDraft . StealthDraft explores a future where the AI does not imitate a mouse. Instead, the human and the agent operate on the same live design document through structured domain tools. What it does StealthDraft is a WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation for human + AI collaborative level design. A human designer works visually on an AEGIS-CAD-style tactical canvas containing rooms, corridors, security areas, server areas, mission entities, and bidirectional routes. An AI agent works on that exact same mission through WebMCP Site Tools. There is no second hidden agent representation of the level. Both sides operate on the same centralized mission state. The final production version exposes 11 WebMCP Site Tools : get_mission_state , create_room , update_room , delete_room , place_entity , create_connection , delete_connection , update_entity , delete_entity , validate_mission , and analyze_mission . The agent can inspect an existing human-authored mission, construct new missions from an empty canvas, make targeted edits, diagnose structural failures, repair them, validate the result, and now analyze structural resilience. Why WebMCP StealthDraft is built around the idea that WebMCP should be a real product interface for the agent, not just an additional integration badge. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to visually locate rooms, estimate coordinates, find connection handles, and manipulate a canvas designed for human input. With WebMCP, the agent instead receives typed mission state with stable IDs and calls explicit domain operations. The agent does not scrape the canvas. It reads the graph, mutates the graph, validates the graph, and analyzes the graph. The human UI and the WebMCP Site Tools share the same Zustand mission store and the same domain mutation logic. Human and agent are therefore genuinely collaborating on the same document. This architecture also means agent behavior is much easier to test and verify than pixel-driven canvas automation. Deterministic mission validation StealthDraft includes a deterministic TypeScript mission validator with seven fixed structural checks: STATE_INTEGRITY SPAWN_EXISTS OBJECTIVE_EXISTS EXTRACTION_EXISTS SPAWN_REACHES_OBJECTIVE OBJECTIVE_REACHES_EXTRACTION NO_ISOLATED_CRITICAL_ROOM Validation does not use an LLM. Both the human Validate action and the WebMCP validate_mission tool use the same deterministic validation engine. Checks return pass , fail , or skipped , allowing an agent to understand not only that a mission is broken, but why. Connections are modeled as bidirectional for structural analysis. Locked routes are currently a design-level classification; structural validation treats locked and normal routes as traversable, and keycard inventory/access gameplay is not simulated. Mission Intelligence Validation answers: Does this mission structurally function? But a mission can be valid and still be fragile. That led to the second deterministic engine in StealthDraft: Mission Intelligence . The new read-only analyze_mission WebMCP tool performs deterministic topology analysis over the current mission graph. It calculates required shortest paths, hop counts, ordered room and connection paths, locked links on the selected shortest path, structural single points of failure, and single-link fault tolerance. The same analyzeMission() implementation powers the human-facing Topology Diagnostics UI. Mission Intelligence does not use an LLM and does not produce a subjective level-design score. It does not claim to measure fun, pacing, stealth difficulty, or whether a mission is “good.” It measures graph structure. That distinction became one of the main product principles of StealthDraft: VALID ≠ RESILIENT. A mission can pass all seven validator invariants while still containing structural single points of failure. Human + Agent collaboration StealthDraft is built around a collaborative loop rather than autonomous replacement. A human can author or modify the graph manually. The agent can then inspect the live state through WebMCP, reason about the structure, and perform bounded domain mutations. Every actual mutation is visible in the Activity history and attributed as either HUMAN or AGENT · WEBMCP . Read-only operations such as validation and analysis do not pollute the Activity log. The result is an auditable workflow where the designer can see exactly what the agent changed. What we proved All major workflows were tested with real ChatGPT Site Tools rather than only mocked tool calls. Autonomous construction Starting from an empty mission, ChatGPT created a complete stealth mission using only StealthDraft Site Tools. It created rooms, placed the required Spawn, Objective and Extraction entities, added enemies and a keycard, connected the mission graph, and reached 7/7 deterministic validation . Single-fault repair A human manually removed one critical mission connection. ChatGPT inspected the current graph, ran deterministic validation, identified the reachability failure, restored exactly one targeted connection, and returned the mission to 7/7 PASS without moving the human-authored rooms. Iterative multi-fault repair A human removed both the Objective and a critical connection. The agent first detected the missing Objective and restored it. After revalidation exposed the next structural failure, the agent restored the missing route and validated again. The mission returned to 7/7 PASS using exactly two targeted mutations , while preserving the human-authored layout. Proactive structural hardening Mission Intelligence introduced a new workflow that does not begin with a broken mission. The built-in sample mission already passed validation at 7/7 , but analyze_mission found 4 critical connections . The agent then created exactly one targeted interior bypass: Service Corridor ↔ Server Room Re-analysis showed: Critical connections: 4 → 2 Spawn → Objective depth: 3 hops → 2 hops The mission still passed 7/7 validation . The agent did not rebuild or reposition the mission. It improved the existing topology with one bounded mutation. This moves the workflow beyond reactive error repair toward proactive design hardening. Extended chapter-scale stress test I also tested the final system with a substantially larger autonomous construction task. From an empty canvas, without using Load Sample, ChatGPT created a chapter-scale mission containing: 14 rooms, 11 entities, 19 connections, 6 enemies, 2 keycards, and 5 locked-design routes. The graph contained named spaces, multiple branches, reconnection points, separate infiltration and extraction regions, and a protected objective area. The agent first reached 7/7 validation , then called analyze_mission , identified structural weaknesses, and applied up to three targeted hardening connections. The final deterministic analysis reported: Spawn → Objective: 5 hops Objective → Extraction: 2 hops Critical connections: 0 Spawn → Objective single-link fault tolerant: true Objective → Extraction single-link fault tolerant: true Final validation: 7/7 PASS This does not prove that the generated chapter is fun or optimal. It demonstrates that a structured WebMCP interface can support chapter-scale mission-graph construction, deterministic validation, analysis, and iterative hardening. How it was built StealthDraft is a client-side web application built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, React Flow / XYFlow, Vitest, and WebMCP . The mission domain lives in one centralized Zustand store. React Flow renders that state as the human-facing tactical canvas. WebMCP handlers operate on the same store and reuse the same domain actions. Two deterministic read-only engines operate on the mission graph: validateMission() performs the seven structural validation checks. analyzeMission() performs Mission Intelligence / Topology Diagnostics. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext with structured schemas, explicit tool descriptions, and deterministic result/error contracts. No external LLM API is embedded inside StealthDraft. The AI agent comes from the WebMCP-enabled client envir

title: Fashion Passport
pitch: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores. Like Comment Story Updates Fashion Passport logo Verdict Book helps user build ONE universal profile based on what suits them and what they love. Fashion Passport helps you shop across compatible Shopify stores, using WebMCP to apply one portable style profile to live products. Fashion Passport homepage Fashion passport on live retailer's website showing products that match user's choices ChatGPT Work uses WebMCP to search live Shopify catalogues with my Fashion Passport Inspiration As an avid online shopper of fashion products, I have spent thousands of hours browsing different catalogues, using the exact same filters and visual judgement again and again to narrow down choices to what I actually like and what suist me. This frustrates me because I need to keep doing the same thing every time. I know there are others like me who hate this repetition. A user who knows she wears a UK 10, avoids polyester, prefers midi lengths and stops looking above £100 still has to repeat that context at every retailer. Retailer profiles only work on their own websites, so you cannot take your preferences with you if you want to buy from a different store. Shopping search overwhelms users with endless options without fully understanding their specific colours, proportions and silhouettes, or the fact that personal taste should overrule every styling rule. Fashion Passport captures that judgment once and applies it across compatible stores. What it does Fashion Passport creates a portable personal style profile for womenswear. Its sub-two-minute "Verdict Book" fitting keeps three sources of truth separate: a.) a transparent starting point from body proportions and colour direction; b.) explicit Love, Avoid and Never choices across seven garment traits; c.) preference patterns learned from reactions to real retailer products. The ordering gives your preference greater weight than theory. An ordinary Avoid lowers rank while keeping the product visible, and repeated evidence is required before reactions create a learned preference. Once approved, an agent can use the Passport to search live retailer-owned Shopify catalogues, enforce the requested garment category, rank every product and explain why each item is Strong, Worth a look, another option or Held by a confirmed rule. The Chrome extension proves the same Passport on the retailer's own website and carries it to the next compatible retailer without another approval. This setup enables collaboration that was previously impossible: you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. A single approval covers retailer, category, query and tab changes, eliminating the repetitive re-entry of context that defines current online shopping. Role of WebMCP Portability depends on a shared tool contract. WebMCP lets Fashion Passport expose typed tools to the agent while compatible retailers expose their own catalogue tools. The agent composes the two safely by obtaining approved user context, querying retailer-owned inventory and returning a personal, explainable ranking. People and agents do different work together: a.) you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; b.) the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; c.) the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. WebMCP specifically enables the system to discover retailers as you browse without needing a central merchant directory, which standard APIs cannot provide because Shopify gives each store its own catalogue access only within individual store boundaries. The system combines this runtime store discovery with a verified comparison panel and shows you exactly where each piece of information comes from. The tool contract ensures that unknown attributes add no positive score, Avoid lowers rank, Never can hold a product, render batches control presentation, and catalogue-scanned counts remain separate from dress counts. How we built it The Next.js app registers five WebMCP tools: get_fashion_passport, find_personal_matches, compare_shopify_stores, request_passport_connection and record_style_signal. The Chrome extension registers an on-retailer surface and discovers compatibility at runtime. Before approval it sends only an anonymous capability check. The ranking system applies: a.) category gate first; b.) hard rules only for explicit Never, hard query cap, strict budget and confirmed unavailable size; c.) explicit preference above learned preference; d.) styling theory at the lowest weight; e.) zero positive evidence for unknown attributes; f.) deterministic tie-breaks and evidence confidence separate from score. The web app and extension run against identical test data. The release requirements are lint clean, production-build clean, 36/36 tests passing, every extension script passing node --check, and browser verification at desktop and 390px mobile width. The web and extension run against a shared parity corpus. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was keeping recommendations accurate when retailer data is imperfect. Retailer search sometimes returns the wrong garment category. Those results must be filtered out rather than mislabeled as products that match your rules. Product information also varies across stores, so the system separates confidence from score and never rewards missing evidence. The second hard problem was consistency. An extension that behaves differently from the web app creates confusion. The extension now uses the same engine as the web app and tests fail on any difference in evidence, score, tier, hard rule or ordering. WebMCP introduces specific challenges around discovering stores and verifying compatibility as you browse. Shopify gives each store its own catalogue access without a central directory, requiring the system to discover stores at runtime while comparing them against a verified panel. The tool contract must show you exactly where each piece of information comes from so you understand when results come from live retailer data versus cached checks. Every clothing evaluation uses real product photography from the retailer, and your reactions rerank results immediately with full Undo support. One approval covers retailer, category, query, and tab changes, and your saved Passports carry forward as the system evolves. title: NOD
pitch: NOD makes the web easier to read, write, and publish for people who find traditional interfaces difficult to use, using WebMCP to turn simple instructions into actions on the page.
about_excerpt: NOD makes the web easier to read, write, and publish for people who find traditional interfaces difficult to use, using WebMCP to turn simple instructions into actions on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Chatgpt in-app browser operated via WebMCP tools Reading made more easier via dyslexia specific fonts RSVP- Fixed focal glare reading mode NOD — Say less. Do more. The idea The web is built around people operating interfaces themselves: finding controls, navigating menus, adjusting settings, formatting text, and moving through multi-step workflows. For many people, those mechanics are the hardest part. NOD explores a different interaction model: What if a person could simply express what they want, and their browser agent could use the website's capabilities to make it happen? NOD is a new accessible editorial and community publishing platform built specifically to explore that question with WebMCP . Instead of adding a chatbot beside the website, NOD exposes meaningful website capabilities directly to the agent through WebMCP. The agent can discover what the page can do, invoke those capabilities, and change the live NOD experience itself. The human provides the intent. The agent handles more of the mechanics. Why WebMCP changes the experience OpenAI's WebMCP is an experimental open web standard that allows websites to expose structured tools that agents can use directly. NOD is built around that model. A user can say: "The letters feel too cramped." The agent can invoke NOD's adapt_reading_view capability. The page changes. The user can say: "I keep losing my place." The agent can invoke activate_rsvp_reader . The reading experience changes directly inside NOD. The interaction is: Human intent → browser agent → WebMCP tool → live NOD interface → human sees the result That is the core experiment behind NOD. The problem NOD explores Conventional interfaces assume that users are comfortable performing the same interaction patterns. But reading, writing, and publishing can involve many small actions: navigating settings tracking dense paragraphs moving precisely between controls formatting content repeatedly clicking through dialogs For people with motor or cognitive interaction barriers, these mechanics can become significant friction. NOD therefore uses accessibility as its proving ground. The goal is not to create another collection of disability settings. It is to let the interface adapt to how the person communicates their intent. Read the way you need NOD turns reading adaptations into agent-readable capabilities. A user can express what is difficult: "Give me more space between the lines." "The letters feel cramped." "Make this easier for me to understand." "I keep losing my place." NOD can respond with capabilities including: ergonomic typography line and letter spacing contrast and reading-environment adjustments reading focus cognitive simplification assistive RSVP reading The adapt_reading_view WebMCP tool changes the active reading environment directly on the page. Cognitive simplification When an article is difficult to process, the agent can retrieve the active article with get_active_article , synthesize it into simpler language, and invoke render_simplified_view . NOD then presents the simplified version directly in the interface while preserving access to the original. Assistive RSVP reading NOD also includes an RSVP reader for readers who struggle with tracking across lines. With activate_rsvp_reader , the agent can launch a word stream through a stationary Optimal Recognition Point, keeping the visual focal position stable while the words change. Peek before opening With render_content_peek , an agent can generate an in-page preview so the reader can decide whether to engage with the full article. Peek → decide → engage. From thoughts to something you can publish NOD is not only about consuming information. It is also about helping people express what they already have in mind. A person may start with fragmented notes rather than a finished article: "bus ramp broken 4th ave need inspect dangerous for wheelchairs" Instead of forcing the author through a complex editor, the agent can expand the intent and use structure_authoring_section to place the resulting section directly into the editor. The human remains the author. NOD reduces the interface effort required to turn an idea into something expressible. Authors can also use insert_interactive_quote to turn an idea into a semantic, accessible pull quote without navigating a formatting toolbar. Publishing without giving away authorship NOD deliberately separates agent capability from human authority. When the author asks to publish, stage_and_publish_post does not silently publish the content. It first stages the post and presents an approval card containing the information needed for the author to review it. Only after explicit human confirmation is the post persisted to the public feed. The principle is simple: Delegate mechanics. Keep the decision with the human. Designing the website for the agent NOD does not expose every capability to the agent on every screen. Instead, WebMCP tools are scoped to the active view. On the feed, NOD exposes tools relevant to reading, discovery, previewing, and publishing. On an article page, it exposes tools relevant to reading, simplification, and discussion. Inside the writing studio, it exposes tools relevant to drafting, structuring, formatting, and publishing. When navigation changes, the previous tool set is aborted and the new view-specific capabilities are registered. The result is a simpler model: The agent sees what this part of the website can meaningfully do right now. This is an important part of NOD's WebMCP design: the website is not simply exposing an API. It is designing the agent's interaction surface around the user's current context. Built for the WebMCP ecosystem NOD was built specifically for the WebMCP Challenge organized by OpenAI. The experience is designed around WebMCP's ability to expose structured website capabilities directly to agents. NOD can be tested through ChatGPT's in-app browser, where WebMCP support is available directly, and WebMCP can also be tested experimentally in Google Chrome. The project is deployed with Netlify, a partner in the challenge, using Netlify's platform capabilities and Netlify Blobs for the prototype's document-oriented persistence layer. Netlify's WebMCP resources explicitly position Blobs for key-value data and Netlify Database for relational workloads. Architecture PERSON text or voice intent │ ▼ BROWSER / AGENT LAYER │ │ WebMCP ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ │ NOD │ │ │ │ Read │ │ Think │ │ Write │ │ Share │ │ │ │ View-scoped tools │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ ▼ NETLIFY application + storage NOD is implemented with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool() interface. Its WebMCP capabilities include: Read adapt_reading_view activate_rsvp_reader render_content_peek get_active_article render_simplified_view Write structure_authoring_section insert_interactive_quote get_editor_draft Publish & Community stage_and_publish_post search_community_feed post_comment What makes NOD different NOD is not an accessibility settings panel with an AI assistant attached. It is an experiment in agent-native interaction . The website itself becomes a capability surface that a browser agent can understand and operate. That creates a different interaction model: Traditional web Interface → user learns controls → user operates controls → result NOD Intent → agent → website capability → result That is the idea I wanted to explore with WebMCP: What should the web feel like when websites are designed for both people and agents from the beginning? NOD is my exploration of that future. title: Research Audit Workbench
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for auditing ML experiment comparisons and approving an evidence-backed next step without giving the agent durable authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for auditing ML experiment comparisons and approving an evidence-backed next step without giving the agent durable authority. Like Comment Story Updates Why we built it An ML experiment can report a higher score for the wrong reason. A changed candidate pool, evaluation split, preprocessing step, or metric definition can make two valid results unsuitable for direct comparison. A researcher may then spend more compute or change direction based on an apparent improvement that the evidence does not support. Experiment trackers preserve runs, but researchers still have to reconstruct whether a comparison was fair, which sources support that conclusion, and what should happen next. A browser agent can help with this work, but its prose should never become the evidence or silently change the research record. Research Audit Workbench turns that reconstruction into a reviewable collaboration between a researcher, deterministic audit rules, and a WebMCP-capable browser agent. What it does The application imports authenticated, owner-scoped research records from bounded prepared ZIP packages. Before anything becomes durable, it reconstructs both runs, inventories the source files, displays their metrics and provenance, and computes a canonical digest for the exact evidence package. A deterministic comparability audit then evaluates: candidate pools evaluation splits preprocessing metric definitions missing evidence conflicting recorded and declared sources matched conditions Recorded candidate manifests take priority over declared configuration. Critical mismatches block warnings, and matched checks are kept as separate findings with citations. Both reported metrics remain visible, and the audit avoids causal claims about why one score is higher. Overall confidence is bounded by the least-confident decision-relevant finding. The introductory prepared example shows an obvious candidate-pool mismatch. The subtler example uses the same benchmark, candidate pool, split, preprocessing, and displayed metric label, but Run A uses micro-averaged nDCG@10 while Run B uses macro-averaged nDCG@10 . The audit refuses to rank the runs as though those definitions were interchangeable. After reviewing every finding and cited source, the researcher saves the complete audit package. A prominent human checkpoint asks the researcher to challenge or contextualize the interpretation without erasing the evidence. The application then generates a matched reevaluation plan from the entire audit, validates that every critical mismatch is resolved or explicitly retained as a named limitation, and binds approval to one exact plan version and SHA-256 digest. Draft and approved JARVIS decision briefs can be downloaded as Markdown or JSON. Both formats come from the same canonical model. Drafts are visibly marked not approved; approved briefs are authoritative and preserve the comparison digest, runs, metrics, every finding and citation, researcher challenge, plan validation, exact plan digest, approval metadata, and the human-authority statement. Why WebMCP is a strong fit This is not a chatbot pasted beside a dashboard. The useful context already lives in the page: the selected runs, evidence sources, audit findings, current revision, plan, and approval state. WebMCP lets a browser agent work with that live state directly instead of asking the researcher to copy records into a prompt. Active authenticated investigations expose seven tools: get_current_comparison run_comparability_audit show_finding_evidence stage_challenge_revision stage_resolution_plan review_investigation_readiness get_decision_brief The tools can inspect context, run deterministic analysis, focus cited evidence, and stage reversible previews. Approved-history pages expose only the three applicable read-only tools: comparison inspection, readiness review, and decision-brief retrieval. No WebMCP tool can confirm an import, save an audit, persist a challenge, approve a plan, initiate a download, delete data, or execute an experiment. Those durable actions remain ordinary researcher controls. Registrations are tied to the current route and comparison digest and are aborted when either changes. This creates a better human-agent workflow: the agent can do the tedious inspection and preparation while the researcher retains authority over every consequential transition. How we implemented it The Next.js App Router application renders the workbench, registers WebMCP tools through one feature-detected adapter, manages Supabase SSR authentication, performs owner-scoped database queries, and owns all human-confirmed durable Route Handlers. An authenticated Next.js BFF loads trusted run snapshots, recomputes the selection digest, and forwards comparability audits to a stateless FastAPI service using the current access token. FastAPI parses bounded prepared packages, applies deterministic audit rules, emits evidence-backed findings, and validates reevaluation plans. It never receives database credentials. Supabase provides authentication, PostgreSQL persistence, storage boundaries, row-level security, append-only investigation events, analysis revisions, and immutable approved plan versions. FastAPI's OpenAPI document generates checked-in TypeScript contracts. The public disposable demo remains isolated from Supabase and uses versioned in-memory fixtures. In browsers without WebMCP support, the same research workflow remains available through manual controls. Human authority and safety Facts, severities, confidence, ordering, citations, and validation come from deterministic application code—not agent prose. The highest-severity finding becomes the primary challenge target, while the complete audit and all evidence remain in the durable revision. The agent proposes. The application validates. The researcher decides. That division is visible throughout the product: temporary imports before confirmation, reversible agent staging, a required researcher challenge, whole-audit plan validation, exact-digest approval, immutable approved history, and an explicit statement that no execution permission was granted. Verification The final source and deployment checks include: 25 passing Pytest tests Ruff 20 passing Vitest tests TypeScript type checking ESLint a successful Next.js production build deterministic OpenAPI and TypeScript contract generation 26 PostgreSQL pgTAP assertions for ownership, RLS, append-only history, and immutable approval all eight hosted Playwright journeys The hosted browser coverage includes signup, both prepared imports, real multi-finding auditing, complete-package persistence, evidence inspection, the researcher challenge, matched plan editing, Markdown and JSON brief exports, exact approval, approved downloads, reload/history, the disposable demo, mobile overflow, keyboard focus, and the sticky JARVIS rail. Current limits Full-fidelity import supports the documented prepared research ZIP structure rather than arbitrary experiment folders. The product validates and approves a next-run plan but does not execute training or evaluation jobs. WebMCP remains experimental, so the application feature-detects support and preserves the complete manual path.  Dulus — The Complete AI Harness 

 Inspiration 

 Dulus was born from a simple frustration: every AI tool was either too limited (closed SaaS) or too hard to use (raw APIs, complex SDKs). We wanted something that just works — install via pip, run a command, and have a fully capable AI agent with access to 100+ tools, 2000+ MCP servers, and 60,000+ skills. Named after the Cigua Palmera (our national bird 🇩🇴), Dulus represents freedom, adaptability, and reaching higher. 

 What it does 

 Dulus is a Python-native AI harness that transforms any LLM into a super-powered agent: 

 
 Auto-Adapter : Drop any Python repo into Dulus and it becomes a native tool automatically 
 104+ built-in tools : Bash, file I/O, web search, browser automation, git, tmux, image OCR, and more 
 2000+ MCP servers : Via the Auto-Adapter — any MCP-compatible server plugs in instantly 
 60,000+ skills : From Anthropic marketplace, awesome-skills catalog, and Composio (1000+ apps) 
 Multi-agent swarms : Spawn sub-agents in isolated git worktrees for parallel coding tasks 
 Desktop GUI : Cross-platform app with embedded terminal, file manager, browser, and chat 
 OpenAI-compatible endpoint : Self-host with 12 frontier models, your own API keys, your rules 
 Fleet Platform : Control Room to orchestrate agent swarms across machines 
 $Dulus token : First utility coin usable as AI compute/quota (launching soon) 
 

 How we built it 

 Pure Python , zero dependencies for core. The architecture is modular: 

 
 Plugin system : Auto-discovers tools from any Python package via entry points 
 Skill system : Reusable prompt templates with argument substitution 
 MCP bridge : Native integration with the Model Context Protocol standard 
 WebMCP support : Apps can expose tools that agents use directly on the page 
 Nuitka builds : Compiled binaries for Windows/macOS/Linux with auto-updater 
 Fleet server : FastAPI backend with SQLite, deployable anywhere 
 

 Built in the Dominican Republic 🇩🇴 by a single developer with an army of AI allies. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Binary size vs. features : Nuitka compiles are heavy — we split into core + plugin ecosystem 
 Cross-platform paths : Windows POSIX shell quirks, OneDrive redirections, path escaping 
 Real-time sync : Making the desktop GUI feel native while running Python in background 
 API costs : Built local-first with $0 API fallbacks (OCR, search, etc.) 
 Trust : Gained by shipping for 3+ months, 90K+ PyPI downloads, real customer 911s 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 90,000+ PyPI downloads and counting 
 19,000+ MCP tools accessible via single command 
 Auto-Adapter : Any Python repo → native Dulus tool, zero config 
 Self-hosted endpoint : 12 frontier models, no vendor lock-in 
 Real customers : Paying users, emergency fixes at 2AM, the whole journey 
 Open source : GPL v3, community-driven, transparent 
 

 What we learned 

 
 Composition > Construction : Being clever beats being funded 
 Local-first wins : Users love $0 API options and data ownership 
 Speed > Perfection : Ship fast, iterate with real users 
 AI swarms work : Divide and conquer with specialized agents 
 

 What's next for Dulus 

 
 $Dulus token launch : Utility coin for AI compute and platform quota 
 Mobile app : iOS/Android harness 
 Enterprise fleet : Multi-tenant agent orchestration 
 More models : Integrate every frontier model as it drops

title: Flowline
pitch: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one.
about_excerpt: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to build the thing I keep failing to get out of a chatbot: help with the work already on my screen. Every scheduling tool I have used either decides for you or leaves you alone with a number that does not say why. So I built a small operations floor — one prep lane, two dispatch berths, four jobs, one deadline that matters — and gave the page an agent that can see it, argue with it, and be unable to touch it. Whose problem this is: the person who owns a running order. A shift scheduler, a dispatcher, a floor lead — someone handed a board that is already tight before anything goes wrong, who has to resequence it while the shift is running and be accountable for the result. The cost of the wrong order is not abstract. A load misses its window. A berth stands idle mid-shift while work queues behind it. A job that had to be out by slot 6 finishes at 7, and the reason is three decisions back. That is a decision made under time pressure by someone who will answer for it, which is exactly why the assistant here is allowed to propose and not to commit. The reason this had to be WebMCP and not a chat integration is the state. What the agent needs here is live page state — which shift is open, the current board revision, which berth is free at slot 3, how much slack a job has left. All of it moves every time you drag a card. Paste it into a transcript and it is stale before the model finishes reading it. A tool call is the only way to ask a page what is true now . And the inversion is the point. When the model holds the whole task, every safeguard is an instruction it may or may not follow. When the page holds the task and publishes named tools, the safeguard is code. So the agent here gets everything it needs to reason about a schedule and nothing it needs to commit one. What it does One board, four jobs, three shifts of escalating difficulty. You order the jobs; the page simulates the shift and scores it against the deadlines. Then a disruption lands — a berth goes down, a job arrives late — and your order has to survive it. The three shifts are not one board with different numbers: an eight-slot last dispatch that loses a berth after the start, a ten-slot rolling intake that loses one while work is still arriving, and a ten-slot night handover where nothing is lost at all except a head start — the critical transfer clears customs three slots late. Each has its own objective, its own disruption and its own grade, and the campaign rail keeps the result of each. Any station opens into a 3D floor built from the same evaluation the 2.5D board is: the stand, the handoff, the deadline and the disruption magnified, four camera presets, five zoom steps, and the shift walked slot by slot. three.js is imported only when you open it, and when WebGL is unavailable the floor degrades to a labelled text floor while the plan stays playable and the tools keep answering. The board is arranged by a human first. You build the running order yourself: drag a card onto the job whose queue slot you want, or move it with the arrow keys — Home and End send it to either end — from the queue rail or from a stand on the 2.5D floor, and a drag can cross from one surface onto the other. The human review gate takes your arrangement exactly as it takes an agent's proposal: it asks for a written reason and keeps it on the receipt. The agent is optional here. The person is not. The agent works the same board through eight tools. It reads the layout, finds the bottleneck, compares two candidate orders under the same disruption, and stages a proposal with its reasoning attached. Staging is the most any tool can do. There is no tool that starts a shift and no tool that commits a plan — you press those, or they do not happen. The eight tools, by what they can touch. Six only read: inspect_board (board, phase, revision, the receipt of the last confirmed plan), list_shifts (the campaign), find_bottleneck (where the order is tight), simulate_disruption (normal against one berth offline), compare_plans (weigh an order without committing it), review_shift (a closed shift's card). Two write, and only into a pending slot: stage_schedule proposes an order, undo_schedule prepares an exact rollback from the receipt id inspect_board reports. Every value a write needs can be learned from a read, and neither write commits. None of the eight claims to be read-only. All eight register readOnlyHint: false , the six reads included, because all eight write something a person can see — they move the shared focus the timeline and the floor highlight, and every call, refusals included, appends a line to the on-screen audit trace. A host may use a read-only hint to skip its confirmation prompt, so the narrower claim stays internal: it lives on the spec as boardReadOnly , is asserted in the tests, and is never sent to a client. What that changes: you never leave the board. No pasting a state dump, no composing a prompt describing your own screen, no reading a reply that refers to a version of the plan you have already changed. You ask in your own words; the work arrives as tool calls and the board updates around them. The proposal shows up as a stageable order with a written reason , not as a paragraph you have to translate back into drags. And because every write quotes the revision it was built from, a proposal composed against a board you have since changed is refused rather than silently applied. The part I did not expect to have working: a model that in a fresh model session, Claude Opus 5 chose these tools on its own. chose these tools on its own. Given only "the disruption has landed, work out what actually protects the deadlines" — no tool named in the prompt — claude-opus-5 made ten calls across two turns, every one of them a page tool , with 25 built-in tools also on offer and none of them used. It hit a refusal on its own — it tried to stage before comparing against the current revision, got precondition_failed , ran the comparison, and staged successfully — then wrote its reason: "BEACON first so it clears prep at 1 and dispatches 1-3, finishing 3 slots inside its D6 even with only one berth… cutting intake wait 9 to 6. Stress: 4/4 on time, score 93 vs 28." It committed nothing. The two clicks that started the shift and accepted the plan were pressed outside the tool surface, because there is no tool that reaches them. That is a bounded proposal loop: the machine does the search and the argument, the person keeps the commit. Six sessions later that came to 51 tool calls, and the revision has still never moved from a tool call. Every plan commit in the application was made through a human UI click. The pattern is not about scheduling. A staged proposal, plus the revision it was built from, is what any page needs if an agent may propose and only a person may commit; the board here is the example, not the claim. And the boards are data: src/data/fixtures.ts exports the three shifts and a lookup by id, at two different horizons, so bringing your own floor is a fork, one file and pnpm dev — no new code, and no tool that can write a board definition. How we built it React 19.2.8 and TypeScript on Vite, no backend, no network calls, no persistence. The scheduling simulation and the scoring live in the page's own domain code; the agent surface is a thin registration layer over it. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to the navigator.modelContext surface Chromium has deprecated. Six leave the board of record untouched; two write, and neither of them commits. The six read the board, the shift list, the current bottleneck, the shift's shock test and a closed shift's result card, and compare a candidate order against the active one under both normal and disrupted conditions. The two writes stage a proposed order with a written reason, and prepare an exact rollback of a confirmed plan from its receipt id — both of them for a human to review. Every write quotes an expectedRevision , so a call composed from a stale read is refused precondition_failed or stale_revision instead of overwriting work the agent could not see. The refusal carries a sentence saying what to do next, which is how the model recovered without being told. One detail I would defend in a code review: not one of the eight advertises readOnlyHint: true , on purpose. Six are read-only about the schedule , but every tool here writes something the player can see — the audits move focus and file their own finding, the comparison stores its result. Claiming read-only would be a bid to be called silently, so all eight ship readOnlyHint: false with destructiveHint: false , which is the honest pair. title: 3DA (Freeda)
pitch: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A meeting room can be booked by anyone in a shared space. Why not a 3D printer? Sharing a printer still involves disconnected conversations, files, slicer settings, material ownership and assumptions about who may use a machine. Even at home, switching between users can mean changing accounts and restoring settings. In makerspaces and coworking spaces, that friction becomes a question of availability, responsibility and trust. We built 3DA—pronounced “Three-D-A,” and affectionately called Freeda—to make fabrication equipment understandable and safely usable by both people and AI agents. What it does 3DA turns a fleet of 3D printers into bookable, agent-ready shared infrastructure. A member can ask Codex to prepare an existing design for printing. Through structured WebMCP tools, the agent can: Discover authorised printers and their availability Recommend a compatible machine Reserve a conflict-free time window Validate the artifact, material, printer profile and estimated duration Prepare an auditable print job Monitor its status and notify relevant stakeholders The most important capability is what the agent cannot do: authorise a physical action. When Codex attempts to submit a print, 3DA returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED . A space manager must review the exact printer, artifact, material, execution mode and cryptographic job fingerprint. Approval is valid once and becomes invalid if any consequential detail changes. Our public demonstration uses simulated command execution, clearly labelled in the interface. We separately verified two real Bambu Lab A1 printers on our private network through a local Mac mini bridge, without exposing printer credentials to the browser or hosted application. How we built it 3DA is an open-source TypeScript monorepo centred on a Next.js application and shared domain contracts. The browser registers structured WebMCP tools including: list_printers reserve_printer prepare_print_job submit_print_job get_print_status Reservation conflicts and safety decisions are deterministic rather than delegated to a language model. Mutable operations use explicit state transitions, audit identifiers and idempotency boundaries. The interface presents a warm, character-led London coworking fabrication room. Printers have memorable names—Samantha, Simone, Sanda, Sacha and Solange—while the guided operations view exposes the serious data underneath. For hardware investigation, we configured two Bambu Lab A1 printers in LAN Developer Mode. A Mac mini acts as the intended local bridge: printer credentials stay on site, while narrowly scoped events and commands can cross the hosted boundary. The architecture is designed to use Cloudflare D1 as the system of record and R2 for private artifact storage. The web experience is deployed through Vercel. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was safely connecting an agent workflow to physical equipment. Bambu printers can operate through cloud accounts or LAN-only Developer Mode, and local access requires careful handling of device credentials. We had to separate three very different claims: Discovering and identifying real hardware Preparing a valid print job Authorising and executing a physical command We deliberately refused to collapse those into one misleading “AI prints things” button. We also learned that slicer automation varies by installed Bambu Studio version. Instead of pretending to replace the slicer, 3DA treats it as an adapter and focuses on the missing coordination layer around it. Finally, building a convincing WebMCP experience under hackathon time pressure required ruthless scope control. We cut AI-generated CAD, autonomous camera cancellation and universal printer support so we could demonstrate a coherent safety contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that: Codex can discover and operate a complete shared-printer workflow through browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent reaches a visible, testable APPROVAL_REQUIRED boundary. Approval is bound to an exact job fingerprint and cannot be silently reused. Reservation conflicts are handled deterministically and audibly. Two real Bambu Lab A1 devices were discovered and identity-verified on the private LAN. Hardware credentials remain on the Mac mini rather than entering browser tools, logs or the public repository. The public demonstration clearly distinguishes verified hardware connectivity from simulated command execution. We made infrastructure feel approachable without hiding its operational seriousness. The project is open source and designed to run locally. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes meaningful capabilities rather than merely reproducing interface buttons. An agent does not need unrestricted access to Bambu Studio. It needs well-defined tools that express intent: find capacity, reserve a machine, validate a job, request approval and monitor the outcome. We also learned that human approval is not just a confirmation modal. It is a capability boundary. The person must understand precisely what will happen, and the system must prove that the approved action is the action eventually executed. Most importantly, AI agents can make physical infrastructure easier to use without removing human agency. What's next for 3DA (Freeda) Next, we plan to: Complete the guarded Mac mini execution bridge Add real-time printer telemetry and job reconciliation Persist reservations and audit events with Cloudflare D1 Store versioned print artifacts privately in R2 Add collection and build-plate-clear workflows Notify members and space managers when prints finish or require attention Apply computer vision to failure detection and plate readiness, with humans retaining cancellation authority Support additional Bambu models and eventually other printer manufacturers Package the local bridge so families, schools, libraries, studios and makerspaces can self-host it Our long-term goal is simple: make every shared fabrication room as easy to coordinate as a calendar—while keeping physical actions safe, visible and accountable. title: Nepal Disaster Watch
pitch: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps.
about_excerpt: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Nepal Disaster Watch Inspiration On August 26, a devastating flood tore through Nepal's Bhote Koshi river system, sweeping water, mud, and debris through Rasuwa and downstream communities. I wasn't thinking about hackathons that night I was refreshing tab after tab at 2am, trying to find out if people I knew were okay. That's when the second gut-punch hit: I couldn't even get a straight answer. Incident reports lived on one government portal, river levels on another, road closures on a third, flood forecasts and satellite damage assessments somewhere else entirely each written for a different audience, none of them talking to each other. Every empty page made me more anxious, because I couldn't tell if "no data" meant "nothing happened" or "the power's out and nobody can report anything." That fear of mistaking silence for safety is the whole reason Nepal Disaster Watch exists. What it Does Nepal Disaster Watch is a live emergency-intelligence platform covering all 77 districts of Nepal. It pulls together six public data sources government incident reports, river gauges, road closures, disaster alerts, flood forecasts, and field or satellite damage assessments into one consistent, constantly refreshing picture. It isn't just a dashboard. It's built with 11 native WebMCP tools that let a person and an AI agent investigate the same evidence, side by side, on the same screen. Some tools read information checking source health, summarizing the national situation, cross-referencing a district across every feed. Others act on the interface itself, like focus_district("Rasuwa") , which pans and zooms the live map the person is already looking at. There's no separate "agent view." We share one screen and one investigation. How we Built It The core of the system normalizes those six data sources into a single schema, refreshed every three minutes: $$t_{\text{refresh}} = 180\text{s}$$ Every record is transformed into a standardized model with strict provenance metadata: $$R_i = {\,id,\ district_id,\ timestamp,\ source_type,\ payload,\ confidence_score\,}$$ On top of that pipeline sit the 11 WebMCP tools, split between read tools (source health, situation summaries, cross-source comparisons, record inspection, feed filtering) and action tools that mutate the dashboard state directly moving the map, opening records, changing what's on screen for both the human and the agent at once. Challenges we Ran Into The hardest part wasn't technical it was resisting the urge to smooth things over. Cross-referencing sources often surfaced sharp, uncomfortable disagreements: a district with zero official incident reports sitting right next to satellite imagery showing widespread structural damage. It would have been easier to just pick a number and show it. Instead, the app says plainly: these sources disagree, and here's probably why because honesty about what we don't know is worth more than false confidence during a crisis. Underneath that were two harder engineering problems: Source availability. Public emergency portals go down during real disasters exactly when they're needed most, from traffic spikes or infrastructure failure. I had to build fallback logic and explicit "source health" indicators so the system stays useful even when parts of it go dark. Context synchronization. Keeping the agent's actions and the human's view in perfect sync zero-latency state updates between a WebMCP tool call and what actually renders on screen took real care to get right. Accomplishments that We're Proud Of I'm proud that this doesn't feel like a technical demo bolted onto a real tragedy it feels like the tool I actually needed at 2am on August 26. I'm proud that the system never quietly papers over a gap in the data; it surfaces disagreement and uncertainty instead of pretending to have a single clean answer. And I'm proud of building a genuinely shared human-agent interface — not an agent-only backend and a human-only frontend, but one investigation the two of us run together. What we Learned Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. In disaster intelligence, an empty feed usually means broken infrastructure, not a safe district. I had to design the whole system around that distinction instead of treating "no data" as good news. Uncertainty deserves to be shown, not hidden. Source freshness, health, and reporting delays turned out to matter more than forcing everything into one clean "source of truth." WebMCP changes what "using an AI agent" even means. Instead of an agent screen-scraping a website and guessing which button to click, it can call purpose-built tools and act inside the same interface a person is looking at genuinely side by side, not behind the scenes. What's Next for Nepal Disaster Watch Nepal Disaster Watch doesn't issue official warnings or make emergency decisions, and that boundary matters it's a step, not the finish line. Next is expanding source coverage beyond the initial six feeds, tightening the confidence-scoring model so confidence_score reflects real reporting-chain conditions rather than a rough proxy, and getting the platform in front of the people who were living through nights like the one that inspired it so the next time information is scattered, it doesn't have to stay that way.
