title: xAgent.ID
pitch: A website and an AI agent onboard that site together: the agent assembles a verified install plan, the owner approves it in the page, and the commands never leave the owner's hands.
about_excerpt: A website and an AI agent onboard that site together: the agent assembles a verified install plan, the owner approves it in the page, and the commands never leave the owner's hands. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Live xagent.id. Every card on screen is the deployed page: real companies, real public evidence, nothing claimed on their behalf. The target published no public proof, so it stays pending. Missing evidence is never converted into a pass. After the click: four commands, bound to a digest of the exact plan on screen, handed to the owner. The page executes none. Machine speed, human authority. Live at xagent.id/agent, with a command and an expected result for every claim in VERIFY.md. One task, three conditions. Without WebMCP: 134,552 bytes over 9 requests. With it: 6,460 over 2. Wall clock: inconclusive. Asked for the install bundle before approval, the page refuses: human_approval_required. The bundle does not exist yet. Chrome's own WebMCP panel, in DevTools, listing this page's eight tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool. Approval is a real browser-trusted click on a visible control. No tool parameter and no page script can assert it instead. Inspiration Onboarding a website to an identity service is a negotiation, not a page of text. It needs the current release, the exact target host, the modules the site is granting, the files that will be written, a rollback path, and a human decision in the middle. We watched both halves of that fail. An agent reading our rendered HTML could only guess at the contract, so it stalled or invented commands. A human owner opened the docs, copied four commands into a terminal, and hoped the version, the host and the grants lined up. Neither party had what it needed, and the one step that genuinely required a person, deciding, was the step that copy-paste quietly skipped. WebMCP suggested the fix. Not "let the agent click the buttons", but: let the page state its contract as tools, and keep the human decision a decision. What it does xagent.id registers eight top-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, so a WebMCP-capable agent can onboard a website together with its owner. inspect_onboarding reports the tool surface, the authority limits and the current step. Read-only. preview_agent_id previews the public Agent ID card for a target website. get_install_plan loads the target-bound install manifest, without commands. choose_verification_method selects public-file domain proof. request_owner_approval asks the human for a visible decision, and waits. prepare_install_bundle returns the approved commands for the human to run. verify_installation reads independent public evidence for the target. get_onboarding_status reports the current onboarding state. Read-only. Only those two carry readOnlyHint, because only those two change nothing. The shape of the journey is the point. The agent does the assembly: release identity, module grants, declared write paths, and a digest of the exact plan. The page shows the owner which files will change and which permissions are being granted. The owner approves on a visible control. Only then does prepare_install_bundle return commands, and it returns them to the owner. The page executes none of them. The agent executes none of them. Ask for the bundle before approval and you get human_approval_required. Not a warning. A refusal. Why WebMCP is the right fit here: the trust boundary already exists, and this keeps it intact. The tools live in the page the owner already trusts, so there is no connector to install, no API key to paste, and no third party standing between an owner and their own website. The agent gets the real contract, bound to one canonical HTTPS origin, instead of its own reading of the rendered page. What people and agents can now do together that neither could do alone: the agent assembles a plan a human would find tedious and error-prone, the exact release, the exact host, the module grants, the files that will be written, and a digest binding all of it. The owner supplies the one thing an agent must never supply, which is the decision. Before this, the owner did the assembly by hand and the decision collapsed into copy-paste. An agent alone still cannot finish, and that is the design, not a limitation. How we built it The tools are one vanilla JavaScript module shipped by the page itself, at /assets/webmcp-onboarding.js. No build step, no framework, and nothing for the owner to install. Approval is the part we spent the most care on. It requires a browser-generated trusted activation on the enabled, visible wizard control, and completion of the permissions-to-install transition on screen. There is no public approval mutator and no writable exported state, so no tool parameter and no page script can assert approval on the owner's behalf. Editing the target, changing the manifest, or a failed refresh all revoke it. For evidence we built two harnesses. The first walks the same task three ways, human, agent without WebMCP, and agent with WebMCP, and aborts the entire run if any request returns anything other than 200. The second drives a real Chrome over the DevTools Protocol with the WebMCP testing flag enabled, discovering tools through document.modelContext.getTools and giving approval with real mouse events at the control's own coordinates. The submission video is that second harness running on a clean cloud VM against the deployed site, with Chrome's own WebMCP panel open in DevTools counting the calls as they happen. Every frame is a recording, and the uncut source recordings are published alongside the film. Challenges we ran into A microtask that arrived too early. Approval worked in our tests and never worked in Chrome. The browser runs a microtask checkpoint between event listeners, so our approval landed while the page was still mid-transition and was discarded. The fix revalidates every precondition on a real timer instead of trusting a single moment. Our tests had passed because they dispatched listeners in an order no browser actually uses; the regression test now reproduces the real ordering. Feature detection that lied. executeTool kept failing with "Failed to parse input arguments" until we found that arguments must be passed as a JSON string rather than an object. A release pipeline that had never once succeeded. Deploying the fix meant first repairing six separate faults in it, ending with a skaffold key that is spelled cloudrun and not cloudRun. Until that was done the correct code existed only on our own machines, which is not the same thing as shipped. Measuring honestly when the numbers did not cooperate. Our wall-clock ranges overlapped between conditions, so we could not claim a speed win. Saying so turned out to be harder than not measuring at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of The refusal works, in a real browser, on the live site. Eight tools discovered, prepare_install_bundle refused with human_approval_required before approval, four commands returned after a real click, and none of them executed by the page. That run is recorded and published. The measured result is specific. To reach the same target-bound install plan, an agent following our own documented public trail takes in 134,552 bytes over 9 requests. Through WebMCP it is 6,460 bytes over 2. That is 20.83 times less material and 4.5 times fewer round trips, and both figures came out identical on every run. What we did not measure is stated as plainly as what we did. Wall clock is reported as inconclusive, because the ranges overlap. Human duration is reported as not measured, because no participant was timed. A test in the repository fails if either one is ever quietly converted into a number. Every claim in our public README has a command and an expected result in VERIFY.md. A reviewer never has to take our word for anything. What we learned The interesting question is not what an agent can do. It is what it must not do. The value of this integration is concentrated almost entirely in the one call that refuses. Everything else is convenience; that one is the product. Works in tests and works in a browser are different claims, and the gap between them was a single microtask. We now treat any test that models browser event ordering as suspect until it has been reproduced against a real browser. Honest measurement is a design constraint, not a reporting step. Once we decided that nothing unmeasured could appear as a number, we had to build the harness so that not measured was a value it could carry all the way to the screen. That changed how we built, not just how we wrote it up. A page can hand an agent a contract instead of prose, and it costs one module. The hard part was never the tool surface. What's next for xAgent.ID — WebMCP onboarding Measure the human path properly. Our comparison paths are scripted, not observed users. title: Packedup
pitch: Plan together, travel better. \nDrop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
about_excerpt:
Plan together, travel better. 
Drop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every time I travel with friends, the same thing happens: someone drops
five hotel options and a dozen restaurant links into WhatsApp, everyone
votes with thumbs-up reactions scattered across different messages, and a
day later nobody can remember what actually won. The votes get buried
under new messages, there's no single place to look back at what was
decided, and by the time we land, half the group doesn't even have a
day-by-day plan — just a chat log full of half-finished decisions. 

 I wanted a place built specifically for that moment: drop in the options,
let everyone vote, lock in a winner, and have it turn into an itinerary
automatically — instead of relying on a chat app never designed for
decision-making in the first place 

 What it does 

 PackedUp is group trip planning built around three boards — Stay, Eat, and Visit. Anyone with a 7-character invite code joins as a guest and drops in a suggestion — a hotel, a restaurant, a hike — for the group to vote on, up or down, in real time. The trip's creator finalizes a winner on each board, and those winners flow straight into a day-by-day itinerary — no re-typing, no digging through chat history to remember what won. 

 No sign-up is required to participate. A guest is identified by a session token stored locally, so joining a trip takes a name and a code, not a password — the whole reason WhatsApp felt easier than "download an app" in the first place, minus the part where votes get lost. 

 The newest layer is agent support: PackedUp exposes create_trip, get_trip_board_info, and add_recommended_suggestion as WebMCP tools — an emerging browser standard (document.modelContext) that lets an AI agent fill in the trip form or drop a recommended restaurant onto a board on a user's behalf, the same way a person would from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js 14 (App Router) for both the UI and the API — Route Handlers sit between the client and Supabase. 

 
 Supabase (Postgres) for data, with row-level security enabled on every table. Guest writes go through a service-role client scoped strictly to server-side route handlers, since a guest has no auth.uid() for RLS to key off of. 
 Zustand, persisted to localStorage, holds the guest session (member_id, trip_id, session_token) across visits. 
 TanStack Query manages server state — trip details, suggestions, members — with short polling intervals standing in for full realtime where it wasn't worth the complexity yet. 
 Framer Motion for the transitions between states (voting, finalizing, empty boards). 
 WebMCP, via the use-webmcp-tool React hook, registers tools directly on the page components where the corresponding UI action lives — create_trip on the landing and create pages, the suggestion tools on the board page — so a tool only exists while its page is actually mounted. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting from "WhatsApp thread full of forgotten votes" to an actual finalized itinerary in three clicks — join with a code, vote, finalize — without ever asking a single friend to make an account. Getting real-time-feeling voting working with plain polling instead of reaching for a heavier realtime setup before it was needed. And shipping WebMCP support early enough to be one of the first trip-planning tools an AI agent can actually operate, not just read. 

 What we learned 

 That an emerging standard is still an emerging standard — WebMCP is real, shipping behind flags and origin trials, but building against it means designing for graceful absence: useWebMCP reports supported: false in any browser without the API, and the app has to be just as usable without an agent in the loop as with one. We also learned, the hard way, that the fastest debugging step for a "healthy app, broken deploy" is checking whether the database itself is still awake. 

 What's next for Packedup 

 Real Supabase Realtime subscriptions in place of polling, an actual MCP server (not just WebMCP) so agents like Codex or Claude Desktop can drive trip creation without a browser tab open, and per-day budget estimates rolled into the itinerary so the group knows the damage before they land.

title: Fix This
pitch: Repairs without the runaround.
about_excerpt: Repairs without the runaround. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rental repairs turn into a runaround: the tenant repeats the problem, the property manager chases safety and access details, and contractor prices, availability, approvals, and confirmation live in separate conversations. Tenants should not need another portal just to get a leak fixed, and an agent should not be allowed to approve its own consequential work. What it does Fix This keeps the tenant in SMS and gives the property manager one shared repair case. A repair agent gathers safety and access facts, follows the building's stored contractor agreements in order, and prepares the next action through typed WebMCP tools. The property manager sees the evidence and explicitly approves one contractor call bound to the contractor, agreed price, and permitted time windows. In the recorded controlled-live run, one allowlisted tenant MMS woke the background agent. The agent triaged the repair and replied in the same thread. WebMCP prepared the stored-agreement path for the manager. After one explicit approval, the contractor heard a fixed AI disclosure and pressed 1 before any audio reached OpenAI. The contractor confirmed a time inside both authorized windows, Fix This booked the visit, and the tenant received the confirmation text. The public judge URL is a separate, resettable synthetic Pennsylvania build. It exposes the same shared-case and WebMCP boundaries without sending a real message or placing a real call. Why WebMCP The public build exposes twelve typed tools over the same workflow API and repair record used by the dashboard. The tools cover case discovery, triage, tenant messaging, preferred-contractor ordering, access evidence, contractor confirmation, and booking. The agent acts on structured state instead of guessing through DOM clicks. The most important tool is the one that does not exist: manager approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP surface. The server rejects booking until the current proposal has matching manager approval, tenant access authorization, and contractor confirmation. What people and agents do together The tenant reports the repair in a channel they already use. The agent handles repeatable fact gathering and prepares the approved-contractor path. The property manager makes the consequential cost and contact decision. The contractor gives affirmative consent before the AI call and confirms the visit. Fix This then records the booking and notifies the tenant in the original thread. That replaces fragmented coordination with one causally ordered, auditable workflow without handing approval to the agent. How it was built Fix This uses React, Vite, TypeScript, Express, Node.js, an atomically written JSON store, Twilio, OpenAI Responses and Realtime APIs, Vitest, and Render. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers thin browser adapters over the same HTTP operations used by the dashboard. The controlled-live route validates provider signatures and exact allowlists, deduplicates wake events, serializes work per repair case, journals outbound effects for retry safety, and keeps the fixed disclosure plus keypad-consent gate outside the model. No raw call audio is retained. How Codex helped OpenAI Codex helped turn the product idea into decision tickets, challenge unsafe or vague assumptions, implement the shared workflow and controlled-live seams, write and run the tests, diagnose provider failures offline, review the deployment boundary, and assemble privacy-safe evidence. The final controlled-live commit passed 119 tests, the production build, and a production dependency audit with zero reported vulnerabilities. Jacob retained the product decisions and every consequential approval, provider mutation, live message, and call authorization. Evidence and source Public synthetic demo: https://fix-this-demo.onrender.com Public repository: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp Controlled-live source: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp/tree/codex/controlled-live-deploy Sanitized end-to-end proof: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp/issues/19#issuecomment-5517032165 Current limitations The public judge build is synthetic and cannot contact real people. The recorded real-provider journey was one bounded, allowlisted controlled-live proof—not a pilot, production launch, or reliability claim. The controlled-live deployment is protected and single-operator; judges should use the public synthetic URL. WebMCP browser support is experimental. The public Render service may cold-start after idle. No measured savings, legal certification, general availability, or autonomous approval claim is made. title: Actuo Expense Manager
pitch: Turns out AI agents can act like human can, just had to teach two apps that don't know each other to actually talk.
about_excerpt: Turns out AI agents can act like human can, just had to teach two apps that don't know each other to actually talk. Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Expense List Add Expense Page Settings page list all function calls history and settings for custom agent settings (Model selection and BYOK Config) Agent Page listing all available tools and a custom chatbot agent that calls 3rd party app tools embedded with <iframe allow="tools">. Dashboard page with a 3rd Party Utility with WebMCP enabled embedded with <iframe allow="tools"> for converting currencies Inspiration I deliver a lot of talks around new and upcoming features of web, across the Indian Developer Community, which involves me spending a great deal of time investigating new features of web platforms so that I can pass them on to our community. Recently I came across WebMCP, and a very simple concept drew my interest. An AI agent shouldn't have to work out what a button does by randomly clicking around a page; instead it should be able to carry out the same actions as a human user, using an actual contract and the same authentication and rules. It seemed like a good idea to base a proper project on it rather than just go through the documentation. My aim was not to launch a well-polished startup; I only wanted to use the standard from beginning to end, discover its shortcomings on my own, and create something tangible to contribute back to the community. That exploration eventually became Actuo. What it does Actuo is a multi-tenant expense management application which includes features such as organizations, roles, budgets, approval workflows, and support for multiple currencies. I designed it in such a way that each significant action taken by a user through the user interface also corresponds to a real WebMCP tool that is registered directly via document.modelContext . Read-only tools: For example, there's search_expenses , get_budget_status , get_spend_summary , and fetch_categories . I've also included a generate_report tool which can be cancelled during the process by means of an AbortSignal , the result being that the server actually gives up on the task rather than the browser simply ignoring the result. Mutating tools: The submit_expense tool has the ability to mutate data; I showed this by using the WebMCP declarative API with no JavaScript involvement, simply employing a regular HTML form on the Add Expense page and including the appropriate tool annotations. State-gated tools: The approve_expense tool appears in the list returned by getTools() only when a signed-in admin has pending expenses that need approving; once the queue is empty the tool disappears. Custom Agent powered by Gemini API: A custom agent can use a functions/tools from third party currency converter app embedded using <iframe allow="tools"> to convert the expense value to base currency. Following snippet can fetch those tools and we can use Gemini API function calling if we are building our own agent. Navigation Tools: Built in navigation tools allowing agents to act exactly like human and navigate between pages while performing tasks. Sample prompts to try Sign in, open the Copilot orb, and paste any of these, each is chosen to hit a different tool or WebMCP aspect from the table below. Try this What it exercises What did we spend on software this month? get_spend_summary — read-only, runs instantly, no confirmation How much budget is left for Travel this month? get_budget_status — read-only Show me all pending expenses from last week search_expenses — read-only, untrusted-content badge What categories do we have set up? fetch_categories — read-only File a ₹1,200 lunch at Barista submit_expense — mutating , stops for confirmation before writing Export last month's expenses as CSV — then hit Cancel while it runs generate_report — cancellable , AbortSignal end to end (as priya@actuo.demo , with pending items) Approve all pending expenses under ₹2,000 approve_expense — state-gated , only registered for owner/admin with a non-empty queue (on /agent ) Convert 200 EUR to INR Cross-origin: discovers and calls a tool from Cambiaro , an independently deployed converter app Sign in as arjun@actuo.demo (member) and try the approval prompt again and approve_expense won't even appear in the tool list, since it's gated server-side by role, not just hidden in the UI. // getting tools for own app await document.modelContext.getTools(); // getting tools for 3rd party app embedded with <iframe allow="tools"> await document.modelContext.getTools({ fromOrigins: ['https://cambiaro.programmersingh.dev'] }); The aspect that interested me most to develop was the /agent screen since it demonstrates interoperability between different origins rather than merely within a single application. It presents as an independent WebMCP-enabled site the currency converter I developed called Cambiaro. Actuo does not own the code for Cambiaro; instead, Actuo calls getTools({ fromOrigins }) on Cambiaro and receives back the actual tool descriptions across the origin boundary, together with all the security annotations remaining unaltered. I confirmed this in real time between two deployed URLs and as a result of calling Cambiaro's currency tool from Actuo the embedded widget on Cambiaro's side was actually updated. How I built it For the frontend I used Angular with support for SSR and PWA, on the backend I used NestJS and for the database I used Supabase. The specifications for each tool are defined just once in a common file as a JSON Schema. This same schema is registered on the client side and employed by the server when validating each incoming request. Thus there is a single source of truth regarding what a tool actually accepts. I always followed one strict rule during the project. Anything that WebMCP makes available at the discovery level is solely for the purpose of improving the user experience and ensuring interoperability, not to serve as a security boundary. Although it is useful to hide the approve_expense function from the discovery level for a non-administrator, the backend still independently checks the caller's role in the database on each and every call, no matter what the client discovers. Challenges I ran into Definitely the most difficult aspect was getting the cross-origin feature to work. It took a great deal of trial and error to work out the settings for exposedTo , fromOrigins , and the iframe's allow="tools" permission policy between the two separately deployed applications. A tool remains invisible to origins other than its own unless its registration specifically lists the consuming origin; that is why Actuo has to pass along its own origin to Cambiaro when the frame loads if the handshake is to work. A further difficulty consisted in making the state-gated tools genuinely secure rather than merely hiding them visually. It is one thing to hide a tool from a list, but much more effort is required to ensure that its disappearance is supported by an independently enforced check, and to prove this by writing tests for someone who is attempting to spoof a role claim. What I learned The most important thing I've learned is that looking at the examples in the specification does not prepare you for the kind of experience you'll actually have when developing a real application. It wasn't until I had gotten deep into the code that I realised how much of the fascinating WebMCP surface area only becomes available when you have actual users, genuine roles, and live data. Features such as state-gating, cancellation, cross-origin discovery, and security annotations simply don't appear in the single-page toy demonstrations. That's precisely the kind of insight I hope to bring back to my GDG talk; I don't just want to show the API, I want to demonstrate what happens when you actually try to use it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Making the cross-origin connection work in both directions. When you invoke the currency converter from Actuo's /agent screen, the currency converter doesn't simply return a fixed figure; you can actually see the state change on Cambiaro, which is a completely separate and independently deployed application. It was only when two applications with different codebases and release cycles started genuinely communicating with each other using just the WebMCP origin handshake that this stopped being merely a specification I was reading and became something real that I could demonstrate. Creating state-gated tools that are truly secure, not just appearing so. While it's a pleasant user experience that the expense approval tool doesn't appear on the frontend when you're not an admin, I made certain that this wasn't just a visual illusion. Each time a request is made, the backend independently checks the user's role. I also prepared specific tests to detect anyone attempting to forge their role claim. title: Inkframe — An Agent-Native Motion Studio
pitch: Compose editable short-form videos with a browser agent: plan scenes, review every change, manage media, and explicitly approve a local MP4 export through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Compose editable short-form videos with a browser agent: plan scenes, review every change, manage media, and explicitly approve a local MP4 export through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inkframe keeps the agent’s proposed edit visible and editable in the same browser timeline. Inspiration Video editors are built for people who can see what is selected, infer whether a drag worked, and recover from an accidental click. A browser agent faces a different problem: it sees controls and pixels, while the project itself is structured state—clips, timing, text, audio, transitions, and export rules. Inkframe explores a better collaboration model. The person defines the creative direction. The agent works through the editor’s real capabilities, and the person reviews every consequential change. What it does Inkframe is an agent-native motion studio for short-form video. It creates editable 9:16 and 16:9 timelines with video, images, captions, audio, and transitions. In the demo, an agent plans a 16-second Vietnam travel Reel, finds matching Pexels footage and licensed Freesound audio, imports those assets into the browser, composes four scenes, adds captions and transitions, validates the result, and reports the required attribution. The finished work remains an ordinary editable timeline rather than a black-box generated file. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Inkframe expose named, typed editor tools instead of asking an agent to imitate a person clicking through the UI. The agent can inspect the project, search stock footage, plan a storyboard without changing anything, compose an approved plan, validate the timeline, inspect attribution, and request local export. The key control point is approval. A storyboard plan returns a one-use token bound to that exact plan. Composition requires the token and explicit confirmation, so a later mutation cannot silently reuse an earlier approval. Export and destructive actions are confirmed too. How we built it Inkframe is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Its reducer-backed editor session keeps separate 9:16 and 16:9 timelines. WebMCP tools are registered through the browser’s model context with strict Zod schemas and JSON Schema inputs. Elah renders the composition in a browser worker and MediaBunny encodes the MP4 locally. Pexels, Jamendo, and Freesound imports retain provider, creator, source, license, and required-credit metadata. Projects and media stay in browser storage; Inkframe does not upload the source media or rendered video to a render server. Challenges we ran into The main design challenge was making the agent capable without making it authoritative. An early lesson was that atomically exposing every editor action is not enough: the agent also needs a safe workflow. We added capability discovery, preview-first storyboards, content-bound approval tokens, isolated variants, bounded tool output, timeline validation, visual QA, attribution reporting, cancellation, and local export verification. We also had to make tools read current editor state at call time, rather than stale state captured when the page mounted. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when tools express product intent rather than DOM mechanics. A browser agent becomes more reliable when it can reason about a project’s actual state and report what changed. The best outcome is collaborative: people direct taste, make approvals, and retain control; agents handle the structured, repeatable editing operations. What's next We want to make visual review and comparison faster, give creators more reusable motion templates, and continue refining agent workflows that are easy to inspect, approve, and undo. The underlying editor predates this challenge. The WebMCP tool surface, approval workflow, live state bridge, validation, attribution, and judge flow were added during the challenge period. title: Autofix
pitch: “AutoFix turns a web application into something an agent can diagnose, repair, and verify—through WebMCP.”
about_excerpt:
“AutoFix turns a web application into something an agent can diagnose, repair, and verify—through WebMCP.”
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 Inspiration
Modern web apps crash on unexpected null checks or bad inputs, causing lost carts, churn, and 3 AM on-call alerts. We asked: Why do biological systems heal wounds in real time, while web apps shatter at the first error? With the new W3C WebMCP standard, we realized we could embed an AI immune system directly inside browser memory to detect, diagnose, and repair broken code instantly.
⚙️ What It Does
AutoFix.run is a self-healing frontend engine that fixes crashes in under 2 seconds with zero page reload:
WebMCP Flight Recorder: Buffers user clicks, DOM mutations, and component stacks.
Gemini Root-Cause Diagnosis: Dispatches crash dumps via WebMCP to synthesize surgical AST patches.
AST Safety Auditor: Blocks prototype pollution, arbitrary network calls, and unsafe evaluations before execution.
Zero-Downtime Hotpatching: Injects the verified fix straight into browser memory, preserving active user state and unfreezing the UI.
Git PR Automation: Generates clean Git diffs and ready-to-merge GitHub pull requests.
🧗 Challenges We Faced
Hotpatching Without State Loss: Swapping code in a running React bundle without refreshing the page or losing user inputs required careful in-memory prototype interception.
Preventing Hallucinations: Constraining Gemini via strict JSON schemas and AST invariant assertions so it only produces surgical, runnable code fixes.
High-Demand API Reliability: Built an adaptive circuit breaker that seamlessly cascades across Gemini flash models if an endpoint hits temporary 503 limits.
🏆 Accomplishments
Achieved sub-1.8s Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) from crash to live heal.
Demonstrated zero state loss across an authentic 2.7k★ React Calculator and an enterprise e-commerce checkout funnel.
Native browser-level WebMCP implementation (window.navigator.modelContext) instead of an external chat wrapper.
📚 What We Learned
WebMCP transforms the browser from a passive display into an active, intelligent host.
Neuro-symbolic design wins: Combining LLM reasoning with deterministic AST security checks is essential for running generated code safely in production.
Production web software no longer needs to be fragile—it can have its own immune system.

title: GridPact
pitch: Where people and agents agree when compute should run.
about_excerpt: Where people and agents agree when compute should run. Like 1 Comment Story Updates arch Inspiration Carbon-aware schedulers already move jobs into cleaner hours, but they decide silently. The constraints that actually matter: this backup stays in Frankfurt, that training must finish by 8 AM and live in people's heads and never reach the scheduler. WebMCP made it possible to turn that into a conversation. What it does Shows your workloads on a timeline against the grid carbon forecast. You state a goal, the agent plans against it. When the goal is impossible, GreenWindow names the colliding constraints and offers the smallest trade that unlocks most of the benefit: shift one deadline by 45 minutes, get 38% of the reduction, keep region and cost untouched. You accept or reject each trade. Anything you lock stays locked. The output is a carbon execution contract: what was preserved, what was relaxed, and the resulting savings. How we built it TypeScript, React, Vite, static, no backend --> WebMCP tools run in the user's own browser session. The planner is a constraint solver over discrete time slots optimizing carbon and cost. Infeasibility explanations come from tracking which constraint killed which window, so the solver can name culprits instead of returning "no solution". Carbon and price forecasts are a bundled 24-hour dataset, so the demo needs no API key. Challenges we ran into The first version let the agent apply schedules directly. It produced better plans that no operator would ever run, because it had no idea which constraints were negotiable. Rebuilding around locks and single-constraint trades was the turning point. Explaining infeasibility properly meant instrumenting the solver, not bolting on a message afterwards. Accomplishments that we're proud of The infeasibility explanation: it tells you exactly why your goals don't fit and what the cheapest way out is. And the demo is honest: state really changes, plans recompute live, and the savings come from the same solver that produced the schedule. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when tools aren't remote controls for existing buttons. The useful ones here have no button at all: test a hypothetical constraint set, find the minimum relaxation. Those are questions, not clicks. What's next for GreenWindow Export contracts in a form the Carbon Aware SDK and Kubernetes schedulers can consume. Real grid forecast APIs with fallback. Multi-region contention when two teams want the same clean window. A review mode, so contracts can be approved by someone other than the negotiator. title: REPLAY
pitch: REPLAY uses WebMCP to let people and agents reconstruct road incidents together without turning uncertainty or inference into fact.
about_excerpt: REPLAY uses WebMCP to let people and agents reconstruct road incidents together without turning uncertainty or inference into fact. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most minor road incidents have no black box. The useful record is usually scattered across photographs, vehicle damage, final positions, approximate timing, and conflicting memories. Traditional forms flatten those relationships into prose. A general-purpose AI conversation can create a different problem: an assumption or inference may gradually sound like an established fact. I built REPLAY to explore a safer form of human-agent collaboration—one where evidence, memory, uncertainty, dispute, and agent inference remain visibly distinct throughout the investigation. What it does REPLAY is a local-first visual workspace for reconstructing minor, no-injury road incidents. People can: Position and rotate vehicles on a calibrated road scene Create and edit timed trajectories Record impacts and vehicle damage Add observations with explicit provenance and certainty Attach and connect local evidence Track unresolved questions Compare alternative hypotheses Run deterministic geometry, motion, and consistency checks Produce JSON, SVG, PNG, and citation-bound PDF exports The project includes four repeatable synthetic scenarios, including a calibrated roundabout and a straight-road case with a path-derived 65–80 km/h approach. REPLAY is intentionally not a forensic simulator, truth detector, or fault-assignment system. Its calculations are transparent review aids based on the recorded inputs. Why WebMCP A screenshot may show two vehicles, but it cannot reliably tell an agent which timed point belongs to which hypothesis, whether a statement is photo-backed or disputed, which geometry is locked, or whether the human has changed the case since the agent last read it. WebMCP exposes those semantics directly from the live page. REPLAY provides a lifecycle-aware inventory of 18–19 structured Site Tools. An agent can read the current case, inspect evidence relationships, run deterministic validation, focus an issue in the visible interface, add attributed observations, compare hypotheses, create a reversible geometry proposal, and prepare a report preview. The agent and human do not work on separate copies. Both use the same validated domain command layer and the same visible case. The authorization boundary is deliberately asymmetric: Agent: read, validate, propose, and draft. Human: attest, decide, confirm, and finalize. An agent proposal remains a visible preview until a person reviews it. No Site Tool can confirm a claim, attest that evidence or uncertainty was reviewed, accept its own proposal, decide fault, or finalize the report. How I built it REPLAY is a static React 19 and strict TypeScript application built with Vite. The domain layer uses Zod schemas and a command engine for validation, optimistic versioning, provenance, locks, idempotency, hypotheses, proposals, consistency checks, undo/redo, reporting, and import/export. The interface includes: An accessible SVG scene editor A synchronized incident timeline Simple and expert workspace modes Evidence, facts, questions, hypotheses, reports, and activity panels Human-only proposal and finalization controls A guided onboarding and Site Tools walkthrough Case data and uploaded evidence remain in the browser through IndexedDB and Dexie. The runtime requires no account, analytics service, location permission, backend, or model API. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) using fixed JSON schemas derived from the same validation rules used by the interface. Durable WebMCP writes are staged, version-checked, saved, and only then adopted by the visible application. Challenges I faced The hardest challenge was preserving one trustworthy state across human actions, agent calls, persistence, and visible rendering. A tool result must not silently overwrite a newer human edit. REPLAY therefore uses case versions, compare-and-swap persistence, semantic idempotency keys, pose-target guards, cancellation handling, and compensation for post-save conflicts. Another challenge was representing uncertainty without turning the workspace into an unreadable collection of warnings. I designed explicit states for confirmed, reported, likely, uncertain, disputed, unknown, and agent-hypothesis content, while keeping provenance and open questions inspectable. Scene geometry also required careful boundaries. REPLAY checks calibrated vehicle footprints, contact placement, road clearance, speed, acceleration, turning, and heading consistency—but labels every result as a deterministic advisory rather than proof of what physically happened. Finally, I had to make the human authorization boundary real rather than cosmetic. The restrictions on confirmation, completeness review, proposal acceptance, and report finalization are enforced inside the domain command layer, not only through hidden or disabled buttons. What I learned I learned that effective agent integration is less about exposing many actions and more about exposing precise semantics, trustworthy state, and clear authority. WebMCP works best when tools are narrow, versioned, attributable, and connected to the interface the person is already using. Read operations should explain what changed—or explicitly state that nothing changed. Mutations should preserve provenance and be safe to retry. Consequential decisions should remain visible and intentional. I also learned that uncertainty can be useful product data. A reconstruction does not need to pretend every question has been answered before it can help someone organize evidence, identify contradictions, and prepare a reviewable record. Accomplishments The final release includes a complete human workflow, native Site Tools, local persistence and recovery, accessible desktop and mobile layouts, four deterministic scenarios, structured exports, and human-gated report finalization. The release passed 463 automated unit and integration tests plus 223 end-to-end browser tests with no failures. The deployed artifact is linked to an exact clean source commit and is verified byte-for-byte after deployment. Most importantly, REPLAY demonstrates an agent collaboration model where AI can contribute meaningful structured work without being allowed to convert its own conclusions into accepted truth. title: Kodi: Agent-Native Tax Workspace
pitch: WebMCP turns Kodi into an agent-native tax workspace, letting external AI securely discover and use its document evidence and tax capabilities without brittle UI automation.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns Kodi into an agent-native tax workspace, letting external AI securely discover and use its document evidence and tax capabilities without brittle UI automation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT discovers Kodi’s seven WebMCP tools while the Kodi document library remains visible side by side. Kodi exposes all seven WebMCP capabilities for document discovery, evidence access, reasoning, and reversible actions. Live Kodi library showing 13 active documents with states and revisions, plus two records currently in Trash. WebMCP searches 2025 utility-expense evidence, then retrieves exact canonical evidence from a selected Kodi document. Kodi answers a Kenyan sole-proprietor tax question using governed knowledge, citations, warnings, and conversation state WebMCP renames a document, verifies the revision, then moves the same canonical record safely into Trash. The trashed record is restored, its original filename recovered, and all seven WebMCP capabilities complete successfully. Kodi Tax Workflow: Kodi works through a tax objective by inspecting evidence, taking actions, preserving progress, and continuing as needed. Manual AI Handoff: Without WebMCP, customers must switch to Kodi, retrieve needed information, and manually carry it back to their AI. Three Ways to Use Kodi: Customers can use Kodi directly, use Kodi’s own AI, or let a compatible external AI access Kodi through WebMCP. The problem Kodi existed before the WebMCP Challenge. I originally built it around a simple idea: what if working through tax could feel more like working with a modern coding agent? When I give a coding agent an objective such as “fix the authentication bug,” I do not have to tell it which file to open, which function to inspect, which command to run or which test to try first. The agent can inspect the environment, use the tools available to it, observe what happens and continue working toward the objective. Tax has many of the same characteristics, only with a very different environment. There are taxpayer facts, documents, evidence, tax rules, calculations, missing information, forms, validations and actions. Traditionally, much of the burden of connecting those pieces falls on the taxpayer or the professional helping them. Kodi was my attempt to change that. Instead of treating tax as a series of screens that someone has to understand and operate manually, Kodi treats it as work to be done . A user can give Kodi an objective. Kodi can work with their documents and evidence, determine what is known, identify what is missing, use tax capabilities where appropriate, ask the taxpayer when information genuinely cannot be resolved, and preserve the state of that work as it progresses. That was already Kodi before this challenge. The WebMCP Challenge started from a different problem. Kodi had become capable of doing useful tax work, but most of that capability was still available only when the customer was actively working through Kodi itself. And the way people are using AI is changing. A business owner may already be working with a general AI assistant while reviewing their business. An accountant may have an agent helping prepare for a client meeting. Someone may be working through a larger financial task that touches email, accounting systems, calendars, business records and tax. If that agent reaches a point where it needs something Kodi already knows how to do, the customer can still end up acting as the connection between them. The capability exists. The intelligence exists. The customer's data exists. But the customer is still doing the integration. That is the problem I wanted to address in this challenge. Why this happens Kodi was designed to be used directly by its customers. Its document library is available through Kodi. Its evidence retrieval is available through Kodi. Its tax intelligence is available through Kodi. Its autonomous Tax Case is available through Kodi. That is exactly what a normal product should do. But there is now another kind of user emerging: the AI agent acting on behalf of the customer. A browser agent should not have to reverse-engineer the meaning of every button, search box and rendered table just to use a capability that the application already understands internally. And the alternative should not be handing an external AI unrestricted access to Kodi's backend. What I wanted was something in between: Give the agent useful capabilities, while Kodi continues to control identity, permissions, data and execution. That is where WebMCP fits. The WebMCP approach For the WebMCP Challenge, I did not rebuild Kodi. I extended the existing product with a new agent-facing interface . WebMCP allows Kodi to describe selected capabilities in a structured form that a compatible external AI agent can discover from the authenticated application. So Kodi can now be approached in three ways: The first two already existed. The third path is what I added for this challenge. And that is where the additional customer value comes from. I am not replacing Kodi's AI with another AI. I am not saying customers should stop using Kodi. I am making the capabilities that already make Kodi valuable available in another context when that is more convenient for the customer. If someone is already inside Kodi, they can continue using Kodi. If they want Kodi to autonomously work through a Tax Case, they can use Kodi's Tax Agent. And if they are already working with another compatible AI agent on a broader objective, that agent can now use selected Kodi capabilities when it needs them. The product stays the same. Its utility expands. title: VocalApply - voice-driven job application
pitch: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Codex working screenshot 3 Codex working screenshot 1 Codex working screenshot 2 Chrome home WebMCP tools listed Application Page WebMCP tools listed VocalApply Inspiration If you watch a visual AI agent try to fill out a job application, it looks like someone trying to click a mouse while looking through a telescope. It takes screenshots, streams images to a vision model, guesses coordinates for dropdowns, misclicks, and retries. Now try navigating that same multi-step form with a screen reader. A screen reader reads top-to-bottom, line by line. When an application has five steps, dropdown menus, hidden accordions, and error labels, someone who is visually impaired has to tab through dozens of irrelevant links and labels just to find the next input. A task that takes a sighted user two minutes can take twenty minutes of listening to raw boilerplate. People also run into this when they have a broken wrist, severe carpal tunnel, or are multitasking with their hands full. Screen readers are slow, and vision bots keep guessing coordinates. We wanted to fix both: What if you didn't need a vision model watching your screen, and didn't need to tab through fifty links with a screen reader? What if you could just talk to the page, and the page exposed its buttons and inputs directly to your voice? At the same time, applying for a job is personal. It is your work history, your salary, and your name on a legal declaration. We wanted a tool that types the repetitive fields, asks you out loud when it needs your input, and deliberately refuses to press submit on your behalf . What it does VocalApply is a careers website paired with a voice agent that runs directly in your browser: Hands-Free Job Search: You speak naturally: "Show me what you have open." The page sets the filter bar, highlights the best match, and reads out why it fits your background. If you say "Not that one," it moves the ring to the next job on the shortlist. Visually impaired users can hear role summaries without tabbing through navigation menus. Form Filling: Say "Apply to that one and fill it in." The page opens the application and fills in your contact information, eligibility, and work history from a saved profile. Two-Pass Input: A profile cannot answer everything, and it shouldn't guess. When the form asks "Why this role, and why now?" or asks about relocation, the agent moves to that field, highlights it in amber on screen, and asks you out loud. You answer, it writes down what you said, and the highlight clears. Spoken Corrections: Say "My salary expectation went up to $130,000." It updates the field immediately and saves it locally for future applications. The Missing Submit Tool: When the form is ready, the agent focuses the submit button and prompts you to review your answers. It will not submit. There is no tool on the page that clicks submit, and no tool that checks the legal disclaimer checkbox. You have to read the declaration and click submit yourself. How we built it VocalApply runs entirely inside the user's browser tab. There is no intermediate application server storing resumes, voice recordings, or personal data. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ): Instead of a camera watching the screen, the page registers tools directly into the browser's model context. When the voice session starts, it asks the page what tools exist and runs them by name. Progressive Tool Scoping: On the job board, the model only has search and navigation tools (6 tools). It cannot access form tools until an application actually opens (9 tools). Keeping the two sets separate prevents the model from getting confused or calling form tools on a board. Live Voice Connections: The app connects directly to Gemini Live over a WebSocket (sending 16 kHz audio and receiving 24 kHz audio) and to OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. You can interrupt the model mid-sentence without echo. Keyless Walkthrough: If you don't have an API key or microphone, a built-in walkthrough drives the same tools in the same order using the browser's speech synthesis, so anyone can test the full interaction immediately. Challenges we ran into Rethinking Accessibility Without Visual Clutter: Standard accessibility tools dump all content into audio sequentially. Building a voice assistant meant figuring out how to summarize jobs concisely so a user isn't forced to listen to five paragraphs of job descriptions just to compare titles and locations. Barge-In and Audio Echo: When using laptop speakers, the microphone picks up the model's own voice and cuts itself off. We had to tune audio threshold levels and scheduled playback queues so interruptions felt crisp without the model tripping over its own speech. Knowing Where to Stop Automation: It is easy to write a tool that ticks every checkbox and sends an application automatically. Deciding not to build that tool was an intentional design decision. We had to make sure the agent could prepare the application thoroughly without taking away user consent. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Better Experience for Low-Vision and Mobility-Impaired Users: Eliminating the need to tab through dozens of form elements or rely on clunky screen scrapers. You ask, it answers, and it fills the inputs cleanly. Safety as Code, Not Prompting: We didn't prompt the AI with "Please do not submit the form." We simply did not write a submit tool. The agent cannot submit an application because the capability does not exist. Direct Semantic Tools Over Computer Vision: Proving that connecting voice directly to web capabilities is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than streaming video to computer-vision bots. What we learned Voice Changes Web Accessibility: For people who rely on screen readers, conversational tools are a massive upgrade over linear DOM navigation. Asking a page to show relevant roles and hearing an immediate summary saves minutes of tedious keyboard navigation. Assistants Should Assist, Not Replace: Users don't want an AI that impersonates them or signs legal documents in their name. The most helpful tools handle mechanical data entry while leaving decisions and final consent to the person. Semantic Page Context Beats Pixels: Web automation that works with structured tools doesn't break when CSS classes change or buttons move. It provides a far more stable foundation than visual bot scrapers. title: RoomCraft
pitch: Design a room with an agent in seconds.
about_excerpt: Design a room with an agent in seconds. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Architecture Tools RoomCraft Rearrange your room with an agent via WebMCP. ▶ Watch the demo video (1:39, narrated) TL;DR Tell RoomCraft what is happening. It changes the room with you. “Eight people are coming over.” The agent adds chairs and rearranges the room. Every piece moves together on the live 3D canvas. “My mom uses a wheelchair.” The agent checks a 90 cm route between the doors, finds the tight spots, and moves what is blocking them. Red paths turn green. Drag the sofa in front of the balcony door. Ask, “What do you think?” The agent sees what you changed, tells you the door is blocked, and fixes it when you ask. It is using the room, not looking at a screenshot. WebMCP lets the agent read the live layout, move real objects, measure gaps, and check clearance inside the page. That is RoomCraft: you arrange the room by hand, by conversation, or both. Try it live Open roomcraft.nihsett.workers.dev in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ). Wait for WebMCP connected in the header. Paste these in order and watch the room react: “I’m hosting a dinner party for eight people tonight. Can you rearrange the room?” “Actually, my mom is coming and she uses a wheelchair. Can you make sure she can get around?” Drag the sofa in front of the balcony door, then ask: “What do you think?” “Fix it.” — or just keep improvising: “Get rid of the sofa,” “add more chairs,” “make the room bigger.” Anything goes. Watch the activity panel on the right log every real WebMCP call as it happens. Source: https://github.com/nihsett/roomcraft What we built RoomCraft is a complete 3D room planner in the browser. A person can orbit the room, select furniture, drag it, rotate it, and remove it. The agent gets 18 always-available WebMCP tools plus four controls for whichever object the person selects. The number is not the point. The behavior is: One shared room. Pointer gestures and WebMCP tools use the same Zustand state. No half-finished rearrangements. RoomCraft validates every object in a batch before moving any of them. The agent keeps up. Human drags and edits are journaled and returned with the next tool result. The room has meaning. The agent receives facing direction, facing target, wall placement, and layout warnings—not just raw coordinates. Constraints show up in the room. Clearance checks draw green and red routes directly across the 3D floor. How we used WebMCP 18 tools on the live room. Read, add, move, rotate, remove, save — every call hits the real state, never a screenshot. Intent, not coordinates. place_facing , place_against_wall — the agent says what it wants, the engine finds valid spots. Atomic batches. Multi-piece rearrangements validate fully first, or nothing moves. Meaning, not raw numbers. Tool results carry facing, wall placement, and layout warnings. Visible constraints. check_clearance draws the real 90 cm route on the floor — red blocked, green clear. You can interrupt anytime. Your drags since the last call ride back as human_actions_since_last_call . One state. Your mouse, its tools. How it works The picture is the whole point: there is one measured room, not two copies. When you drag the sofa, the agent’s next read already shows the new position. When the agent rearranges for eight guests, the room you are looking at is the room it changed. RoomCraft is a React and TypeScript single-page app rendered with React Three Fiber. It has no backend. Layouts can be saved in the browser. Built with WebMCP — the agent's hands on the live room: 18 tools, zero screenshots. React Three Fiber — the live 3D canvas. Zustand — one shared state for human and agent. TypeScript + Vite — fast, typed, no backend. Cloudflare Workers — where the live link lives. What's next Your actual floor plan. Upload it. RoomCraft rebuilds the room. Real furniture catalogs. Real sizes. Real prices. Agent picks what fits. More room types. Bedrooms, offices, kitchens — the same shared-state magic. The loop stays: say it, drag it, done. title: Mausam
pitch: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Interactive map close-up - Zoomed view of the MMR map with rainfall intensity scale Desktop landing view - Mausam header with live status and the Mumbai rainfall intelligence map Mobile layout - Mausam on a phone-sized viewport, showing header and map Full product page - End-to-end scroll of the Mausam site, from hero through map and supporting sections MMR rainfall map - Full Mumbai Metropolitan Region choropleth with locality labels and intensity legend Mausam Mausam (pronounced "mow-sum") is the Hindi word for weather or season. I chose the name because this project grew out of Mumbai's unpredictable monsoon. In Hindi, people often ask, "Mausam kaisa hai?" , or "How is the weather?" My project tries to answer the more useful version of that question: What changed? Where is the rain moving? Does Borivali face the same risk as the rest of Mumbai? Is this worth interrupting someone for? Inspiration Mumbai's weather rarely behaves like a simple forecast. During the monsoon, the sky can change within minutes. One suburb may get intense rain while another stays almost dry. A forecast that says "rain in Mumbai" may be technically correct and still be useless to someone deciding whether to leave home. That gap inspired Mausam. It watches several sources, compares new evidence with the last report, and sends an update only when something has changed. I started with one question: Can I build a weather service that remains alert without becoming noisy? What it does Mausam produces two complementary weather reports for Mumbai: A near-term nowcast covering approximately the next three to six hours. A five-day outlook comparing GFS and ECMWF forecast models. The primary nowcast combines: IMD PPI-Z and SRI radar frames; Windy rain-accumulation imagery; short-range GFS and ECMWF frames; readings from Borivali and Kandivali East; scraped rain statistics; local weather-station observations; and the previous report’s state. It evaluates Borivali separately from the wider Mumbai Metropolitan Region because rainfall can vary significantly across the city. The five-day pipeline compares GFS and ECMWF at five forecast horizons: $$ 2\ \text{models} \times 5\ \text{horizons} = 10\ \text{forecast frames} $$ Mausam delivers the result through email, Discord, a local alert banner, and an Astro website. It also chooses when to check again. Dangerous conditions get a faster follow-up; stable conditions can wait. The website also exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_weather_nowcast get_weather_outlook get_forecast_reasoning A compatible browser agent can call these tools to read the forecast as structured data instead of scraping the page. How I built it I built Mausam over five months with Bun and TypeScript. Each month solved a problem that appeared once the previous version started running in real conditions. April: Building the evidence pipeline The first version downloaded radar images and stored them in S3-compatible object storage. I wrote utilities to find the latest image, convert it to a compact JPEG, compare it with the previous frame, upload new evidence, and safely remove old objects. That led to the rule at the center of the project: $$ \text{Analyse} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if evidence changed} \ 1, & \text{during the morning guarantee} \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ Weather sources often publish the same frame more than once. Analysing every copy would waste multimodal model calls and send repetitive notifications. Mausam compares the image bytes first. A morning exception still guarantees one baseline report each day. Once that worked, I connected the images to a multimodal weather agent. I added rain observations, local station data, saved summaries, email delivery, Telegram alerts, and BullMQ scheduling around it. By the end of April, Mausam had evolved from an image-processing script into a continuously scheduled weather service. May: Making scheduling dependable In May, I focused on the less exciting part that decides whether an automated service survives: failure handling. The pipeline schedules another attempt when a source fails or an image has not changed. Active-hour checks stop jobs from running at unsuitable times, while severity-based delays revisit urgent conditions sooner. This was when scheduling became part of the weather decision rather than a fixed cron interval. June: Adding rendered maps and Discord Some weather sources do not provide a direct image. Windy renders its accumulation map inside a web application. I added Puppeteer to open the page, wait for the weather layer, take a controlled screenshot, and pass it through the same pipeline as a downloaded image. A shared ingestion helper means the rest of the application does not need to know where an image came from. Discord replaced Telegram as the technical reporting channel. A separate gRPC integration handles delivery, so communication failures stay outside the weather analysis process. I also added Uptime Kuma heartbeats and automatic startup jobs so Mausam could run unattended. July: Expanding from hours to days The original system only answered, "What happens over the next few hours?" In July, I added a second pipeline to answer, "What could the next five days look like?" It finds the newest usable GFS and ECMWF runs, resolves changing Tropical Tidbits image URLs, and collects frames at approximately (+24), (+48), (+72), (+96), and (+120) hours. All ten images are staged before analysis. If one required frame cannot be prepared, the incomplete set is removed instead of mixing different or partial model runs. Running the system exposed another problem: a retry could repeat actions that had already succeeded. I strengthened the workflow with: Zod-validated configuration and model output; Redis-backed previous-report state; decision caching using evidence-derived run identifiers; delivery locks and completion markers; follow-up-job deduplication; and separation between queue construction and process side effects. The model interprets uncertain weather evidence. Regular application code controls persistence, delivery, retries, and scheduling. This boundary keeps free-form model behavior away from side effects. August: Building the web experience In August, I started retaining the two newest frames from each primary source. A pair of images shows basic movement and development that one snapshot cannot. I also compressed primary evidence to reduce multimodal input cost. The estimated image-token load fell from roughly 50,000 tokens in the earlier high-frame case to around 7,500: $$ 1-\frac{7{,}500}{50{,}000} =0.85 =85\% $$ I extended the agents with structured website fields and Zod validation. Using bun:sqlite , I persist nowcasts and outlooks for an Astro and React frontend. The stored data includes separate Borivali and Mumbai/MMR alert levels, headlines, rain probability, peak timing, confidence, station observations, source summaries, daily outlook cards, model comparisons, and detailed reasoning. The website presents the current alert, local conditions, five-day forecast, source summaries, model comparison, and reasoning. I also integrated an interactive Mumbai Metropolitan Region map. It connects report data to localities and visualizes alert severity, rain intensity, forecast movement, and differences across the region. The last addition was WebMCP. When a browser exposes document.modelContext , the React application registers three focused, read-only weather tools. Each returns bounded structured data and labels the result as AI guidance. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the complete website, making agent interaction a progressive enhancement rather than a dependency. The full path now looks like this: $$ \text{Weather sources} \rightarrow \text{Evidence pipeline} \rightarrow \text{Structured reasoning} \rightarrow \text{Reliable delivery} \rightarrow \text{Web experience} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP interaction} $$ Challenges I ran into Inconsistent weather sources Some sources provide files. Others need browser rendering. Forecast URLs change with model initialization times, and station or rain-statistics endpoints can fail on their own. I wrote source-specific resolvers behind one ingestion interface. A missing required radar frame stops the run. An optional source can fail without taking the whole forecast down, and Mausam uses retained evidence where appropriate. Detecting real changes A newly published file does not always contain new weather. Running the agent on identical frames would consume resources and wear out the person receiving alerts. Exact byte comparison is predictable, but it has a trade-off: an encoding change can look new to the system even when the two images look identical to a person. Preventing duplicate alerts A run may successfully send an email and then fail while posting to Discord. Retry

title: Gulawo Tendering Workspace with a Built-in WebMCP Agent
pitch: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved.
about_excerpt: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved. Like Comment Story Updates demo demo demo Inspiration East African SME contractors don't lose government tenders on price. They lose on a missing PPDA certificate. A deadline buried in a procurement portal. A compliance gap nobody caught until it was too late. That admin, the finding, the tracking, the checking, the paperwork, is exactly what beat the teams that could actually do the work. Gulawo exists to close that gap. What it does A contractor signs in, uploads a real certificate, hands a tender to the agent, and the agent works the whole pipeline inside the app. It searches open tenders, pulls the full brief, scores fit against the company's actual profile, checks the document vault against the compliance checklist, and scans the bid security against the stated guarantee so the fatal gap is caught before anyone submits. The agent proposes. The human approves. Nothing touches the bid until someone clicks Approve. How we built it Next.js and React for the workspace, and a WebMCP layer that declares six tools in the manifest and registers the same six on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool dispatches to a typed function that runs real SQL against the live database, so the workflow is identical whether a human drives the cockpit in the browser or an agent calls the tools from ChatGPT's embedded browser with WebMCP enabled. It degrades gracefully if the API isn't there and is guarded by a session cookie. Challenges we ran into Making it watchable. The unbounded agent route we tried first was slow and unreliable, so we made the recorded path deterministic and database-backed, and bounded every step so one slow call could never blow the three-minute limit. A recording quirk taught us what the eye actually follows. A new tool's result is prepended above older ones, and an early cut scrolled the bottom card into view while the narration described the new one. Fixing the recorder to center the card it was talking about, and to actually reveal the proposal and the kanban, took more patience than the app itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of Credibility over confidence. Every WebMCP tool is deterministic. It returns structured JSON computed from real SQL against real tenders, the real compliance rule set, and the real uploaded documents. If the tool says a UGX 12 million bid security is short of the required two percent, that's arithmetic against an actual tender record, not a comforting guess. And human approval isn't a checkbox. Lookup tools run freely, but nothing persists until a person approves. What we learned For a contractor, credibility beats confidence. An agent that sounds sure about compliance is worthless if it's wrong and costs them a bid. That's why Gulawo doesn't guess. And we saw firsthand what people and agents can now do together that was hard before. Before, an assistant could only read whatever the page rendered. Now a small contractor gets a defensible answer in seconds. Is this tender worth it? Are we legally ready to bid? Is there a compliant draft held for sign-off? Instead of hours of paperwork or a disqualification. What's next for Gulawo Turn the six tools into a persistent compliance watchman. Let the agent monitor open tenders against the vault continuously, alert the contractor the moment a new tender matches, and keep draft proposals current as tenders change. Grow the readable tender pool beyond Uganda into Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda, and let the vault check itself against each market's rule set. And push deeper on the collaborative loop that WebMCP makes possible. The agent works the pipeline in the same session, with the human holding the final say, all the way to submission.
