 Inspiration 

 Initially, I wanted to create a head-to-head competitive game for two players. However, after experimenting with Codex to control a webpage via WebMCP, I abandoned that idea due to excessive latency and slow response times. 

 This led to the creation of SplitSight—an escape room game consisting of three stages. The human player can see real-time visual cues that are not captured in the system's output, while the AI ​​agent can check the game state and operate mechanisms that the human cannot control. Neither party can escape alone; success requires cooperation. 

 Feature Overview 

 SplitSight guides the human and the AI ​​agent through three interconnected rooms: 

 
 Mirror Chamber: The human identifies and shares a flashing symbol; the agent reads this information and adjusts the angle of the mirrors. 
 Portrait Gallery: The human focuses on a flashing portrait; the agent uses the shared information to open the corresponding hidden compartment. 
 Twin-Door Hall: The agent analyzes structural information regarding two exits, while the human observes real-time "guardian markers" and selects the corresponding door; the agent can only open the door if its proposal aligns with the human's decision. 
 

 Every action—reading, selecting, blocked attempts, mechanism changes, and successful outcomes—is recorded in a shared causal log, with the source (human, agent, or room) clearly marked. The interface also indicates whose turn it is and what needs to be done next. 

 Technical Implementation 

 Implemented using Codex and "vibecoding"; the specific technology stack was also selected by Codex. 

 Challenges Faced 

 The biggest challenge was choosing the concept; I actually discarded three other ideas before settling on this one. 

 Achievement I'm Proud Of 

 Implementing the entire project using the "vibecoding" workflow. 

 Lessons Learned 

 Make frequent use of AI and Codex.

pitch: e-nvoice — Free client-side Factur-X / EN 16931 e-invoicing for the 2026 French mandate.
about_excerpt: e-nvoice — Free client-side Factur-X / EN 16931 e-invoicing for the 2026 French mandate. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In September 2026, French businesses must start emitting electronic invoices (freelancers and small companies join in September 2027). As my wife is a freelancer, I wanted to first understand the rules and requirements. Then I looked what was available for freelancers to generate invoices. I found that most of the available tools were either too complex or too expensive. So I decided to build a free, client-side tool that could generate Factur-X / EN 16931 invoices. Apart from creating a compliant invoice, the main part of the tool would be to connect it to a platform like Chorus Pro, but I didn't work on that, I only built the invoice generator and added a WebMCP API for it. So anyone can call my invoice generator through the WebMCP API and generate an invoice in a compliant way. What it does e-nvoice is a free, 100% client-side app that generates Factur-X / EN 16931 invoices: a PDF/A-3 with embedded UN/CEFACT XML, ready for Chorus Pro. No server, no API key, no data leaving the machine. It covers B2B/B2C, four currencies, and French legal mentions — and exposes everything as four WebMCP tools agents can discover, validate with, compute, and generate with end to end. How we built it I started from scratch with a prompt trying to understand the new legislation and what the steps are to create a compliant invoice. Then I started to build the application using React 19 + TypeScript + Vite. I delegated the PDF and XML development to the AI, then I started looking into WebMCP and how to use it. title: CoWriter
pitch: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page.
about_excerpt: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page. Like Comment Story Updates CoWriter in session Inspiration Co-writing with an AI these days usually mean pasting your script into a chat window, getting a lot of text back and then copying these into your document. You loose formatting and context for every round trip. I wanted to see what happens when the agent isn't a chat window, but a real collaborator working on the same page as you are, through the same interface as you use. WebMCP made that possible: expose the app's real actions as tools, and an agent can write directly into your live document instead of describing what it would write. What it does CoWriter is a small screenwriting tool: it has a Story Bible panel (title, logline, theme, genre, tone), a real act-by-act Outline panel (paste in your own — Act 1 with its beats, Act 2 with its beats, and so on, including acts with no scenes written yet), that breaks acts and scenes into real screenplay format (sluglines, action, character cues, dialogue). It has a character bible, and a loose idea board where you can tweek ideas on the go. Every action on that script; revising the premise, importing or editing the outline, adding a scene, editing a line, revising a character, dropping an idea, reordering scenes, checking the whole thing for consistency — is exposed as a WebMCP tool ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). The agent is not clicking around a UI it has to guess at; it's calling the exact same functions the interface calls, and the result shows up on your screen instantly, on the same live document. You can keep editing by hand at any moment if you wish to. Crucially, get_script 's description tells the agent to call it first, always. It returns the human-authored, act-by-act outline and the Story Bible up front, so every scene the agent drafts, and every consistency check it runs, is explicitly grounded in the story's real throughline and theme. It does not guess at what happens next from whatever scene happens to be open. The outline (the plan) and the written scenes (what's actually on the page) are kept deliberately distinct, the way a real writer's outline and draft are. You can ask, in plain language, "write a tense scene where she finds the letter, no dialogue yet" — the agent calls add_scene and it appears, correctly formatted, right in front of you. You read it and asks for some more edit if you want it tweeked, and the agent calls edit_scene on that exact scene. The character bible updates the same way as new characters get introduced. And check_consistency hands the agent every dialogue line labeled by speaker plus the full character bible in one structured payload, so it can catch things like a character's voice contradicting itself across acts — the kind of full-document consistency pass that's genuinely tedious for a human to do by re-reading, but natural for an agent to do well. Nothing about the human side of the app changes because an agent is present — you can type directly into any line at any time, exactly like a normal document. That's the point: one shared script, two collaborators, no export/import step between them. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — no framework, no build tooling, no backend. All 12 WebMCP tools are registered in a single readable file ( script.js ) so the integration itself is easy to inspect end to end. Data persists to the browser's local storage. Tool responses are serialized as compact JSON to keep the token footprint of every agent call low. Challenges we ran into Keeping the outline and the written scenes as two genuinely separate sources of truth, rather than letting them silently collapse into one, took deliberate design. It would have been simpler to let the agent treat whatever is on the page as the plan, but this would have let scenes drift from the story's real throughline. Instead, get_script always returns both, and the agent's own tool descriptions tell it the outline is the plan and the scenes are what is actually been written — they won't always be in sync, and that is intentional. Getting an agent to actually call a tool rather than just answer a writing request conversationally in chat also took some care in how the tool descriptions were phrased — an ambiguous prompt can be satisfied just as easily by the model generating prose in the chat window as by it calling add_scene on the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve WebMCP tools, all grounded in one shared Story Bible, with a UI that never has to know or care whether the human or the agent made the last edit. Watching a scene appear live on the page, correctly formatted and fitting the outline is genuinely satisfying to demo. What we learned That grounding matters more than raw capability. An agent that can call add_scene isn't useful on its own. It is useful because get_script forces it to read the outline and premise first, every time, so what it writes actually belongs in the story. What's next for CoWriter Multi-scene consistency diffing — let check_consistency compare against the previous run's report so an agent can flag only new contradictions instead of re-surfacing everything each time. PDF/Fountain export of the finished screenplay. Multi-document projects — more than one script per browser profile, with a lightweight project switcher. Real backend/cloud persistence, so a script isn't tied to one browser's local storage. A visible scene-level undo/history stack for agent-made edits. A richer character bible — arcs, relationships, and a "first appearance" pointer the agent can use to catch characters who show up before being introduced. A more efficient architecture for managing token consumption for each 'get_script' tool call. title: Easy Query
pitch: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you.
about_excerpt: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you. Like Comment Story Updates demo1 demo2 demo3 Inspiration Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Pain: Writing complex SQL requires expertise. Solution: Using WebMCP, the agent can help users write accurate SQL queries. Pain: Most AI assistants and data tools operate in separate contexts. Users are forced to repeatedly copy information between tools and manually apply every suggestion. Solution: The agent works directly in Easy Query, eliminating constant copy-pasting between tools. Pain: Long, deeply nested SQL queries maintained by multiple people are difficult to understand, modify, and debug. Solution: WebMCP gives the agent access to the full query, schema, errors, and results to explain the logic, make changes, and verify the fix. How it creates a better user experience Pain: Basic file viewers such as Excel are easy to use but building complex queries quickly becomes awkward. Solution: Easy-to-use GUI features such as: infinite scrolling, search, sorting, and filtering. Pain: On the other hand, database tools are powerful but intimidating. Solution: Easy Query gives users the power of SQL and AI through a familiar table interface, making advanced data analysis far less intimidating. Pain: Formats such as Parquet are difficult to inspect. Solution: Easy Query displays them directly in a fast, familiar table. Pain: Most AI tool's chat history buries earlier queries and results. Revisiting an earlier query means scrolling through the conversation, finding the right response, and interrupting the current discussion to refine it. Solution: Every query and result appears in a browser-style tab that users can inspect, edit, rerun, rename, and reuse. What people and agents can do together Every query and result remains visible and editable, making advanced analysis accessible without taking control away from experienced users. Either the user or agent can independently perform full data analysis. They can also collaborate: the user guides the question while the agent handles complex SQL and iterative debugging. Because both operate on the same live workspace, either can immediately continue, refine, or verify the other's work. What it does Easy Query loads CSV, TSV, Parquet, JSON, and JSONL files into DuckDB-Wasm and lets users explore them entirely in the browser. Users can write DuckDB SQL themselves or ask a WebMCP-enabled agent to: Discover tables, columns, and relationships Write joins, aggregations, CTEs, and window queries Execute SQL and inspect complete results Diagnose errors and revise queries Create, rename, activate, and close workspace tabs Every query and result remains visible in a tab, allowing the user to inspect, edit, rerun, and learn from the agent’s work. How we built it Easy Query is built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, CodeMirror, Apache Arrow, and DuckDB-Wasm. Files are loaded into an in-memory DuckDB database, while virtual scrolling keeps large query results responsive. We implemented WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API. The application exposes structured tools for inspecting the DuckDB catalog, managing workspace tabs, reading and writing SQL, executing queries, and retrieving help. These tools operate on the same Svelte state and DuckDB connection used by the visible interface. When an agent creates a query tab or runs SQL, the result immediately appears for the user. When the user edits or renames a tab, that updated state is available to the agent. Challenges we ran into Tables, SQL, active tabs, query results, and schema changes must remain synchronized between the user interface and WebMCP tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end WebMCP workflow rather than a collection of isolated demo commands. An agent can discover an unfamiliar dataset, create a query, run it, inspect an error or result, revise its approach, and leave the finished analysis visible to the user. We are also proud that Easy Query supports two collaboration styles. An agent can complete an analysis autonomously, or it can behave as a copilot by drafting SQL and waiting for the user to review and execute it. What we learned We learned that WebMCP tool design is product design, not just an implementation task. Delegating it entirely to a coding agent can produce tools that work technically but create a confusing user experience. Human judgment was essential for defining clear capabilities and boundaries. For example, explicitly identifying DuckDB as the SQL dialect and separating database tables from workspace tabs made agent behavior far more reliable and predictable. What's next for Easy Query Next, we want to grow Easy Query into a broader, local-first data analysis workspace: Add charts and maps so people and agents can turn query results into clear trends, relationships, and geographic insights. Explore additional query paradigms, including dataframe-style transformations and specialized languages for graph or time-series data. Support more data sources, including local SQLite and DuckDB databases, plus optional remote databases through secure, user-controlled connectors. A live dashboard where you and your agent can design and manage your restaurant

 Inspiration 

 After first learning about the WebMCP Challenge, I ran through a list of ideas I always wanted to try building: an outfit generator, a groceries tracker and recipe book, a sleep productivity app, and others, but none of these seemed to really fit the use case. Then, while sitting down at a restaurant with a few friends, a waiter accidentally brought us the wrong item. An honest mistake, something that I'm sure most people have experienced, and one of the difficulties that come with managing a restaurant. After coming home, and following a bit of research into restaurant software, I decided to build a live restaurant manager, where a manager can operate from a live view of their restaurant, aided by an agent to lessen the workload on the employees. That product is now Sous. 

 What it does 

 Sous is a live dashboard where you and your agent can design and manage your restaurant. 

 Starting with design mode , both a manager and an agent can rearrange and edit the floor layout to design or match their restaurant. Each table has its own controls, with the ability to change the size, number of seats, name, and waiter section. With WebMCP integration, the agent could simply be given a picture of the restaurant and call tools to match the in-app layout to the real thing. 

 Service mode is where you actually run the restaurant. Assigning tables, taking orders, delivering orders, and managing all the work in between happens here. Humans can perform all the functions, but the agent side is where it shines. By connecting the agent to a Yelp waitlist, a live feed, or other sources of information, it can automatically track and manage everything that is happening within the restaurant, with all the changes reflecting visually for the manager to see. WebMCP allows the agent to manage all the smaller functions, with only physical interactions left to employees, lessening the friction that comes with running the restaurant. 

 How we built it 

 As I am non-technical, this project was mostly built with the help of Claude. The app runs on React, Vite, and TypeScript, and all changes on it are saved locally to the user's browser without the need for logging in, so there is no backend or database. It runs similarly to the apps seen in OpenAI's WebMCP showcase. 

 WebMCP's whole author-facing surface is registerTool : a name the agent calls, a description it decides with, an inputSchema for the arguments, and an execute that runs. Sous makes that call once, over a table of 30 definitions, rather than writing thirty literal copies of it, so grep registerTool src/webmcp.ts finds the wiring, and src/tools.ts holds the tools themselves. 

 Challenges 

 Since this was my first time building an app, naturally it was filled with challenges, especially since I don't have a technical background. One of the biggest problems I came across was realizing midway that the app did not really match my vision. While AI has been a huge help in this challenge, I had essentially allowed it to build everything from scratch, without providing a list of exactly how I wanted the app to look and function. The main canvas in the middle took multiple iterations, including hours spent in Claude Design, before I arrived at something I believed fit the app. 

 Takeaways 

 As I mentioned above, I had multiple other app ideas before Sous, but I never got myself to actually build them out until now. The WebMCP Challenge finally pushed me to build my first app, and that experience is definitely my biggest takeaway from this challenge. Also, while I knew about APIs and MCPs before, this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, and seeing and building the possibilities myself makes me excited for the future of this technology. 

 What's next for Sous 

 Sous is an app I built on a whim with Claude Code, but it does help solve a problem that many restaurants face. Past this challenge, Sous could be integrated with existing POS systems in restaurants and other software like Yelp or Stripe, in order to help it move past simply being a dashboard and become an all-in-one app for restaurant management. Likely, this would include building out the backend, so that will be another learning opportunity for the future.

title: webmcp.utlovat.se — Non-Partisan Election Fact-Checking
pitch: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026.
about_excerpt: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026. Like Comment Story Updates Utlovat.se WebMCP landing page explaining that agents can sort Swedish election evidence but cannot recommend a political party. tlovat.se research brief for healthcare, showing a recorded unclear position for Moderates, 12 evidence records for Social Democrats, Evidence cards in an Utlovat.se research brief, each with a Swedish quote, publication date, four-year cost range, source link, archive copy Inspiration During democratic elections, voters are inundated with conflicting claims, manifesto promises, and shifting party positions. When citizens in general, and first time voters in particular, turn to AI assistants for guidance, your average, I have and answer for everything, general-purpose LLMs present a dangerous hazard: they risk hallucinating plausible quotes, confusing past election cycles with current platforms, and inventing policy stances where parties are actually silent . In high-stakes civic decision-making, an AI summary is not enough. Citizens need evidence, not a verdict. And to be encouraged to question the feasibility of the "five minutes to Election Day" promises. utlovat.se (meaning "As Promised" in Swedish) is aims to be an independent, non-partisan election platform tracking over 2,000 promises and 700+ reviewed parliamentary actions for the 2026 general election. We (actually there is only me and my assisting agents) were inspired to build on OpenAI's WebMCP because it offers the missing piece of the agentic web: a standardized, browser-native protocol that allows a website to expose its immutable, verified evidence directly to AI agents . A perfect fit with how youths of today consume information. What It Does With WebMCP utlovat.se transforms from a static website into an active, agent-native truth layer. Through WebMCP, an AI assistant using a WebMCP-enabled browser gains access to 7 specialized tools in total (5 global + 2 contextual): Grounded Deterministic Search (search_verified_evidence): Queries exact manifesto commitments, returning verified quotes, publication dates, transparent cost approximations (≈), and linked Wayback Machine archive copies when available (we have set a 100% archive target and are very close to achieving it). Interactive Evidence Boards (build_research_brief): Generates side-by-side comparative cards on /granska and /webmcp without recommending any party. (Absolute neutrality in all aspects are paramount) Human-in-the-Loop Protocol Verification (get_evidence_board_status): Ensures that evidence remains strictly unverified until a human visually inspects the primary citations and marks the board as confirmed. Parliamentary Trail Tracing (trace_promise): Connects a 2026 election promise to Handlingsvågen's (our Swedish feature name) database of reviewed Swedish Parliament (Riksdagen) voting records and motion histories. Multi-Party Fiscal Matrix (show_party_comparison): Opens the interactive comparison matrix on /jamfor, accounting for joint coalition proposals without double-counting costs. Contextual On-Page Tools (trace_current_promise, build_current_question_brief): Dynamically activates contextual tools when browsing individual promise pages or topic questions. Honest Silence & Gap Transparency: Explicitly reports when a party has no recorded stance on a query, rather than treating a bounded empty result as proof of a position. How We Built It We built the WebMCP integration natively into utlovat.se using TypeScript, Astro, and Tailwind CSS: WebMCP Client-Side Tool Registry (site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts): We registered our 7 tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool, defining JSON schemas with strict parameter typing and non-partisan output structures. Cryptographic Data Hashing: Every tool response includes an authoritative data_hash (SHA-256), anchoring conclusions to a fixed, verifiable dataset snapshot. Web Archive Links: When available, a political quote includes a linked Wayback Machine archive copy, making the source trail inspectable and more resilient to link rot. (And also makes it possible to highlight a change in stance in any question). Parliamentary Open Data Bridge: We engineered client-side JSON API endpoints (/api/v1/promise-traces.json) linking election promises to Swedish Parliament document IDs (e.g. data.riksdagen.se/dokument/HB023145) and chamber voting roll calls. Dedicated English Surface (/webmcp): Built a dedicated English hub with the 5 global WebMCP tools, clear testing prompts and cost-range badges. The 2 contextual tools become available after navigation to an individual promise or topic page. Challenges We Faced Enforcing Strict Epistemic Neutrality: The primary challenge in election technology is preventing algorithmic bias. We designed tool descriptions and read-only output structures that explicitly instruct agents not to declare "kept/broken" verdicts, rank parties, or make subjective recommendations. Honest Silence Reporting: In standard RAG pipelines, an empty search return is ambiguous. We had to architect bounded search semantics so that if a party has no promise on a topic, the agent explicitly returns a structured gap report rather than extrapolating. Sometimes silence speaks a thousand words. Zero-Self-Certification for Human-in-the-Loop: We had to ensure agents could not fake human verification. The get_evidence_board_status tool queries the live DOM state, which only transitions to confirmed ✓ when the physical user clicks the inspection button. Anti-Double-Counting in Coalition Manifestos: Calculating joint party proposals required shared commitment keying so coalition proposals are not counted twice in fiscal matrix calculations. New Additions Developed Exclusively During the Hackathon (from August 25, 2026): 1. Prior Work (Before August 25, 2026): The core Swedish public-information website, Utlovat.se. Its foundational dataset of Swedish election commitments and public evidence, including data/promises.json and Handlingsvågen. Existing non-partisan calculations and Swedish public-facing comparison templates. 2. New Additions Developed During the Hackathon (August 25 – September 3, 2026): Browser-native WebMCP integration ( site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts ): Seven read-only client-side tools—five global tools and two page-contextual tools—registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . English Challenge Surface ( site/src/pages/webmcp.astro ): An English entry point, “Evidence, not a verdict,” with a testing guide and direct display of cost ranges marked with ≈ , their basis, and the four-year assumption where applicable. Visible Research Brief and Evidence Board ( /granska , site/src/pages/granska.astro ): A shared human–agent research surface that renders published quotes, dates, source links, archive copies where available, recorded unclear positions, and bounded gaps. It creates deep-linkable research briefs without recommending a party. Human review boundary ( get_evidence_board_status ): The agent can read whether the person has marked the visible evidence board as reviewed, but cannot mark it reviewed itself. Unread material remains explicitly unverified. Parliamentary action tracing ( /api/v1/promise-traces.json ): A read-only evidence chain from a published campaign promise to its source, archive copy, and recorded, human-reviewed parliamentary actions where available. The tool does not decide whether a promise was kept or broken. Automated WebMCP verification ( site/scripts/test-webmcp.mts , site/scripts/test-webmcp-retest.mts ): Tests of the published browser client, tool registration, evidence fields, archive filtering, visible uncertainty, neutral boundaries, English topic matching, shared links, and contextual tools. Open-source licensing : Apache-2.0 was added to the root repository during the hackathon. Frozen competition release : A separate public repository, bambapappa/utlovat-webmcp-challenge , preserves the final static competition build independently of the continuing election-information service. Its manifest records the selected source commit, data hash, and output hashes before the competition cutoff. Transparent implementation history : The public Git history records the WebMCP implementation commits from August 26 onward, while the separate snapshot repository records the freeze and release procedure. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Hackathon premiere: This marks the moment of my first ever participation in a Hackathon. Evidence-Bounded Civic Fact-Checking: WebMCP keeps tool outputs tied to published quotes, source URLs, archive copies when available, and a verifiable data hash. Complete 4-Step Parliamentary Accountability Chain: Users and agents can trace a promise from a party manifesto directly to permanent web archives and the official Riksdag voting prot

Like Comment Story Updates Same request, two outcomes: SeriesSafe preserves all five customized occurrences; a conventional edit loses all five. Inspiration Every calendar app offers "this and following" when you change a repeating event. What it actually does is end the old series and create a new one — and everything you had customised about future occurrences goes with it. This is not our claim. It is how the platforms describe their own behaviour. Google's Calendar API guide implements the change as two requests and states that instances after the target are reset. Microsoft's MS-OXOCAL specification says that when a recurrence pattern changes, future exceptions are cancelled and their exception objects removed. Microsoft's own admin guidance warns organisations about exactly this loss. So when a teacher moves a Tuesday class to Thursday from September, the two public holidays they had cancelled quietly become classes again, the make-up session already moved to a Wednesday disappears, and the guest lecturer's room booking goes with it. Nobody is told. There is no diff, and no undo that brings the exceptions back. What it does You give SeriesSafe an .ics export and an ordinary sentence: "From September, move my Tuesday class to Thursday — but keep the holidays I cancelled, the make-up I already moved, and the guest-lecture room." It reads the series graph behind the calendar grid, re-anchors every future exception onto the new pattern, shows the same request applied two ways — SeriesSafe's way and the conventional way, with the losses itemised — verifies nine invariants against the serialized .ics bytes, and only then makes committing possible. Everything runs in the tab. No calendar account, no upload, no server. How WebMCP is used A calendar UI renders occurrences . The structure that defines them — which Tuesday is a cancellation rather than a gap, which event is a detached override rather than a separate meeting, which ordinal anchors a given exception — is never in the DOM. An agent working from pixels cannot recover it, and cannot tell a silently-lost exception from one that was never there. SeriesSafe registers eleven tools on document.modelContext . Nine are always present; two appear only when they are safe: load_calendar → list_recurring_series → inspect_series → list_series_exceptions → simulate_series_split → stage_series_split → validate_staged_split → commit_staged_split → undo_series_split , plus compare_with_conventional_edit and export_calendar_ics . Two design decisions carry the weight: There is no fix_my_calendar tool. The agent must read the structure, propose a change, look at what the dry run says it would cost, then stage, validate and commit. It has to change course on intermediate results — an unsupported rule part, an override that cannot be re-anchored, an end date that would silently cost a meeting. Dynamic registration is the safety boundary, not a UI state. commit_staged_split is not disabled before validation; it does not exist. Calling it returns "No tool named commit_staged_split is registered right now." After a commit it is withdrawn again and undo_series_split takes its place. This is covered by an automated test. How we built it TypeScript and Vite, no runtime dependencies. An RFC 5545 parser that retains every property it does not understand, so "nothing was lost" is provable rather than aspirational. Recurrence expansion walks the wall clock in the event's own zone and converts each occurrence to UTC separately, so "every Tuesday at 19:00" stays at 19:00 across a DST transition. The core idea is week-anchored alignment : an exception moves to the corresponding slot in the same recurrence week. A cancellation on a Tuesday becomes a cancellation on that week's Thursday, because "that week is off" is indexed by week, not by calendar date. When a week cannot be matched one-to-one, SeriesSafe refuses the change rather than guessing. A detached override is re-anchored the same way but keeps its own start time — a make-up already moved to Wednesday 16 September stays there; only the slot it hangs from moves. That single distinction is what stops it from being either absorbed into the new pattern or duplicated beside it. Challenges An RDATE nearly corrupted every later exception. Explicitly added dates are not part of the recurrence pattern, so counting them in the ordinal shifted every subsequent exception by one week — cancelling the wrong class. Fixed by aligning on pattern slots only. Moving the weekday silently dropped the final meeting. Inheriting a fixed UNTIL while moving Tuesday → Thursday ends the series a week early, because the last Thursday falls before the last Tuesday. Our own validator caught it: "25 kept + 16 moved = 41; originally 42." Rather than pick a behaviour silently, SeriesSafe now exposes the trade-off — preserve-count (default) keeps every meeting and lets the end date shift; keep-end-date is refused when it would cost a class. Both are regression-tested. Put through adversarial review rounds, and every finding reproduced The engine was handed to an independent reviewer with one instruction: find defects, and treat "nothing found" as a failed review. Fourteen rounds followed, each attacking the fixes from the last. Every finding was reproduced by execution here before a line was changed, and each is now a regression test. The first round returned six blocking findings. The common thread was that the headline claim — we prove nothing was lost — was stronger than what the validator actually checked: Across the rounds, the recurring shape was that a check measured something adjacent to what it claimed: A three-year modelling window rewrote a five-year weekly series as a finite run less than two-thirds its length, dropping a cancellation four years out. All eight invariants passed. A UTC series was re-emitted without its Z , becoming floating local time and moving the event for every viewer outside the writer's zone. All eight passed. "Verified byte-for-byte" compared NAME=value and an alarm count , so a reminder retimed from 30 minutes to 5, or an attendee stripped of name, role and status, read as intact. All eight passed. Carrying exceptions by flat position put a Thursday cancellation on the following Monday when the boundary week held a different number of meetings under each rule. All eight passed. FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=1MO was expanded as the first of the month rather than the first Monday — diverging from ical.js — and the edit was approved. An RDATE that coincided with a rule slot was treated as an addition, pulling a real occurrence out of the pattern. Alignment is now anchored to the week rather than a position; expansion follows the rule's own COUNT or UNTIL ; value types are preserved; the fingerprint is a canonical deep comparison including parameters and nested components; and anything the engine cannot expand exactly is refused instead of approximated. The supported surface got narrower and honest: FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=1MO means the first Monday, and an engine that renders it as the first of the month is not entitled to edit it. The second round confirmed seven of those closed — and found that some of the fixes had introduced their own problems. A date boundary derived from one offset lookup landed an hour early across a DST change. The engine had started writing a rule it could not itself expand. And the fix for open-ended series was too strict in the other direction, rejecting 199 of 486 perfectly ordinary moves; it is now an equal-length prefix comparison, and a 405-case sweep across five zones, three week-starts and three intervals passes clean. Rounds three through six continued the same way, each attacking the last round's fixes. The blocking count fell 6, 4, 2, 1, 2, 1 — and the fixes themselves kept needing fixing: the guard against impossible dates began rejecting two legal ones, a leap second and any four-digit year below 0100, which JavaScript maps into the 1900s. Three rounds in a row then found the same shape of bug — something riding on an EXDATE or RDATE going missing — and the reason each one reached the file was that the date lists were never compared at all. Fixing the third instance was not the answer; comparing the lists was. Rounds nine and ten were asked a different question — not "can the output be tampered with undetected" but "does SeriesSafe ever write a wrong calendar from ordinary input" — and that turned out to be the more productive framing. It found seven real defects, two of them in the headline demo. The sample's guest lecture, which changed room but was never rescheduled, was being left on the old Tuesday while its anchor moved to the new Thursday. The most instructive finding came last: three defects lived in code paths the README had already declared out of sco
video_transcript_excerpt: This is a language school's calendar, a weekly Tuesday class running from March to December. Over the term, the teacher canceled public holidays, moved one session to Wednesday as a makeup, and booked a different room for a guest lecture. Now the timetable changes. From September, Tuesday becomes Thursday. In Google Calendar or Outlook, you would choose this and following, and those future exceptions would be silently thrown away. That is documented behavior. Google's API guide says following instance changes reset later exceptions, and Microsoft's protocol removes them when the recurrence pattern changes. This page exposes the calendar structure to an agent through Web MCP. Watch the eight tool calls. It loads the calendar, lists the series, inspects the rule, and asks specifically what is at risk after the 1st of September. It simulates before it touches anything. Here is the result. The same request applied two ways. Series safe preserves five things. A conventional this and following edit destroys all five. Both counts are read back from the resulting calendar files, not predicted. It also caught something subtler. Moving Tuesday to Thursday while keeping the old end date required cost a class because the last Thursday falls after the old end. The default keeps every meeting and explains the shifted end date. Ask it to hold the original date instead, and it refuses. Nothing was changed. It would rather decline than produce a calendar it cannot vouch for. Before committing, it checks nine invariants against the actual serialized ICS bytes, not its own plan. The past is untouched. Cancellations stay cancelled. Overrides survive exactly once at their own time. And attendees, alarms, and private properties carry across. Before validation, commit stage split is not disabled. The tool does not exist. Only after all nine checks pass does it appear in the registry. The class is now on Thursdays. The holiday cancellations moved to the correct Thursday slots. The makeup is still Wednesday, September 16th, not absorbed and not duplicated. The guest lecture is Thursday, October 22nd, with its room intact. Five things a normal calendar edit would have destroyed are still here. With one click undo. Series safe. Save weekly ICS surgery entirely in your browser. Exposed through web MCP and MIT licensed.

title: WEBMCP
pitch: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates One button, one autonomous pass over twelve open procurement notices. No further human input. Seven tools registered through document.modelContext. Every agent call is mirrored on the right, in the human view. Every criterion ruled met / gap / unclear with its evidence, four integrity flags with their reasoning, and a dated bid plan. An agent raised the bid ceiling through update_supplier_profile and the board re-ranked live: this notice moved 17 to 41. The board ranked by fit, with the reasoning trace beside it: every tool call, its output and its latency. Inspiration Across the EU roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else — a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. TenderLens does that pass. The WebMCP layer is what lets somebody else's agent do it too, on the same page, in front of the human it is working for. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. For every open notice the agent opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board — 87 down to 17 across twelve notices — and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The full reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen is five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: SHORT_WINDOW , THIN_COMPETITION , VENDOR_CONCENTRATION , SPEC_LOCK and INCUMBENT_LOCK . None is presented as proof of wrongdoing. Each carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bid/no-bid is a conversation, not a query. The questions a bid manager actually asks are open-ended and chained — what closes this week that we can actually win? which of those look rigged? what would we qualify for if our turnover were three million instead of one-point-eight? — and every answer changes the next question. That is exactly the shape of work an agent is good at and a filter UI is bad at. But it is also work with consequences. A supplier who skips a tender because an agent said "weak fit" has lost a contract on the strength of a sentence. So the human has to stay in the room, looking at the same board the agent is reasoning over. WebMCP is the only arrangement that gives you both. The tools live on the page the human is already looking at. The agent gets typed JSON — fit scores, verdicts with evidence strings, flags with rationale — instead of scraped DOM text, and every call it makes is mirrored into a panel on that page, in the human's field of view, while the board itself re-ranks in front of them. No API key, no OAuth handshake, no separate agent-facing copy of the product to drift out of sync. How it creates a better user experience Three things change: You ask, instead of filtering. "Show me everything closing inside ten days with an integrity flag" is one sentence. In the UI it is four controls and a sort. You can see what the agent did. Every tool call appears in the Agent activity panel with its arguments and a one-line result. The verdict is auditable in the moment, not after the fact. The page answers with the page. search_notices outlines the matching rows on the board. update_supplier_profile re-ranks it live. The agent's answer and the human's screen are the same object, so there is nothing to reconcile. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The what-if is the one that did not exist. update_supplier_profile lets the agent change the profile every notice is scored against — turnover, headcount, certificates, capability areas, bid ceiling — and the entire board re-ranks in the human's browser while they watch. Ask "what would an ISO 27001 certificate be worth to us?" and you do not get an estimate; you get the actual board you would have had, recomputed by the real engine, with the notices that moved outlined. That is a joint action. The agent supplies the question and the argument, the page supplies the ground truth and the recomputation, and the human sees both at once and decides. Before WebMCP you got one or the other: a chatbot that could reason but only about text you had pasted to it, or a dashboard that held the truth but could not be asked anything. The same applies to the integrity work. A journalist can now walk an agent across a portal — screen these, tell me which buyers concentrate awards — and every claim the agent makes is anchored to a screen_integrity call whose output is sitting on screen next to the claim. How I implemented WebMCP Seven tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , in edge/webmcp.ts : tool what it does search_notices rank open notices by fit; filter by category, country, days left, fit band, or integrity flags get_notice one notice in full: every criterion with its verdict and evidence, flags, bid plan, optional raw dossier screen_integrity the five single-bidder detectors with the reasoning behind each flag get_bid_plan dated plan worked backwards from the deadline, owner on every step get_supplier_profile the profile every notice is scored against update_supplier_profile change the profile and re-rank the board — the what-if tool run_sweep the whole pass over every notice, returning the ranked board Each registration carries a real JSON Schema — enums, descriptions and required fields on every property — because the schema is the only instruction the visiting agent gets. Every execute returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(...) }] } , so the shape holds across clients. Three implementation decisions are worth naming: Tools call the product, not a demo path. Each execute hits the same /api/notices , /api/notice/:id and /api/profile endpoints the page itself uses. There is no agent-facing copy that can drift out of sync with what the human sees. Every call is visible. record() writes each invocation — name, arguments, one-line result — into the Agent activity panel on the page. Tool calls also act on the view: search_notices outlines matching rows, update_supplier_profile and run_sweep re-rank the board. Writes are validated, not trusted. update_supplier_profile goes through applyProfilePatch in edge/agentapi.ts , which range-checks every field and ignores anything it does not recognise. An agent can explore the profile space; it cannot corrupt it. Registration degrades cleanly. If document.modelContext is absent the pill reads "WebMCP not detected" and the page works as an ordinary web app. The tools are also exposed on window.__TL_TOOLS__ , and every tool in the list has a run button beside it that fires the identical execute() — so a judge without a WebMCP-enabled browser can still see each tool run and log its result. How I built the rest TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the agent itself runs as a Supabase Edge Function on Deno. The front end is a single static page on GitHub Pages that talks to that function over CORS-open JSON and SSE, which keeps the page a plain document a judge or an agent can open with nothing in the way. The agent core — orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types — depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and the Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board. The side effect is that the hosted demo runs with zero API keys — which is also why a judge can open it, and a visiting agent can use every

title: Floorplay
pitch: A floor plan you and your agent edit together, in 2D and 3D, doorways included.
about_excerpt: A floor plan you and your agent edit together, in 2D and 3D, doorways included. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I've moved apartments four times and every time the same thing happens. I open a chat, describe the room, get a nice paragraph about "creating a cozy reading nook by the window", and then I stand in the room with a tape measure and none of it fits. The bed blocks the door. The desk is in the dark corner. Meanwhile the planner apps that can actually draw a room have no idea what I asked for. So the idea was pretty simple: put the drawing and the agent in the same place. Not a chat with a picture attached. A real plan that an AI agent can read and change, next to me, while I drag things around too. What it does Floorplay is a room designer where you and an AI agent work on the same floor plan. On the left there's a plan that looks like something an architect would hand you: grid, thick wall bands with the doors and windows cut out, swing arcs, dimensions. On the right the same room in 3D, and you can walk through it at eye height. Eight rooms come already furnished because staring at an empty rectangle is the worst part of any planner. There's a catalog of 139 pieces with real sizes and prices. The whole room is exposed to the agent as WebMCP tools. Sixty of them, plus four that show up only while you have something selected. It can read the plan, ask where a bed would fit, place and move things, paint a wall, resize the room, cut a window, move the camera, or lay out a whole option. When it proposes a layout you see it as ghosts on the drawing with a little card. Hover to preview, accept or reject. Everything else it does lands straight on the plan, goes into a ledger next to your own edits, and any step can be reverted. Late in the week I added homes. You can put rooms next to each other on one sheet, they snap edge to edge and refuse to overlap, and if you cut a doorway through a shared wall it opens in both rooms. Then you can walk from the living room into the bedroom in 3D. The part I like most is small. Ask the agent "what do I see from the door?" and the camera actually walks to the door and the answer comes from what is in that view. No guessing. How we built it It's a Vite + React + TypeScript app, no backend, three.js for the 3D through react-three-fiber. I built it in three days with an AI coding agent doing most of the typing and me doing most of the complaining. Underneath there's a plain TypeScript engine that doesn't know the UI exists. It computes footprints and overlaps, whether a door can swing, whether you can reach everything, walkway width on a 10 cm grid, a rough daylight model, budget, and it can invert every operation so undo is exact. Homes sit on top of that: snapping, overlap checks, and a doorway stored as one record that owns an opening in two rooms. The WebMCP part registers every tool on document.modelContext with a schema and a readOnlyHint where it applies. The selection tools live in their own group behind an AbortController, so when you click a different chair the old group is torn down and a new one registered. All the editing tools share one write path, which means they all answer the same way: what happened, what's now broken, the new numbers. That turned out to matter more than anything else I did. Since most browsers don't have document.modelContext yet, the app has a fake one built in and a dev panel (Cmd+Shift+D) where you can call any tool by hand. Honestly that's where I spent most of the time. There are 309 tests and a Playwright script that runs the real app through 44 screenshots. Challenges we ran into The first time I opened the DevTools WebMCP panel it was empty. Every tool registered without an error, and Chrome just didn't list any. It took most of an afternoon to learn the page needs to be origin isolated, which is two headers ( Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) ). Two lines in the Vercel config. At the start the agent placed furniture by guessing coordinates and it was awful. I tried writing better tool descriptions and it barely helped. What helped was giving it real answers: a suggest_positions tool that returns ranked spots with a reason for each, and every edit reporting the violations it caused. Once it could see that the bed now blocks the door, it fixed it on its own. When I added homes, the walls between rooms poked into each other's floors, because each room draws its walls just outside its own rectangle. Fine alone, wrong the moment two rooms touch. Now a shared wall is drawn as two halves, one on each side of the line. I also built a "Propose first" switch that turned every agent edit into a card you had to approve. It sounded responsible. In practice it just made the agent feel slow, and undo already covers the risk, so I took it out again the same day. And on the last day I noticed you couldn't move a window at all. Not by dragging, not from the editor, not from a tool. Nobody had ever needed to during testing. That's fixed now. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can do anything I can do in the app. It never has to say "please click this for me". The plan looks like a drawing, not a toy. Early versions looked like they were built for kids and that bothered me more than any bug. Homes with doorways. Cutting one door and seeing it appear in both rooms, then walking through it in 3D, was the moment the project felt done. What we learned The number of tools is a vanity metric. What the tools return is what changes the agent's behaviour. Give it computed facts in every answer and it stops needing instructions. Selection-scoped tools are worth the setup. "Move the thing the user just clicked" removes a whole class of wrong-id mistakes. And an agent dropped into a page needs the same thing a new colleague does: a short tour. There's a get_guide tool for exactly that. What's next for Floorplay The Buy tab already lets the agent find where to buy each piece you don't own. Real store listings and price tracking would make that useful for real. After that: more home templates, more than one floor, and a share link so two people and one agent can work on the same flat. title: FlowLens
pitch: Workflow intelligence, in focus
about_excerpt: Workflow intelligence, in focus Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration FlowLens was built for the WebMCP hackathon to solve a core problem in automation debugging: most debuggers require humans to manually translate visual context back into text. We wanted to turn human focus into a typed, temporary tool surface where selecting a failed execution path automatically bounds the evidence an agent can inspect, enabling precise diagnosis and safe repairs without copying node IDs, payloads, or timestamps. What it does FlowLens is a deterministic workflow flight recorder that allows operations specialists to: Run automation workflows and visualize execution traces on an interactive canvas Select exact failed execution paths (normalization and condition steps) Expose selection-bound WebMCP tools that capture immutable run, step, node, selection, and workflow versions Let browser agents inspect bounded evidence and propose the smallest safe repair Preview patches with visible diffs before any mutation occurs Apply approved patches with single-use tokens, rerun fixtures, and prove results with before-and-after comparisons Maintain a complete audit trail with undo capability The hero defect demonstrates a subtle bug: normalization emits customer.segment while the condition reads customer.tier , causing VIP customers to reach the standard queue without throwing errors. How we built it FlowLens is a static React application built with: React + TypeScript for type-safe component architecture @xyflow/react for the interactive workflow canvas with finite node types Vite for fast development and production builds Zod for strict JSON Schema validation Lucide React for consistent iconography @polar-sh/checkout for embedded Pro feature paywall The architecture follows a clean domain-driven design: Domain layer ( src/domain/ ) contains workflow types, validation, simulation, patches, and redaction Application layer ( src/app/ ) manages state through a typed reducer with command facade Feature layer ( src/features/ ) provides canvas, header, panel, paywall, and sidebar components WebMCP adapter ( src/webmcp/ ) handles dynamic tool registration with AbortController cleanup The deterministic simulator traverses directed graphs producing bounded trace steps without real side effects. The repair engine accepts only restricted operations (like replace_condition_field ) with preview, approval tokens, version guards, and reversible history. Challenges we ran into WebMCP API evolution : The specification was still evolving, requiring feature detection for both document.modelContext and optional toolchange events independently Selection lifecycle complexity : Managing selection-bound tools that need to abort on workflow edits, selection changes, or component unmounts required careful AbortController coordination Security boundaries : Implementing bounded outputs, secret-like field redaction, version guards, and single-use approval tokens while maintaining usability Deterministic simulation : Building a simulator that produces realistic traces without actual side effects, queues, or network operations Paywall integration : Balancing a local admin bypass for demo purposes with production-grade Polar checkout that requires trusted backend authentication Accomplishments that we're proud of Complete WebMCP integration : Successfully implemented 16 tools (10 base, 4 selection-bound, 1 approval, 1 conditional undo) following Chrome security guidance Deterministic testing : 19/19 Vitest unit tests and 2/2 Playwright E2E tests passing, including real in-app WebMCP calls Apple-inspired UI : Dark graphite interface with glassy chrome, crisp hierarchy, restrained color, and reduced-motion support Safe mutation model : Non-mutating preview, visible diffs, human approval, single-use tokens, and reversible history Production-ready build : TypeScript strict mode passing, static bundle deployable to Vercel or any static host Comprehensive documentation : Architecture, security model, WebMCP inventory, and eval corpus all documented What we learned WebMCP patterns : The imperative API requires careful lifecycle management—tools must register dynamically, capture closure state, and clean up with AbortController Selection as context : Turning visual selection into typed API boundaries is more powerful than traditional copy-paste debugging Deterministic simulation : A bounded simulator can provide sufficient evidence for diagnosis without requiring real integrations Security by design : Version guards, bounded outputs, and single-use tokens prevent many classes of attacks while maintaining usability Static architecture : A well-designed static app can deliver complex functionality without backend dependencies What's next for FlowLens Additional workflow types : Expand beyond the CRM escalation hero flow to support more automation patterns Richer patch DSL : Add more safe operations beyond replace_condition_field while maintaining boundedness Authentication backend : Implement trusted server authentication with Polar webhook verification for production entitlements Multiplayer collaboration : Enable shared workspaces with real-time collaboration on workflow debugging Advanced analytics : Add workflow performance insights, failure pattern detection, and optimization suggestions Expanded WebMCP coverage : Support additional WebMCP features as the specification evolves Built With node.js typescript webmcp Try it out flowlens.quytn-ebuy.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Hector Ta Like Share this project: Updates Hector Ta title: Your AI Can Now Choose Your Health Tests: medtests webmcp
pitch: Your AI can now discover the right health screening, ask the right questions, and guide you through it — using WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Your AI can now discover the right health screening, ask the right questions, and guide you through it — using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI can already talk about your symptoms. But when it needs a structured screening tool, the experience breaks. 

 You leave the conversation, search for a test, complete it on another website, then bring the result back. 

 We wanted to remove that gap. 

 What if a health website wasn't just readable by an AI — but actually usable by it? 

 What it does 

 Medtests makes structured health screening tools available to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 An agent can discover available screenings, retrieve the questions, guide the user through them, score the answers, and return the structured result. 

 For example, instead of only answering: 

 "Could these symptoms be ADHD?" 

 an AI can use Medtests to start a relevant screening flow and guide the user through it. 

 The user doesn't have to figure out which page to open or copy information between an AI and a website. 

 How we built it 

 We turned Medtests from a traditional website into an agent-accessible website using WebMCP. 

 The browser exposes five tools: 

 
 list_screenings 
 get_screening 
 score_screening 
 get_crisis_resources 
 get_chat_analysis_protocol 
 

 The tools are registered through the browser's WebMCP interface using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 The application is written in JavaScript and deployed on Cloudflare Workers with Wrangler, with deployment through GitHub. 

 The important architectural decision was simple: 

 Instead of building another chatbot, we made the website itself callable by AI agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Health screening is a good example of why agent interfaces need structure. 

 An agent shouldn't have to scrape a webpage and guess what a button, question, or score means. 

 We had to turn human-facing interactions into explicit tools with predictable inputs and outputs, while keeping the existing website useful for humans. 

 We also had to separate screening from diagnosis. Medtests provides structured screening tools and results — not medical diagnoses. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working WebMCP layer on top of a real health website. 

 The same resource can now serve two users: 

 Humans can use the website. Agents can use the tools. 

 No separate AI product is required. 

 That is the part we're most excited about. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes what a website can be. 

 For the last 30 years, websites have primarily exposed interfaces for humans: pages, forms and buttons. 

 Agents need something different: capabilities with names, schemas and structured results. 

 Once those capabilities exist, the website stops being something an AI merely reads. 

 It becomes something the AI can use. 

 What's next 

 Medtests is the first use case. 

 The bigger idea is to make useful parts of the web agent-native — so an AI can move from explaining what someone could do to actually helping them do it. 

 The web was built for humans to click. WebMCP lets agents act.

title: Erwin's Survival
pitch: A jungle survival browser co-op game where you explore, gather resources, build a base and an external AI agent places base defenses through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A jungle survival browser co-op game where you explore, gather resources, build a base and an external AI agent places base defenses through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Game Overview Day time resource collection by player Dusk time base defenses setup by external ai agent using webMCP Night time base defense from red slime enemies. Game win screen Game lost screen when Erwin's health drops to zero Inspiration Every WebMCP demo we saw was a dashboard or a form filler. We wanted to build something where the AI had to act, not just read. A survival game where the human explores and the AI plans defenses felt right. The first version had the AI doing everything through WebMCP tools (gather water, eat food, chop wood). That was boring. Typing "gather water" to an AI when a key press does the same thing is unnecessary friction. We pivoted so the AI only acts at dusk, for defense planning. What it does A browser survival game with two players: a human and an external AI agent. They cooperate through WebMCP tools. Three game phases, repeating for 3 days: Phase Who acts What happens Morning Human (keyboard) Cut jungle, collect wood/stone/rope/herbs/berries/water, make medicine, build base. Dusk AI agent (WebMCP) Read threat intel, place spike traps, barricades, fires around the base. Night Human (keyboard) Aim bow, fire arrows at incoming slimes, repair barricades. Win condition: Survive 3 nights. Base still standing. Lose condition: Base destroyed (night) or health hits 0 (morning). WebMCP tools exposed: Tool When available What it does get_game_state Always Returns health, inventory, position, defenses, phase get_planning_context Dusk only Returns expected monsters, defense options with costs place_spike_trap({side}) Dusk only 2 wood + 1 stone. Kills up to 2 slimes. One use. build_barricade({side}) Dusk only 3 wood. Blocks slimes. 3 durability. Survives across nights. set_fire({side}) Dusk only 1 wood + 1 herbs. Kills 1 slime per wave. Lasts 1 night. Tools auto register at dusk and auto unregister when night falls. The AI must act within a 90-second window to plan base defense during dusk. Example scenario: The AI reads get_planning_context , sees "Night 1, 4 slimes expected from 2 sides," then calls place_spike_trap and build_barricade with {side: "north"} or {side: "south"} . Each call costs resources and updates the game map live. The first night has 4 slimes, second has 6 and third night having 9. Each dusk, the AI replans before night falls. Why WebMCP Why this use case fits WebMCP: The dusk phase is a planning problem with multiple variables: 4 sides to defend, 3 defense types, limited resources, player health and a different number of enemies each night. A player with keyboard cannot solve that in 90 seconds but if they use Natural Language with an external AI agent - the possibilities start to open up. WebMCP lets the game expose the board as challenges to overcome via tools, and any external AI agent can pick them up. How it creates a better user experience: Without the AI, the player would need a separate UI for defense placement: dropdown menus for side selection, buttons for each defense type, a cost calculator all on top of a ticking time countdown. With WebMCP, the player says "plan the defense" or "gives a short braindump of the defense" and the AI handles all of it. The game becomes one where the player and external ai agent are dependent on one another. What was impossible before: A browser game could not hand off a planning decision to an external AI mid-session. The AI had no way to read game state or call game functions. WebMCP added that channel. Now the game exposes get_planning_context and the AI reads it, decides, and acts, all within the same browser tab the player is using. How we built it Solo build over 3 days (Sept 1-3, 2026). Vanilla JS + HTML Canvas + Vite. No React or other frameworks used. Direct registerTool() / unregisterTool() calls. Deployed on Vercel as a single page site. There is no backend. Feature detection for both ChatGPT and Chrome: navigator.modelContext ?? document.modelContext . Tested with Chrome 152 WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector extension from Chrome Web Store (offered by François Beaufort). Day 1: Nailed the project requirements, architecture, full game loop (move, health decay, fog of war, inventory, win/lose). Day 2: The pivot to dropping AI-driven resource gathering and addition of morning/dusk/night phases. The external AI agent comes in during dusk time. Day 3: Defense WebMCP tools, night combat with animated slimes, arrows, bow sprites, visual polish (cabin, roads, defense art, pond tiles, animated jungle). Challenges we ran into The first design had the AI call gather_water and eat_food via WebMCP. It worked but was also pointless since a keyboard press does the same thing faster. Scrapped on day 2. ChatGPT uses document.modelContext while Chrome uses navigator.modelContext . So we used a one line of feature detection. Spritesheets from different artists use different layouts (rows vs. columns for direction). Erwin faced north in all 4 directions until we checked the actual pixel layout. We drew red gridlines over the spritesheet to map which column was which direction. Column 0 was north, column 2 was south, and columns 1 and 3 were mirrors of each other, so we located the eye pixels to tell east from west. The timer variable was decremented twice per tick — once at the top of the loop and again inside the action branch. Deleting the second decrement fixed the 4-second window, but that exposed a second bug: arrows now had time to fly, and fast frames made them skip over slimes without hitting. We fixed that by moving arrows in small 0.34-tile sub-steps and testing for a hit at each one. Procedural map generation rules fought each other. Trails carved through jungle, then jungle rings around resources closed the trails. Fixed by ordering the generation steps. Accomplishments that we're proud of The dusk phase works where the player(human) must tell the AI "plan the defense" and barricades, spike traps, and fires appear on the map as they watch. The game went from colored squares to pixel art with animated jungle canopy, slime enemies, a cabin, and a bow. All of this was achieved in one day. We really Locked In for this one. The 5 WebMCP tools with parameterized inputs, real resource costs, and phase-based registration/unregistration. Complete 3-day loop start to finish, playable without an AI agent via debug panel fallback. The pivot decision on day 2: AI plans strategy, human presses buttons. That separation made both halves better and got them to work together. What we learned WebMCP is best when the AI does what a keyboard cannot. For games, this meant getting the AI to plan, in a short window, where it needs to consider multiple factors such as expected enemies, player health and inventory. Tool quality over tool count. 5 tools with a clear lifecycle loop where each tool has an impact. A bug can hide behind a feature that is too fast to expose it. Adding arrow flight time surfaced a timing bug that instant shooting never triggered We started with CC0 Kenney tiles (free, safe to redistribute). Two paid packs we liked said "redistribution prohibited," so we dropped them. The final mix was one free character sprite (nogardlab Stardew Farm) and three ToffeeCraft packs ($3.20 total) that allowed redistribution. Different artists, different styles, but a character always stands out from terrain, so the mismatch was not noticeable. What's next for Erwin's Survival Sound effects for resource collection, defense placement, slime attacks Slime attack animation when they reach the barricade Mobile touch controls Procedural map generation Leaderboard for fastest 3-night survival More defense types (walls, moats) The pattern behind the game This game shows a co-op pattern that works beyond games. The pattern Game example Real-world example Human browses structured data Erwin explores the jungle A doctor reviews patient charts AI reads state through tools get_planning_context returns threat intel AI reads lab results, medications, allergies AI acts through parameterized tools place_spike_trap({side: "north"}) AI orders a specific test or flags a drug interaction Tools register based on context Defense tools appear at dusk, disappear at night Prescription tools appear when viewing a patient, disappear on the dashboard Neither can finish alone Human collects resources, AI places them Doctor knows the patient, AI catches what they might miss WebMCP makes this possible. The website exposes tools. The AI discovers and calls them. The human stays in control. The game is the demo. The pattern is the point. title: My Calendar Planner
pitch: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times.
about_excerpt: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Scheduling meetings with large teams can be a pain, even when everyone is available. When you need to account for different schedules, locations, time zones, focus time, or other factors, things can get unwieldy very quickly. Existing assistants often force people to choose between manually coordinating everything and granting broad write access. We wanted to show a better default: give the agent just enough structured context to help, then keep the final decision visible and human-owned. What it does MyCP is a seeded shared-calendar demo for a distributed launch team. A browser agent uses WebMCP tools to inspect narrowly scoped context, find one-time or weekly availability, and rank meeting options. A weekly proposal checks every requested occurrence against private busy time, protected focus blocks, work patterns, travel buffers, and time preferences without revealing why another person is unavailable. When one weekly check-in conflicts with the manager’s existing meeting, it can stage one bounded reschedule for that instance without moving the existing event. The same pattern works for time away: the agent can prepare one compact change-set draft containing a private absence, proposed cancellation of the manager’s owned meetings, and a transfer to an approved delegate. It cannot apply any of those changes or send notifications. The person reviews a before/after diff in the calendar, opens a confirmation dialog, and explicitly adds the event. That API path requires the reviewed draft revision, a five-minute one-time confirmation, and an idempotency key. Private events remain generic Busy blocks outside the owner’s access. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite for the calendar interface. A Cloudflare Worker for static assets, same-origin API routes, and the WebMCP headers. Cloudflare D1 for persistent seeded-demo state with revision-checked writes. Zod schemas shared at the command boundary. WebMCP imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Vitest coverage for scheduling, redaction, draft lifecycle, confirmation, idempotency, and rate limits. WebMCP Usage MyCP registers fourteen intent-level tools rather than exposing DOM selectors or database access. get_calendar_context provides bounded calendar/team identifiers, while get_user_scheduling_profile reads a purpose-limited profile with meeting preferences, recurring focus blocks, and office/remote work patterns—never a home address, live location, or private events. propose_recurring_schedule validates one weekly local-time slot across 2–26 occurrences and can return no more than four explicit, reviewable exceptions. get_events_in_range and propose_time_away_changes return only active events the user owns, while create_time_away_change_set_draft can only stage—not apply—cancellations and approved-delegate transfers. Read tools are annotated as read-only. Tool outputs carrying calendar content are marked untrusted and limited to 1.4 KB of UTF-8 data; the adapter returns compact events and candidate slots, or a safe truncation response. commit_event is intentionally blocked so an agent cannot bypass the human confirmation flow. Challenges we ran into The key challenge was making the agent useful without making it overly powerful. We separated recommendation, draft creation, and final commit; applied server-side ownership and revision checks; and designed bounded result shapes that still give an agent enough information to continue safely. Persisting the deterministic demo across Worker isolates also required an explicit D1 persistence boundary rather than relying on in-memory state. Accomplishments that we're proud of From a design standpoint, it took some time to really hone in on what would make this tool useful. At first it was basically a scheduling assistant that didn't do much more than what Outlook can do now. However, once I started experimenting with recurring meetings that need occasional alterations, I realized that there are scenarios I run into all the time in real life that MyCP would actually help with. What we learned I mostly got a much better understanding of what could be possible with WebMCP and I'm already thinking of other ways to implement it in my day job. What's next for My Calendar Planner One area where this tool could be incredibly useful is with room management as well as meeting management. Bringing in systems to manage space bookings and maintenance in a large organization, like a university, could really help alleviate pain-points for scheduling that involve lots of difference factors. From a technical standpoint, we could add real authentication, provider OAuth, per-user notification preferences, RSVP-aware recurrence exceptions, delegate acceptance, outbound notifications, and a normalized D1 schema. Those additions would preserve the same visible-draft and explicit-confirmation boundaries.
