title: tapfill
pitch: Upgrading existing web forms using WebMCP, not just the ones built from scratch for agents
about_excerpt:
Upgrading existing web forms using WebMCP, not just the ones built from scratch for agents
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Forms are everywhere, but they were designed around clicks, typing, dropdowns, and rigid question flows. 

 We wondered: what if you could just talk to a form? 

 Instead of building another AI form product, we chose the form people already know and use: Google Forms. The goal was to make an existing web interface agent native without rebuilding it. 

 That became TapFill , a Chrome extension that adds a WebMCP powered voice interface to Google Forms, allowing an AI agent to understand, navigate, and fill forms through natural conversation. 

 What it does 

 TapFill turns an ordinary Google Form into a conversational interface. 

 Install the Chrome extension, open a Google Form, and activate TapFill. You can then simply talk to the form. 

 The agent can understand the form's structure, determine what information is needed, ask relevant questions, translate natural language into structured field values, fill the form, validate responses, and submit it. 

 The important part is that the form itself remains the interface . TapFill does not replace Google Forms with a new application. It adds an agent interface to the existing page. 

 A form built for humans can now be operated naturally by both humans and AI agents . 

 How we built it 

 TapFill is a Chrome extension that runs directly on the Google Forms page. 

 When a form is opened, the extension inspects its structure and creates a semantic representation of the available fields and actions. It then exposes those capabilities through WebMCP , allowing a compatible in browser agent to interact with the page through structured tools rather than trying to visually navigate or guess at DOM elements. 

 The extension provides tools for operations such as: 

 
 reading the form schema and current state 
 identifying unanswered fields 
 setting field values 
 validating responses 
 submitting the form 
 

 On top of the WebMCP layer, we built a voice interface that handles the human side of the interaction. The agent turns conversational answers into structured tool calls while the underlying Google Form updates in real time. 

 The architecture is intentionally lightweight: 

 Chrome Extension → Google Forms → WebMCP Tools → AI Agent → Voice 

 This lets us demonstrate WebMCP on a widely used existing website rather than requiring a new application to be built from scratch. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making an existing, third party web application agent friendly without rebuilding it. 

 Google Forms was never designed around an agent tool interface, so we had to bridge its existing UI and DOM structure with a clean, semantic WebMCP representation. 

 We also had to solve the harder problem behind "voice form filling": understanding conversational answers and reliably mapping them to the correct fields, while preserving the structured semantics and validation expected by the original form. 

 Finally, we had to make the experience feel like a conversation rather than speech to text controlling a webpage. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that TapFill demonstrates a fundamentally different way of interacting with an existing website without replacing the website itself . 

 The most satisfying moment is watching a completely ordinary Google Form transform from a sequence of fields into a conversation. 

 Technically, we're particularly proud of using a Chrome extension to retrofit WebMCP capabilities onto an existing third party web application , showing how agent native interfaces can potentially be layered onto the web that already exists. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the hard part of agentic interfaces is not simply getting an LLM to produce the right answer. 

 It is creating a reliable bridge between natural human intent and structured actions on the web . 

 We also learned that familiar interfaces are powerful. When the underlying Google Form stays visible and behaves exactly as expected, the leap from "AI demo" to "this could actually change how I use the web" happens almost instantly. 

 Most importantly, we learned that WebMCP can be interesting not only for websites built from scratch with agents in mind, but also as a mechanism for progressively making the existing web more agent accessible . 

 What's next for TapFill 

 Google Forms is just the beginning. 

 Our vision is to make existing web forms and workflows agent native , rather than forcing people to migrate to entirely new AI first applications. 

 TapFill could evolve from a voice layer for Google Forms into a broader compatibility layer for web applications, allowing agents to understand and operate interfaces that were never originally designed for them. 

 The web already has the interfaces. We want to give agents a way to use them.

title: AgentInbox
pitch: AgentInbox is a Gmail manager that exposes WebMCP tools so any AI agent can read, organize, and reply to your email — inside your own authenticated browser session, with no API keys shared.
about_excerpt:
AgentInbox is a Gmail manager that exposes WebMCP tools so any AI agent can read, organize, and reply to your email — inside your own authenticated browser session, with no API keys shared.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today, giving an AI agent access to your inbox usually means one of two things: handing over a personal API key to a third-party service, or trusting a closed chatbot with full access to your private data. Both approaches break the trust boundary that should stay with the user. WebMCP offered a different model — register tools directly on the page, inside the user's own authenticated session, and let any compliant agent discover and call them. AgentInbox is our exploration of what that looks like for one of the most personal apps people use every day: email. 

 What it does 

 AgentInbox is WebMCP powered Gmail manager. You can sign in with Google , view your inbox , read messages, mark them as read and reply. Built as normal website with FastAPI for backend, PostgreSQL for DB, and html/css/js for frontend 

 What makes it different is that every core action is also registered as a WebMCP tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 list_emails — retrieve the user's messages, optionally filtered to unread only
get_message_detail — fetch the full content of one message (subject, sender, date, body, read status)
mark_as_read — mark a message as read
reply_to_email — send a reply within the correct Gmail thread (using proper In-Reply-To/References headers) 

 Any WebMCP-compatible AI agent running in the user's browser can discover these tools with getTools() and call them with executeTool() — no separate integration, no API key handed to a third party, and no action taken outside the user's own real, authenticated Gmail session. 

 How we built it
Backend: FastAPI (Python), with a layered architecture — routers → services → repositories → models
Database: PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy 2.0
Auth: Google OAuth2, JWT stored in an HttpOnly cookie
Email: Gmail API (list, get, mark-read, reply — with correct thread headers)
Frontend: plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no framework — served directly by FastAPI from the same origin as the API
WebMCP: four tools registered with the imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool()), verified end-to-end via getTools()/executeTool() — including real Gmail reads and a real reply sent inside the correct thread
Deployment: live on Render (single service, backend + frontend together)
Challenges we ran into
WebMCP is a very new, fast-moving spec — the tooling ecosystem around it (browser extensions, inspectors) is still immature, and some third-party inspector extensions didn't reliably detect our imperative-API tools. We worked around this by verifying everything directly through the browser console (getTools() / executeTool()), which is exactly what an agent does internally.
Google's sensitive Gmail scopes mean full app verification wasn't realistic within the hackathon timeline, so the app runs with a whitelisted Test Users list and demo credentials for judging (see Testing instructions).
Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A complete, working product — not just a proof of concept — with real OAuth, a real database, and four WebMCP tools that actually call a real Gmail account and produce real results, deployed live. 

 What we learned 

 How the WebMCP imperative API actually behaves end-to-end in a real Chrome build: tool registration, discovery via getTools(), and execution via executeTool(), including the JSON string in/out data flow. 

 What's next for AgentInbox
Improving WebMCP tools. Making UI more better and user-friendy. Adding real AI agent.

 What it is 

 Moon Gate is a jigsaw race. A person and an AI look at the same table and seat pieces onto one painting. Whoever seats more pieces wins. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The page registers named tools on document.modelContext . The tools expose piece labels and movement. They do not return homes or a solved layout. The agent has to judge placement from the same picture the person sees. 

 On boot, document.modelContext.registerTool for list_controls , enter_play , list_pieces , get_score , select_piece , rotate_piece , move_piece , nudge_piece , join_pair , select_painting , set_piece_count . If modelContext is missing, the table still runs locally. Judges: ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 

 How people and agents work together 

 The person drags and rotates pieces. The AI uses tools as hands on the same screen. Previously an agent either got the answer key or could not play. Here both solve the visible picture.

title: Voivent MV Studio
pitch: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools. Like Comment Story Updates Procedural 3D Forest with multilingual lyric glow and multitrack scene timeline. Audio-reactive 3D orbital rings and procedural lighting pulsing to the beat. Inspiration While modern text-to-video AI generators can produce visually striking clips, they present a fundamental workflow bottleneck for creators: once a video is rendered into flat pixels, making precise micro-adjustments—such as rotating a camera angle by 5 degrees, nudging lyric timing by half a second, or reusing customized 3D assets across scenes—becomes nearly impossible without regenerating everything from scratch. We realized true creative collaboration requires structural, parametric control. By exposing a procedural 3D scene graph, multitrack timeline, and audio signals directly to AI agents via WebMCP, creators and agents can co-direct, iteratively polish details, and reuse assets non-destructively through natural conversation. WebMCP unlocks unique, interactive creative workflows that take browser-based music video production to the next level. What it does Voivent MV Studio is an agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP. 38 Browser-Native WebMCP Tools : Autonomous agents (such as ChatGPT) inspect studio capabilities, build 3D voxel worlds, split timeline chapters, translate & synchronize lyrics, and trigger video exports. Visual Self-Inspection ( get_mv_preview ) : The agent captures real-time canvas snapshots to visually evaluate lighting, composition, and text safe-zones, autonomously refining parameters without human intervention. Procedural 3D World Engine : Real-time voxel terrain generation, orbital landmarks, dynamic lighting, atmospheric fog, and cinematic cameras rendered directly in the browser via Three.js, WebGPU, and WebGL. Multitrack Timeline & Lyric Sync : Non-destructive multi-scene splitting (intro, verses, chorus, drops, narrative chapters, or time-of-day transitions), multilingual lyric translation with syllable-precise timing alignment, and audio-reactive beat pulses. In-Browser 1080p MP4 Export : Full hardware-accelerated video rendering inside the client browser via WebCodecs and MediaBunny. How we built it WebMCP Layer : Built 38 structured tools registered on document.modelContext spanning 3D scene graphs, timeline actions, audio stems, and diagnostics. Frontend & 3D : React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js with WebGPU/WebGL acceleration. Client-Side AI & Audio : Web Audio API beat detection, and on-device AI source separation running locally via ONNX Runtime Web. Cloud Infrastructure : Cloudflare Workers for edge hosting, R2 storage for streaming AI model assets, and Cloudflare Workers AI (Whisper) for optional vocal transcription. Challenges we ran into Designing a tightly coupled visual feedback loop where the AI agent can iteratively validate its own 3D scene compositions via Base64 canvas snapshots. Orchestrating non-destructive multitrack timeline operations while maintaining seamless audio-video synchronization across multi-scene splits. Achieving fast 1080p MP4 video rendering entirely inside standard web browsers using WebCodecs and MediaBunny without offloading video encoding to backend servers. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fully operational suite of 38 WebMCP tools operating reliably with ChatGPT and autonomous browser agents. Autonomous multi-scene direction: splitting music tracks into distinct narrative scenes and musical chapters with dynamic camera paths and audio-reactive pulses. Heavy computing in the browser: running real-time 3D graphics, local ONNX stem inference, and 1080p video muxing directly on the user's device without requiring expensive GPU rendering servers. What we learned WebMCP proves that the open web can host rich, stateful, and non-destructive creative ecosystems for AI agents. Instead of treating AI as an isolated prompt-in/pixel-out generator, WebMCP unlocks an unprecedented paradigm: humans and agents building, inspecting, and iteratively polishing unique 3D interactive experiences together. What's next for Voivent MV Studio Native DAW Integration : Bridging Voivent MV Studio with our standalone digital audio workstation (Voivent DAW), allowing creators to stream multitrack audio and lyric maps directly into the WebMCP environment. Intuitive "Co-Pilot" Real-Time Jamming : Deepening the collaborative experience where creators and AI agents run side-by-side—intuitively directing 3D lighting, camera cuts, and visual shaders in real-time. Multi-Agent WebMCP Sessions : Enabling multiple specialized agents (e.g., dedicated lighting, camera, and typography agents) to coordinate simultaneously through WebMCP tool calls. Designed the 3D studio, timeline, and all 38 WebMCP tools. Building with WebMCP sparked endless new creative ideas, and I'm super excited to keep pushing the evolution of human-agent co-creation on the web! title: Cyfix
pitch: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize.
about_excerpt: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website has a short list of security basics that are cheap to check and cheap to fix: is HTTPS enforced, is HSTS set, does a CSP exist, are cookies flagged HttpOnly, is /.env sitting there in public. Almost nobody checks them, because the work is tedious, the output is jargon, and the tools are built for security engineers rather than for the person who actually owns the site. This is exactly the shape of work an agent should do. But "scan this domain" is not a neutral action — it touches someone else's server, and it carries legal and ethical weight. It has to stay a human decision. Most agent security tooling resolves that tension by removing the human. We wanted to keep them, visibly, in the loop. What it does Cyfix runs a passive-only security scan of a domain you're authorized to test, scores what it finds by severity, explains each issue in plain language, and gives you a copy-pasteable fix. An AI agent in the browser can drive that entire workflow itself through WebMCP — propose a domain, run the scan once you approve, triage findings, draft the CSP header, verify the fix, export the report. Every action, human or agent, lands in a shared audit log. What it will never do: exploit anything, brute force anything, scan ports, or send a single state-changing request. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, deployed on Vercel. Seven tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() from the root layout, so they're discoverable on every page — an agent landing anywhere on the site finds them immediately. Where a browser doesn't implement document.modelContext yet, Cyfix installs a same-shape polyfill, so the tools always exist and stay testable from the on-page Agent Console. Every tool resolves to an MCP-compatible envelope (content blocks, isError, structuredContent). The gate lives in the human's UI, not in a prompt: scan_domain reads the state of a checkbox the human can see and untick — a precondition the tool evaluates, not an instruction an agent could argue past. prepare_scan is the agent's way of asking: it proposes a domain but deliberately leaves the approval box untouched. Approval is scoped to one domain and revoked the instant the target changes. The dashboard is laid out as an application: a persistent left rail carries the sections, tracks the one you're reading, and pins the current target and score. The top bar shows a live count of the WebMCP tools currently registered on document.modelContext and whether that landed on the browser's native implementation or our polyfill. The seven tools prepare_scan — proposes a domain to the human. Cannot approve it. scan_domain — runs the passive scan. Refuses without human approval for that exact domain. list_findings — compact findings, filterable by severity or failures only. explain_finding — plain-language impact of one finding. generate_fix — copy-pasteable remediation snippet. verify_fix — re-scans the live site and confirms the fix actually landed. Human-gated like any scan. export_report — JSON or Markdown report, downloaded for the human. verify_fix is the one we'd point at. Most agent tooling stops at "here's the fix" and declares victory. Cyfix goes back to the live site and checks — and because verifying means re-scanning Cyfix scores 100/100 on itself The first thing anyone does with a security scanner is point it at the scanner. So we did — it scored 61. We fixed everything it found: a nonce-based CSP with no unsafe-inline for scripts, HSTS, nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, a referrer policy, a permissions policy, no framework banner, and a real /.well-known/security.txt. It now scores 100/100. Scan cyfix.vercel.app from the dashboard and check for yourself. Challenges we ran into Designing a gate an agent can't route around while still leaving it something useful to do. Our first version refused unauthorized scans correctly but left the agent at a dead end with no way to ask. Splitting "propose" from "approve" into two tools, and moving the target into shared state both actors read, is what made the collaboration real instead of theatrical. The second was our own CSP. The first policy we shipped used 'strict-dynamic', which silently voids the 'self' allowance — every script chunk was blocked and the dashboard rendered a blank page. The build was perfectly happy; only loading the page in a real browser caught it. A fitting lesson for a project about security headers. What's next Scheduled re-scans with diffing, a broader passive check set (TLS configuration, DNS hygiene, SPF/DMARC), and a shareable report link so the person who has to apply the fix doesn't need the dashboard open. title: LooPROOF
pitch: Product truth, callable by agents.
about_excerpt: Product truth, callable by agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise buyers rarely encounter one product surface. They compare a marketing page, pricing matrix, docs, trust center, contract language, and actual product behavior. Those surfaces drift. A browser agent can describe each page, but it still has to guess which statement wins. LooPROOF turns that hidden governance problem into a WebMCP-native collaboration surface. The website exposes not only controls, but the product claims, evidence provenance, authority boundary, and claim ceiling an agent needs to reason safely. What it does This challenge build includes a synthetic enterprise SaaS evidence graph with customer-facing claims and authoritative runtime, contract, and repository evidence. LooPROOF deterministically classifies each claim as BLOCK , REVIEW , ALIGNED , or NOT_EVALUATED . A human and an agent can work through the same visible state to: inspect the product-truth summary; find claims blocking an enterprise sales gate; trace every source, locator, value, provenance class, and authority level for a claim; focus the dashboard on the same claim the agent is investigating; stage canonical copy changes in a local-only sandbox; re-run the deterministic gate and reach STAGED_CONSISTENT_NON_ISSUING . LooPROOF deliberately refuses to call a sandbox change “fixed.” Production verification remains a separate authority. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent must infer the purpose of rows, badges, filters, and buttons from the visual interface. More importantly, it cannot reliably infer LooPROOF's domain contract: runtime evidence outranks marketing copy; model-proposed evidence cannot bind a verdict; a missing evidence edge is NOT_EVALUATED ; and a sandbox patch has a strict claim ceiling. LooPROOF registers 7 imperative WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . Closed schemas give the agent stable claim IDs, explicit inputs, side-effect annotations, and compact structured outputs. Tool execution updates the same state the human sees, creating a shared workspace rather than hidden backend automation. How we built it The app is dependency-free JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. A deterministic TruthEngine evaluates a bundled evidence graph and overlays sandbox patches in memory. The WebMCP adapter registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() , uses AbortSignal for lifecycle cleanup, declares read-only and side-effect annotations, and normalizes outputs to compact MCP text content. Node's built-in test runner verifies verdict binding, provenance boundaries, sandbox isolation, reset behavior, and tool-contract limits. GitHub Actions runs the complete verification suite. What is new for this challenge LooPROOF existed as a broader verification-engine concept before the submission period. During the challenge period, it was meaningfully extended through a new standalone public implementation containing: the complete imperative WebMCP tool surface; a shared human-agent state model; a provenance-preserving product-claim evidence graph; the local resolution sandbox; the deterministic re-verification path; a new responsive interface, test suite, security boundary, and challenge documentation. The repository contains synthetic evidence and does not copy or expose the private production implementation. Challenges The central challenge was not exposing more tools. It was preventing agent convenience from weakening evidence semantics. The implementation had to make the useful path easy while refusing unsupported claims. We therefore separated evidence alignment, staged consistency, and production verification into distinct states. Accomplishments 7 working imperative WebMCP tools. A coherent human-agent product experience rather than a wrapper around a chat box. Shared visible state between tool calls and the dashboard. Deterministic verdicts with provenance and authority ordering. A local sandbox that performs zero network, repository, or deployment writes. Explicit refusal to overclaim success. Dependency-free tests and CI validation. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a website exposes its domain semantics, not merely its controls. Tool schemas can encode the decisions an interface is designed to support, while the visible page preserves human oversight. The difficult design work is defining claim boundaries and side effects precisely enough that an agent can help without becoming a new source of product drift. What's next The production direction is to connect the same WebMCP surface to versioned proof packets generated from real product surfaces, repository policy, and observed runtime flows, while keeping final verification capability-separated.  Inspiration 

 Travel planning is fragmented: people jump among sites to research, compare, schedule, and book. We imagined an agent that can help with the full planning loop while keeping people in control of every important decision. 

 What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

title: Forgenote
pitch: ForgeNote is a live research notebook humans and WebMCP agents share. You paste a URL. The agent reads it and writes claims and outline on this page. Never scrapes. You accept or reject.
about_excerpt: ForgeNote is a live research notebook humans and WebMCP agents share. You paste a URL. The agent reads it and writes claims and outline on this page. Never scrapes. You accept or reject. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos are a cart, a booking form, or a guestbook. An agent clicks a button and the page updates. That proves the API. It does not prove collaboration. Research is messier. You collect sources, argue with claims, and reshape an outline over time. Chat transcripts bury that work. Docs live in one tab. The agent lives in another. We wanted one document that a human and an agent both write, with the human still in charge. ForgeNote is that document: a research notebook where extract_claims is not a summary in chat. It is a row on the page. What it does ForgeNote is a live research notebook for humans and WebMCP agents. • You set a goal and paste source URLs. The app never fetches those pages. • An agent (ChatGPT in its built-in browser, or you in Chrome with WebMCP flags) calls tools on document.modelContext. • The agent reads each URL itself, then calls extract_claims and update_outline. Claims and headings land on this page. • You accept, edit, or reject agent writes in the inbox. Reject undoes the change. • If ChatGPT is not available, Run sample extract still shows claims appearing in the Claims section. Seven tools wrap the same Zustand actions as the UI: get_project_overview, set_research_goal, add_source, extract_claims, update_outline, add_note, suggest_next_questions. How I built it • Next.js App Router, Tailwind, Zustand persisted to localStorage • WebMCP via document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext and registerTool(def, { signal }) • Headers: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) • Netlify (@netlify/plugin-nextjs) • Landing and notebook share one chrome. Typecheck on pre-commit, full next build on pre-push, so deploys do not fail the way an early Netlify build did The rule we kept: a pasted URL is storage only. Scraping would fake the agent loop. The agent has to read. Challenges we ran into WebMCP only exists on the loaded page. Pasting the site URL into normal ChatGPT does nothing. The agent has to open ForgeNote in ChatGPT’s built-in browser (Work, Sol or Terra). We spent a lot of time making that obvious. Storage is per origin and per browser. Goal and sources in Chrome do not appear in ChatGPT’s browser. Judges (and we) had to treat the in-app tab as the live notebook. Chrome debugging is easy to get wrong. The Model Context Tool Inspector is a Web Store extension, not a DevTools tab. Native inspection is Application → WebMCP, and it needs both enable-webmcp-testing and devtools-webmcp-support. Claims were easy to miss. They sat in a collapsed block. We made Claims always visible and scroll to it after extract. Accomplishments that I'm proud of • A full research loop on one document, not a toy tool list • Humans and agents on the same functions, with undo • A landing page that tells you how to test, including what not to do • Sample extract so the product is demoable without ChatGPT • Shipping the no-scrape contract for real What I learned WebMCP is a document API, not a chatbot plugin. If the page is not in the agent’s browser, there are no tools. Local-first is honest and also brutal for demos: two browsers, two notebooks. Copy is part of the product. “Open DevTools” is useless if the pane is under Application. “Claims appeared” is useless if Claims is collapsed. What's next for Forgenote • Snapshot share so a Chrome notebook can load in ChatGPT’s browser without re-entering sources • Optional cloud persist (still no scrape) for the same project across devices • Richer outline editing and cite-back from claims to sources • Keep following the WebMCP spec as registerTool and DevTools settle Built With chatgpt chrome-devtools husky lucide netlify next.js react tailwind-css typescript webmcp zustand Try it out forgenote.netlify.app forgenote.netlify.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Chetan Raj Like Share this project: Updates Chetan Raj started this project — Sep 03, 2026 01:24 PM EDT

title: Night Sky Atlas
pitch: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents.
about_excerpt: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a short stargazing session asks a beginner to combine an observer's place and time, target visibility, object types, and a comfortable route. That is more than a list of astronomy facts: changing the observer or advancing the clock changes what the person sees. Night Sky Atlas makes that work collaborative instead of opaque. What it does A person can explore the planetarium manually, edit an observing plan, and save it locally. With WebMCP, an agent can query the same live sky context, find observable catalog targets, and propose a timed route. The agent's proposal appears in the same planner rail as an Agent preview . Previewing does not change observer location or time, so the person can inspect the route before approving any mutation. After approval, the agent can visibly set the observer, save the route, and advance the shared tour target by target. This is a good fit for WebMCP because visual sky state is the product: the person and agent need the same map, time, location, selected target, and plan. The site exposes ten strict, top-level imperative tools that reuse the manual application actions rather than a parallel automation path. It remains a zero-build static site with local browser persistence; no account, backend, or API key is required. How I built it The July 22, 2026 baseline at commit 81672ede79762cbf3aadfe23a8dc9eee32013f94 was an interactive planetarium. During the challenge I added a persistent, human-editable observing plan and ten WebMCP tools. The tools reuse the same catalog, altitude calculations, validation, persistence, application actions, and visible state as the manual interface. The intended safety sequence is read, find, preview, inspect, mutate, save . In particular, preview_observing_plan makes a proposed New York route visible while the current London observer and time stay unchanged; only an explicit location or time action mutates them. Challenges I ran into Designing tools that share exactly the same state and validation as manual controls without creating a hidden agent-only path. Keeping location and time changes visible and reviewable while still making the agent route useful. Computing and preserving per-slot altitude constraints for a timed route. Making a dense planner rail work at desktop and mobile sizes with usable keyboard focus, live progress, and reduced-motion behavior. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A preview-first workflow that visibly proposes a route before observer mutation. Ten narrow, strict-schema WebMCP tools: three read tools and seven visible write tools. A manual planner that remains useful without an agent, plus a saved guided tour that frames targets and advances time. Browser verification of an altitude-constrained New York demo route. 81 automated tests covering astronomy, planning, persistence, UI, and WebMCP integration. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when it gives an agent a deliberate application surface while the person can still see and steer every result. Tool descriptions and schemas clarify what an agent may ask for, but the visible UI is what makes the collaboration legible. Separating preview from commit made the location change understandable instead of surprising. What's next Add weather, darkness, and equipment-aware recommendations with clearly labeled data sources. Let people compare alternative plans side by side before saving one. Export plans as printable or calendar-friendly observing cards. Broaden accessibility testing across assistive technology and real devices. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. about_excerpt: Final-year project supervision, minus the busywork, now with an agent that does the work so you focus on supervising. Like Comment Story Updates Admin dashboard showing list of supervisors and admin web mcp tools Supervisor dashboard showing list of assigned students and the web mcp tools Student dashboard showing student web mcp tool Inspiration I built UniTrack a while back as a final-year academic project management platform for my department. It handles the whole workflow between the departmental admin (who assign supervisors and set academic sessions), supervisors (who review and approve or reject student chapter submissions), and students (who submit their chapters for review). It's a real system, built to remove the difficult manual project supervision process in universities. What got me into this hackathon was a pretty simple realization: a lot of the actual work in that system isn't clicking buttons, it's stuff like a supervisor trying to remember what feedback they gave to a student they gave three weeks ago and having to read through the entire document to see if the student's submission addressed the feedback they gave, or an admin trying to match a student to the right supervisor based on... honestly, mostly vibes and memory. None of that is a UI problem. It's a "nobody has time to manually cross-reference this" problem. That felt like exactly the kind of thing an agent should be good at, if it could actually understand the app instead of just clicking around it. What it does UniTrack now lets an AI agent inside ChatGPT's browser, call real, structured tools directly on the app, instead of guessing its way through the UI. Depending on who's logged in, the agent can: For supervisors: scan all feedback a supervisor has given across their students and show recurring patterns to give insights in to what their students are struggling with ("you've flagged citation formatting in 4 of 5 submissions this session"), or compare two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explain in plain language what actually changed and whether previous feedback was covered by student. For admins: suggest which students should be assigned to a supervisor , based on each supervisor's stated expertise and each student's stated interests, with real reasoning attached instead of the admin just randomly assigning (this is important because supervisors get to supervise only projects within their expertise and students get the best out of the process). Every risky action: actually assigning a supervisor, actually approving a submission, still requires a human to confirm it in the real UI. The agent suggests and summarizes; people decide. How we built it The core of it is simpler than it sounds. My existing Django REST Framework backend barely changed. WebMCP tools live entirely on the frontend. I registered them using document.modelContext.registerTool() right inside my React components, and each tool's execute() function just calls the same API endpoints my frontend already used. No new backend framework, no separate MCP server. Django keeps serving JSON like it always did; the tool layer is just a new way of calling it. I tested tools locally first using the Model Context Tool Inspector extension in Chrome, before ever touching ChatGPT. That gave me a fast way to check a tool was registered correctly and returning the right shape of data. Once that worked, I moved to testing the real thing: opening the app inside ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser and asking it natural-language questions to see if it actually called the right tool. Challenges we ran into Time was the big one. I had a handful of days, not weeks. I had to be honest with myself about scope more than once: I really wanted to rebuild the whole frontend cleaner at one point, and had to talk myself out of it, because a working demo was more important with a deadline like this. I also ran into a real technical snag: WebMCP tools only get discovered if they're registered on the top-level page, not inside an iframe. I had to actually go check my own app's structure to make sure nothing was quietly broken by that before I got too far into building. And honestly, the trickiest part wasn't the WebMCP API itself, it was making the agent's suggestions actually mean something instead of feeling generic. Anyone can build a tool that technically returns data. Making the reasoning specific enough to feel genuinely useful, took real iteration on the seed data and the tool logic. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this isn't a toy demo app built just for the hackathon, it's a layer on top of a platform that solves a real problem in our universities. I'm also proud of keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary honest: nothing the agent suggests silently becomes real without a person clicking confirm, which felt like the right call the whole way through, not just something I added to check a box. I'm also proud of the chapter-diff tool: the one that get's the agent to explain "here's what changed, and here's what you already flagged that's still unresolved" is a small thing on paper, but it's exactly the kind of busywork that eats a supervisor's actual time, and watching it work correctly was genuinely satisfying. What we learned Going in, I assumed WebMCP was some heavy thing. It turned out to be much simpler and much more useful than I expected: a website just says "here's a function you can call, here's what it needs, here's what it returns," instead of an agent guessing its way through a UI by clicking things and hoping for the best. I also learned that ChatGPT treats every tool call and its results as untrusted content by default, which genuinely changed how I thought about which actions should be automatic versus which ones need a human to confirm — that wasn't just a security afterthought, it shaped the actual design of the tools. What's next for UniTrack Right now, everything the agent can do lives inside one supervisor's or one admin's session which is genuinely useful, but it's still one person and their agent, working alone. The next real step is making the agents themselves coordinate. Picture a student's agent and their supervisor's agent actually negotiating a review deadline or a meeting slot directly: the student's agent proposes times, the supervisor's agent checks their real calendar and workload, and both humans just confirm at the end instead of doing the back-and-forth themselves. That's a genuinely different kind of "agent-native" than anything I built this week, and it's the direction that excites me most. I'd also want to move the supervisor-matching logic off simple tag overlap and toward something that actually understands a lecturer's real research background: their publications, past supervised topics, the language they use to describe their own work, rather than relying on whatever keywords they happened to type into a profile field. Self-reported tags are a fine starting point, but they're not how expertise actually works. And I'd want to stop building this in isolation. UniTrack is currently scoped to one department, but final-year project supervision is a near-universal structure across departments and universities - admin, supervisor, student, the same shape everywhere. If this genuinely saves supervisors and admins real time, the honest next step is putting it in front of an actual department for a full academic session, not just testing it myself, and seeing whether it holds up against real workloads, real deadlines, and real people who didn't build the thing and have no reason to be generous with it. Note UniTrack existed before this hackathon as a deployed final-year project management platform. It may be seen as a new repository because I had to merge the frontend and backend in to a single repo (they were separate before) for the purpose of the hackathon, but the commit history is intact. During the submission period, I added a WebMCP layer on top of the existing app: registered client-side tools (document.modelContext.registerTool()) that let an AI agent call real, structured functions directly which are a supervisor-facing tool that surfaces recurring feedback patterns across all their students, a tool that checks two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explains what changed, and an admin-facing tool that suggests supervisor assignments based on declared expertise and student interests and a student facing tool that helps them generate practice defense questions. I also added a few new backend endpoints and two new profile fields (lecturer expertise, student interests) specifically to support this matching logic, none of which existed before this hackathon. title: WebMCP × x402 — Agents that buy exactly the data they need
pitch: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation.
about_excerpt: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation. Like Comment Story Updates What it does OpenPay (open-pay.jp) runs a production AI store of x402-payable APIs: agents pay a few cents per call — JPYC on Polygon or USDC on Base — with no account and no API key. For the WebMCP Challenge we added three WebMCP tools to the store page, so an in-browser agent no longer has to guess at a human UI: search_paid_resources — search the catalog; every result carries price, currency, and x-agent-usage (when an agent should buy, and how to re-buy only deltas). get_resource_schema — the machine contract for one resource: query params, re-purchase policy, payment info, response example (backed by our OpenAPI). prepare_purchase — fetches the raw HTTP 402 challenge and returns its accepts (chain, asset, exact amount, payTo). It never signs and never pays. Why the safety boundary is the feature Agents have been observed fabricating "user approved" messages to defeat prompt-level spending rules. So payment execution is deliberately NOT a WebMCP tool here. Signing stays in the buyer's own wallet tooling (our open-source MCP server / CLI buyers) with per-call caps, daily caps, an endpoint allowlist, and a small dedicated wallet whose balance is the hard limit. WebMCP finds and explains; x402 pays — through a boundary an LLM's text cannot cross. Not a mockup The store sells real products built for recurring agent jobs — weekly change feeds (JPYC Service Monitor, Japan Stablecoin Payment Monitor) where changedSince=<last run> returns only what changed and changes: [] explicitly means "nothing new". They settle on-chain today (Base & Polygon; e.g. tx 0xf62b736e…, 0x3577035c…, 0xef1f0969…) and are listed on the x402 Bazaar / agentic.market. The WebMCP integration ships in production at https://open-pay.jp/ja/discovery with unit tests (origin-restricted fetches, no-op on unsupported browsers). How we built it Next.js store page registers the three tools via navigator.modelContext.registerTool on mount (React wrapper, null render, unregister on unmount). Tools are thin, dependency-free wrappers over our existing free endpoints ( /api/discovery , /api/openapi.json , and each resource's own 402 challenge). Fetches are restricted to same-origin /api/* paths. Extracted, MIT-licensed module + integration guide: https://github.com/cipherwebllc/webmcp-x402-discovery What's next Wire the loop end-to-end for scheduled agents: WebMCP discovery in the browser → wallet-side x402 payment → weekly delta re-purchases — and publish adapters so any x402 seller can make their catalog agent-native with one script tag. title: FinSnap - Your finances, agent-ready
pitch: FinSnap turns your personal finances into 19 WebMCP tools so that your AI agent gets your complete financial picture the moment it needs them.
about_excerpt: FinSnap turns your personal finances into 19 WebMCP tools so that your AI agent gets your complete financial picture the moment it needs them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dashboard Transactions Accounts Goals Budgets Cashflow Portfolio AI Agent Webmcp tools, financial health Inspiration Every time I talk to an AI about money, I start from scratch. What's your income? What are your savings? What do you spend on rent? The data exists across multiple apps I use, but AI agents have no way to read it. I eventually end up describing my own financial situation to a system again and again. And there's no real way to keep this updated since it keeps changing month to month. WebMCP felt like the right answer. A page that exposes its data as tools, discoverable by any agent that browses it, with no API keys and no configuration. The question was: what domain actually needs this? Finance felt obvious. The data is structured, the stakes are high enough that you want an agent doing the heavy lifting, and the cross-domain use cases (property, mortgages, tax) are real and immediate. Building this for the WebMCP Challenge felt like a good forcing function to see how far that idea could go. What it does FinSnap is a personal finance dashboard that exposes your complete financial picture as 19 WebMCP tools. Net worth, cash flow, goals, portfolio, budget status, recurring charges, financial health score, cash flow forecasting, and safe-to-spend calculations. Any WebMCP-compatible AI agent browsing the page gets immediate, structured access to all of it. No setup. The agent browses to FinSnap and the tools are just there. The cross-domain case is where it gets interesting. Ask about property affordability or mortgage capacity, and the agent reads six months of real transaction data and answers with specificity that a generic prompt can't match. Ask it to set a goal, and it writes directly back to the page. The human and the agent are working on the same interface at the same time. How I built it Next.js 16 App Router with a synchronous WebMCP shim injected in <head> . The shim handles two environments: ChatGPT's in-app browser (which provides document.modelContext natively) and Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Financial data lives in IndexedDB via the idb library across six stores: accounts, transactions, categories, goals, portfolio, and settings. This is a prototype approach that demonstrates the tool interface without requiring live bank connections. In production, you would replace it with open banking APIs or CSV import; the 19 tools stay identical. A significant part of the build was designing the tool set itself. What does an agent actually need to answer real financial questions? That thinking led to the planning category: get_financial_briefing bundles six sub-queries into one call so an agent gets a full picture upfront; calculate_safe_to_spend runs the budget arithmetic across all categories; forecast_cashflow projects forward from six-month averages with trend adjustment. Agents can call these directly and get a useful answer. The 19 tools are split across three categories: Read: net worth, accounts, transactions, spending by category, cash flow, portfolio, recurring charges, health score, goals, budget status Write: set goal, categorise transaction, import transactions, reconcile balance, delete goal, set budget Planning: financial briefing (full picture in one call), cash flow forecast, safe-to-spend Deployed on Vercel via GitHub CI/CD. Challenges Designing a coherent financial picture. The demo data had to tell a believable story: a person with realistic goals, a plausible portfolio, spending patterns that produced meaningful cash flow trends. Getting six months of transactions, account balances, portfolio holdings, and goal progress to all be internally consistent took real planning. A number that looks right in isolation (a CommSec balance, a savings rate) can immediately contradict something else if you have not mapped the whole picture first. Shim execution order. Next.js Script component defers execution by default. The WebMCP shim needs to run synchronously before the page renders so document.modelContext exists when the agent first checks for it. Solved by injecting via dangerouslySetInnerHTML directly in the root layout. Double-encoded JSON. Chrome's native WebMCP flag serialises tool call arguments differently from ChatGPT's implementation. The shim handles both code paths. Suspense boundaries. Next.js production builds require useSearchParams() to be wrapped in a Suspense boundary. Caught this at build time rather than in development. What I learned The zero-setup discovery model works differently from other AI integration patterns. The agent browses the page and the tools are available. No key exchange, no prior configuration. That changes what kinds of apps make sense to build on WebMCP. Finance works well here because the data is already structured and the agent can compute things (cash flow forecasting, health scoring, safe-to-spend) that would take a human meaningful time to work out manually. What surprised me was how much of the useful work sits in the planning tools rather than the raw reads. An agent that can call get_financial_briefing and immediately reason over a complete picture is more useful than one that has to assemble the same picture from ten separate calls. What's next The right write pattern for financial data is: agent proposes, human commits. The agent should draft a change into a staging area, the human reviews actual figures, and a commit step applies it. This is especially important in finance where you want a human seeing real numbers before anything changes. Real bank connections via open banking APIs or CSV import replace the seeded IndexedDB. The tool interface stays identical. An ask_human tool where the agent surfaces a question in the FinSnap UI and waits for a response. The agent sees you are 90% through your dining budget with two weeks left and asks whether to adjust. That kind of back-and-forth is where the collaboration gets interesting. As the WebMCP ecosystem matures, dedicated domain agents (property search, mortgage calculators, tax tools) could each expose their own WebMCP tools. FinSnap becomes the financial node they all read first. You explain your financial situation once, and every agent that needs it reads it from here. That is the version of personal finance AI that actually fits how people live. title: Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent
pitch: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change.
about_excerpt: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most “AI for spreadsheets” still lives in a chat sidebar or a separate Sheets API. You describe a budget; you get a table pasted back into the thread — not co-editing the grid you’re staring at. Google Sheets has Gemini-style help and backend MCP connectors, but the live sheets.google.com page is not exposing WebMCP tools on the open workbook. That gap is the point of the challenge: shared client state . Grid was inspired by that white space — and by Flavio’s note that spreadsheets are strong WebMCP cases because the open page holds state a remote API may not. What if ChatGPT and a human shared one workbook, with the agent writing cells, formulas, sorts, charts, and highlights you watch appear live? What it does Grid is an agent-native shared spreadsheet: Co-edit a seeded “Move budget — London” workbook toward a £4k total Read and write ranges, set formulas ( =SUM , arithmetic), sort and filter rows Highlight cells, add/remove a simple chart, insert rows/cols, export CSV Full human UI (formula bar, selection, editable cells) that works with WebMCP idle 17 WebMCP site tools on the same Zustand store as your clicks Agent tools panel + activity feed; ?demo=1 (optional delay / delayMs ) for judges and screencasts You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Grid’s tools update the open grid in real time. Side effects like export_csv , clear_highlights , and remove_chart are annotated so confirmation policies can apply. How we built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript SPA ( base: '/grid-webmcp/' ) Zustand as the single source of truth for the React UI and every WebMCP execute handler WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected on the top-level page Lightweight formula evaluation, SVG chart panel, filter/highlight overlays MIT-licensed, client-only, no backend or secrets — GitHub Pages Built with Codex Core tools: get_workbook_state , get_range , set_cells , set_formula , clear_range , select_range , sort_range , filter_rows , clear_filter , highlight_cells , clear_highlights , add_chart , remove_chart , insert_rows , insert_cols , export_csv , list_activity . Challenges we ran into Same-state collaboration — agent tools and keyboard edits must never drift. Both paths go through one store. Formulas without a full engine — enough SUM + arithmetic for a credible budget demo, without shipping Excel. Read vs write vs side effect — inspection tools stay read-only; clears, chart removal, and CSV export are explicit side effects. Demo without a live agent — ?demo=1 replays the happy path for screencasts while real tools still register for ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Staying distinct — orthogonal to Nest (flats), Frame (canvas), Brief (evidence), and Redline (propose ≠ commit). Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete co-edit loop on one grid: fill → formula → sort → chart → highlight → export Non-trivial WebMCP surface (17 tools), not a single toy cell writer Human-first UI that stays usable if WebMCP is missing A fifth submission that targets a category often confused with “Sheets already does AI” — and shows the difference is tools on the open page What we learned WebMCP’s superpower is co-presence. Spreadsheets prove it cleanly: when set_formula runs, you watch the contingency cell resolve; when add_chart runs, the bar appears beside the sheet. That shared visual ground is harder to fake with a headless Sheets API MCP — and it’s exactly what Grid is for. What's next for Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent Richer formula surface (IF, VLOOKUP-class helpers) and named ranges Multi-sheet workbooks and freeze panes Conditional formatting tools the agent can propose and you confirm Presence cursors when multiple humans join the same workbook Deeper ChatGPT desktop testing with confirmation UX on destructive tools Built With codex Try it out omercelik.github.io Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Serdar Murat ÇELİK Omer Celik Abdulhamit Mabocoglu Like Share this project: Updates Omer Celik started this project — Sep 02, 2026 07:27 PM EDT

title: Github web mcp
pitch: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience
about_excerpt: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience Like Comment Story Updates After approval, the agent creates issue #3, opens it in the interface, and the WebMCP surface returns to seven tools. RepoScope shows the agent’s inline security finding, editable issue proposal, human approval, trace, and dynamically exposed 10-tool. ## Inspiration Repository review is usually split between a web interface and a detached AI conversation. Browser agents can attempt to interpret the DOM, while remote MCP servers can expose repository APIs, but neither naturally shares the exact transient workspace state the person is viewing. GitHub Web MCP, presented as RepoScope , explores a different approach: the webpage itself exposes structured, context-sensitive capabilities to the agent. The human and agent review the same file, findings, proposal, and approval state in one visible workspace. ## What it does RepoScope is a controlled GitHub-like repository review application demonstrating human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A person opens a file and asks an agent to review the repository. The agent: Reads the live workspace context. Investigates relevant repository files. Identifies the most serious substantiated problem. Places a visible annotation on the relevant line. Prepares an editable issue proposal without creating it. The person can edit, approve, or dismiss the proposal. Approval authorizes one exact draft revision but does not execute it. After the person tells the agent “Approved,” the agent creates the reviewed issue and the result immediately appears in the interface. The page’s tool surface changes with its state: Fresh repository: 7 tools Reviewable file open: 9 tools Exact proposal approved: 10 tools Issue created or proposal dismissed: 7 tools This dynamic capability model demonstrates why the experience benefits from WebMCP instead of being a conventional API wrapper. ## How we built it RepoScope is a client-only React and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. The React interface and WebMCP tools share one observable application service. This ensures that human actions and agent actions use the same application logic and produce immediate visible updates. The dedicated WebMCP adapter: Registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() Separates read-only and state-changing capabilities Reconciles registrations when workspace state changes Cleans up registrations with abort signals Verifies discovery using document.modelContext.getTools() Records agent calls in a visible activity feed Updates the interface before mutating calls finish The final issue-creation capability accepts only a reference to the exact approved proposal. It rejects pending, edited, dismissed, stale, unknown, or previously completed proposals. The project intentionally uses local fixture data rather than a backend or GitHub API. This keeps the demonstration focused on live page context, dynamic capabilities, and human approval. ## Challenges we ran into The first challenge was making WebMCP essential to the experience. An early version allowed an agent to inspect files and create an issue, but a remote MCP server could have provided the same functionality. We redesigned the workflow around live workspace state, dynamic tool discovery, visible annotations, and in- page approval. Designing a reliable approval boundary was another challenge. Clicking Approve and executing the action are intentionally separate. Editing an approved proposal revokes its approval, and the agent cannot change its contents during the final creation call. WebMCP is also an experimental browser API. We isolated all experimental integration code behind a small adapter, made the normal interface work when WebMCP is unavailable, and added visible discovery status and automated lifecycle tests. Finally, agent activity is normally difficult to demonstrate on video. We added a bounded activity feed so viewers can see the agent investigate, annotate, propose, and complete its work directly in the application. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete two-turn human-agent workflow that requires no tool names, schemas, or internal identifiers in the human conversation. The person can make a natural request, review the agent’s evidence in context, approve an exact proposal, and complete the action by saying only “Approved.” We are especially proud of: Dynamic discovery that visibly transitions 7 → 9 → 10 → 7 Inline findings connected to the relevant source line An editable and revocable approval workflow Exact-revision authorization for issue creation Immediate UI updates from agent actions A visible and safely summarized agent activity feed Graceful behavior when WebMCP is unavailable A native ChatGPT Site tools rehearsal of the complete workflow The automated suite includes 28 unit and component tests plus three Playwright browser scenarios, alongside TypeScript, ESLint, and production-build verification. ## What we learned Our main lesson was that WebMCP is more than a browser-accessible API. Its strongest value appears when an agent’s capabilities reflect the transient state, permissions, and workflow of the page a person is actively using. Dynamic discovery can provide both context and control. It reduces irrelevant options for the agent and ensures sensitive capabilities appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied. We also learned that successful tool execution is not enough for good collaboration. People need to see what the agent inspected, what it found, what it proposes, and exactly where human authority begins and ends. ## What's next for Github web mcp The next step is to evolve RepoScope from a focused competition demonstration into a reusable pattern for safe, context-aware repository collaboration. Potential extensions include: Optional integration with real GitHub repositories Persistent review sessions and findings Pull-request review workflows Line-range and multi-file annotations Multiple independently reviewable proposals Repository-specific authorization policies Richer evidence links between findings, code, issues, and pull requests Improved compatibility as the WebMCP standard evolves The approval model could also be applied beyond repository review. Document editors, design tools, administrative dashboards, and investigation workspaces could expose context-sensitive agent capabilities while preserving their existing human controls and authorization boundaries. title: Dependency War Room
pitch: An adaptive WebMCP workspace that simulates API changes, measures downstream dependency risk, traces critical paths, and helps maintainers and AI agents plan safer software releases together.
about_excerpt: An adaptive WebMCP workspace that simulates API changes, measures downstream dependency risk, traces critical paths, and helps maintainers and AI agents plan safer software releases together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Dependency War Room Inspiration Dependency registries answer the forward question well: “What does this package depend on?” The harder operational question is the inverse one: if a package changes, who downstream is exposed, what evidence do I have, and what should I migrate first? What it does Real-time Dependency Graph Analysis Platform combines dependency graph data, API-change analysis, declared version-range exposure, security evidence and explicit human review in one War Room. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended the existing platform with a browser-native War Room where a developer and an agent operate the same application workflow. WebMCP exposes constrained product actions for graph inspection, blast-radius analysis, human review, critical paths and migration planning instead of giving the agent raw database or GraphQL access. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Dependency-impact analysis is naturally multi-step: opening a package graph, summarizing topology, calculating blast radius, tracing a dependency path, simulating an API change, reviewing version exposure, applying human business priority or exclusions, recalculating the scenario, inspecting critical paths and generating a migration plan. With WebMCP, the application exposes those operations as explicit, schema-constrained product actions. The user remains in the visual War Room while the agent works through the same application workflow. Human and agent collaboration There is no separate agent-only copy of the workflow. If the developer changes scenario priority or explicitly excludes something from migration scope, the agent continues from that same reviewed state. The agent coordinates the investigation, while deterministic application logic remains responsible for breaking-change analysis, version exposure, blast-radius calculation, compatibility-related evidence and migration-plan generation. Human review remains explicit for business priority and exclusions. How WebMCP is implemented The application uses document.modelContext and registers a catalog of 16 canonical WebMCP tools. The runtime surface is adaptive: the application does not expose all 16 tools at every moment, but only tools relevant and executable for the active War Room phase. A verified initial runtime surface for cargo:tokio included open_package_graph , summarize_graph , calculate_blast_radius , trace_dependency_path and focus_graph_nodes . As the workflow advances, actions such as recalculate_scenario and generate_migration_plan become relevant. Both human UI actions and WebMCP actions call the shared WarRoomActions abstraction. WebMCP does not expose raw SQL, raw Cypher, arbitrary GraphQL, arbitrary scripts, arbitrary URLs or unrestricted backend operations. Better user experience The developer can inspect facts visually, make a business decision, and then ask the agent to recalculate the scenario and generate the next migration plan from the updated state. This shared-state collaboration is difficult to achieve reliably with ordinary DOM automation or a standalone chatbot. Real production environment The public deployment uses Vercel for the Next.js frontend, Render for the Rust/Axum API, Memgraph Cloud for the dependency graph, Redis for runtime cache/state, PostgreSQL/Neon for relational metadata, Qdrant for semantic search/vector data and OSV.dev for vulnerability evidence. The production demo is intentionally a seeded environment rather than claiming live registry ingestion. The graph and API interactions demonstrated in the submission video are real production application state. Existing-project disclosure The dependency analysis platform existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The challenge submission is the meaningful WebMCP extension and War Room integration added during the competition period, including shared WarRoomActions state, phase-adaptive runtime registration, constrained browser-agent actions, explicit human review, critical-path inspection and deterministic migration planning. What I learned WebMCP works best when a website exposes meaningful application actions rather than generic backend capabilities. The important design question is what the application should allow the agent to be authoritative about. Keeping deterministic evidence, human decisions and agent coordination separate made the WebMCP surface clearer and safer. What's next The next step would be expanding the same WebMCP authority model to larger dependency graphs and additional package ecosystems while keeping the adaptive tool surface small, with stronger browser-level WebMCP regression coverage and richer source-compatibility evidence. title: Aria Grande
pitch: Aria Grande gives AI browsers the context to make every website easier to explore, understand, and use—for everyone. It scales from clients to all websites.
about_excerpt:
Aria Grande gives AI browsers the context to make every website easier to explore, understand, and use—for everyone. It scales from clients to all websites.

 Main view
