title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: ScholarSathi
pitch: ScholarSathi helps Indian students simplify scholarships with WebMCP-powered AI that finds eligibility, checks documents, prepares applications, and keeps humans in control.
about_excerpt:
ScholarSathi helps Indian students simplify scholarships with WebMCP-powered AI that finds eligibility, checks documents, prepares applications, and keeps humans in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 In India, many students depend on cybercafes , jan suvidha kendra to complete scholarship applications. Government portals can involve confusing eligibility rules, long document checklists, repeated data entry, and multiple application stages. Students pay for assistance 50 inr to 100 inr and still not understand why they qualify, what is missing, or what happens next. 

 We wanted to create a safer alternative: a shared workspace where an AI agent can handle the complicated preparation work while the student remains informed and in control. 

 ## What we built 

 ScholarSathi helps students: 

 
 discover representative scholarship programs; 
 assess eligibility using deterministic rules; 
 identify missing information and documents; 
 prepare and validate an application draft; 
 request explicit human approval; 
 submit and track a simulated application. 
 

 WebMCP is fundamental to the product. ScholarSathi exposes focused tools that an AI agent can discover and compose, rather than forcing the agent to guess how buttons and forms work. Tool calls update the same visible interface the student uses, creating shared state between the human and the agent. 

 ## How we built it 

 ScholarSathi is a static application built with semantic HTML, modern CSS, vanilla JavaScript ES modules, and local JSON-style data. It uses browser localStorage for privacy-safe demo persistence and requires no backend, account, external API, or LLM service. 

 The application includes: 

 
 a deterministic eligibility engine; 
 shared profile, document, application, and civic-service state; 
 validation and readiness checks; 
 a two-phase human approval workflow; 
 idempotent simulated submission; 
 responsive and accessible UI;

 Inspiration

 What it does 

 AddaSwift makes the Actions Ring context-aware for websites. On Gmail, the ring shows Archive, Snooze, Compose. On GitHub - Merge PR, Request Review. On Notion - New Page, Search. It also surfaces bookmarks and quick-launch links. Everything configures through Logitech Options+. 

 How we built it 

 An Actions SDK plugin built on PluginDynamicCommand that updates the ring at runtime based on the active browser tab. A bridge layer - a desktop app paired with a Chrome extension - communicates browser context to the plugin. We reach websites through three stacking layers: native keyboard shortcuts, DOM element targeting, and WebMCP integration. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The web has no universal API for "what can I do here." Mapping the static ring to dynamic web content while keeping it responsive was the central design challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Contextual ring updates that feel immediate as you switch tabs. 

 What we learned 

 PluginDynamicCommand is more flexible than it first appears. The gap between what users can do on a page and what's programmatically accessible is exactly why WebMCP matters.

title: Taxis
pitch: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A friend of mine was organizing a crypto event, and after we got the venue, we were standing in a large empty hall trying to figure out where everything should go. Where should the rooms or different areas be? Where should the furniture go? How much space do we actually have? Most of the planning was happening in our heads and through conversations. That made me think about how we plan physical spaces today. We have AI agents that can reason about complex problems, but they usually cannot directly work with the structured space we are looking at. I wanted to build something where a person could brainstorm with an agent, see ideas take shape directly on the canvas, and have both the human and the agent work on the same space at the same time. That idea became Taxis. What it does Taxis is a spatial planning canvas for designing physical spaces. You can use it to plan a house, office, event, restaurant, exhibition, warehouse, studio, or other physical environments. The key idea is that both the human and the AI agent can work on the same plan. A person can manually create, move, resize, rotate, duplicate, and delete rooms and objects while an agent can perform these same types of spatial operations through WebMCP. The human does not have to wait for the agent to finish before making changes. Both can contribute to the same evolving plan. For example, while an agent is arranging rooms, a person can add doors, adjust objects, or make other changes themselves. We demonstrated this by giving the agent a plot of land and asking it to create a practical bungalow layout with rooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The result can then be inspected and edited directly on the canvas. How we built it Taxis is a browser-based spatial planning application built with TypeScript and Vite. The application represents rooms and objects as structured spatial data, including their dimensions, positions, rotations, and other properties. We expose the application's spatial operations as WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an agent to interact directly with the application's structured state, including creating, moving, resizing, rotating, duplicating, and deleting spatial elements. This means the agent is not generating an image of a floor plan. It is directly manipulating the actual objects inside the application. WebMCP provides the interface that allows an external agent to work with the same application state that the human is editing. Challenges we ran into One of the more difficult parts was making resizing and reshaping reliable. At one point, when resizing certain objects, the pointer interaction could incorrectly switch between resize and reshape behavior, causing the cursor to loop between the two interaction modes. We had to refine the interaction logic so that the application could correctly distinguish between resizing an object and reshaping it. Another challenge was making the spatial operations reliable when they are being performed through agent tools. The application has to maintain a consistent structured state while rooms and objects are being created and modified. We also had to make the WebMCP tools clear enough for an agent to understand what operations were available and how they affected the spatial canvas. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working spatial planning application where a human and an AI agent can interact with the same structured canvas. We are particularly proud of the fact that the agent is not simply generating a static floor plan. It can directly manipulate the objects inside the application while the human can continue editing the same space. We demonstrated this by using an agent to plan a bungalow on a 20m × 30m plot of land, including bedrooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The same underlying system is not restricted to houses. The spatial canvas and its agent tools can be applied to many different types of physical spaces. What we learned We learned that the most interesting part of agent integration is not simply asking an AI to generate something. Giving an agent access to the structured state and actions of an application changes what the agent can actually do. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful spatial operations so that an agent could work directly inside the same environment as the human. We also learned that human and agent collaboration does not have to be a handoff where one finishes and the other takes over. Both can contribute to the same evolving workspace. The human can make subjective decisions and adjustments while the agent handles spatial operations and repetitive work. What's next for Taxis The current version is a foundation for a broader spatial planning system. Next, we want to improve the spatial reasoning capabilities of the agent, including better constraint checking, collision detection, capacity planning, and more intelligent arrangements. We also want to expand the types of spaces and objects that can be represented, making Taxis useful for everything from homes and offices to retail spaces, warehouses, exhibitions, studios, and other physical environments. The long-term goal is to make Taxis a general-purpose spatial workspace where people and agents can plan, experiment, and build together. about_excerpt: TheraSync is a WebMCP mental-health intake co-pilot: it triages concerns, matches therapists, detects crisis language, and requires human consent before booking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Mental-health intake is a sensitive workflow. People should not be forced through a generic booking flow before crisis signals are recognized, availability is checked, and consent is respected. We built TheraSync to explore what happens when AI agents can use a website’s real tools while the human remains in control. What it does TheraSync is a WebMCP-powered intake and therapist-matching co-pilot. An agent can: Triage a person’s narrative Detect crisis and self-harm language Match therapists by specialty and modality Find recurring appointment slots Prepare a booking for human review Crisis signals immediately stop routine scheduling and display emergency support options. Booking cannot be committed until a person reviews the summary and explicitly approves it. How we built it The app uses a React and TypeScript frontend, an Express backend, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose. We exposed two WebMCP tools: triage_and_match_therapists commit_intake_booking The backend owns the authoritative safety checks, slot locking, consent validation, and database commit. The frontend supports the fallback window.__WEBMCP_TOOLS__ registry and progressive WebMCP browser APIs. Challenges we ran into WebMCP APIs are still evolving, so different environments expose tools through different browser APIs. We normalized the tool schema and supported multiple registration shapes. We also had to ensure that crisis detection could not be bypassed by calling the backend directly, and that a booking could not be committed without an exact slot lock and explicit human consent. Accomplishments that we’re proud of We built a complete agent-to-browser-to-server workflow with: Crisis safety interception Structured therapist matching Recurring slot availability Two-phase slot locking Human-in-the-loop booking approval PostgreSQL persistence A polished demonstration experience What we learned WebMCP is more than exposing functions to an agent. The best agent-native experiences need clear contracts, visible state changes, graceful errors, safety boundaries, and meaningful moments where the person remains in control. What’s next for TheraSync Next, we would add secure authentication, timezone-aware scheduling, audit logs, real provider integrations, stronger clinical safety escalation, privacy controls, and secure notification delivery. This prototype uses a fictional therapist directory and is not intended for real clinical care. title: Full Loop
pitch: Can an agent finish what it started? A WebMCP lifecycle audit that people and their agents fix together.
about_excerpt: Can an agent finish what it started? A WebMCP lifecycle audit that people and their agents fix together. Like Comment Story Updates Audit Corpus Agents Inspiration I run LaunchLoop (launchloop.xyz). We run developer programs like hackathons and accelerators that help companies get builders using their technology, mostly in gaming and AI. We also perform transformations for our clients, getting them ai-ready. And when we have some extra time, we build/incubate our own products, one of them is Methora.io, which is about getting AI-assisted work all the way to done instead of just started. So a WebMCP hackathon was right up our alley. I browsed the public directories of WebMCP-enabled sites to see what people were connecting. What I found was that most sites had tools for searching, pricing, signing up and checking out (the start of the funnel). But very few had tools for cancelling, returning, or closing an account. I couldn't find anyone measuring that, so I built something that does. I don't think WebMCP really works until an agent can do everything a human can on a site. And you can't fix what you can't measure, so hopefully Full Loop helps WebMCP take the next step! What it does Full Loop takes a website's WebMCP tools and sorts them into eight stages of a customer relationship: Discover, Evaluate, Commit, Use, Modify, Reverse, Exit, Support. It shows which stages the site covers and gives it a score. If an agent can commit on a user's behalf (buy, book, sign up) but has no tool to cancel, return or leave, the site is flagged as an open loop. I ran it over the 475 sites in the public webmcp.com directory, about 2,989 tools in total. 148 sites let an agent commit. 144 of those give it no way to undo. No site in the directory has an exit tool. The page also registers eight WebMCP tools of its own, so you can do the audit through an agent in ChatGPT's browser instead of clicking: audit_site and audit_tool_list run the audit and render it on the page find_sites_by_stage , compare_sites and get_corpus_stats answer questions about the directory (for example "which travel sites let you cancel a booking?", which currently returns nothing) draft_missing_tools writes registerTool stubs for the missing stages into an editor on the page set_stub_code lets the agent rewrite a stub in that editor while you edit it too add_review_note lets the agent leave a short note on a stage card Tool calls are logged on the page so you can see what the agent did. How we built it It's a static site: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. There's no backend and no AI API. The classification is a set of regular expressions run over tool names and descriptions, checked in a fixed order (Exit and Reverse first, so cancel_order doesn't get caught by the generic order rule). The scoring weights each stage. Stub templates are picked by stage and site category. The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Each has a JSON Schema inputSchema and an execute function that updates the DOM and returns JSON in content[0].text . The directory data is a snapshot fetched by a small Node script and committed to the repo, so the site doesn't depend on webmcp.com being up. I tested it in ChatGPT's in-app browser with Codex on GPT-5.6 Sol. Challenges we ran into Word boundaries in regex don't work on snake_case. \bpolicies\b never matched search_shop_policies_and_faqs , so the tool fell through to matching on its description, which mentions "return policy", and it got filed under Reverse. That made a lot of Shopify stores look like they had closed loops when they didn't. Splitting names into words before matching fixed it, and the open-loop rate went from 77% to 97%. Deciding what counts as Reverse also took some thought. Shopify's cancel_cart undoes a cart, not an order, so I put it under Use. The number would have looked better the other way, but it would have been wrong. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 97% figure is reproducible from public data, and as far as I can tell nobody had computed it before. The site works the same whether or not an agent is present. And it has no dependencies, no keys and no server, so there's nothing to break during judging. What we learned With WebMCP the page doesn't need its own model. The agent in the browser supplies the reasoning and the page supplies data and functions. Once I understood that, I stopped trying to add an AI API and the project got simpler. Also, the WebMCP ecosystem right now is mostly acquisition tooling. Sites are giving agents the ability to start things that the same agent can't finish. What's next for Full Loop Full customer flow mapping with green/red lights for which parts are active on WebMCP. I'd also love the audits to be live, and connect to an orchestrator. That way someone can see what is possible with all of the WebMCP sites, while also having a good idea about what is not possible. Also, any site going live on WebMCP should have the full customer journey, so I hope Full Loop becomes integral in ensuring that everyone is setting up WebMCP... THE RIGHT WAY! And I want to bring the lifecycle idea back into Methora, where a job shouldn't count as complete unless it can also be reversed, validated, insured or exited. title: Agent Quote Desk — WebMCP Procurement for Shopify
pitch: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote.
about_excerpt: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Quote Desk completes a live supplier comparison: $42.90 saved (12.1%). Instant product-page fit check using live WebMCP page context, with no network request. The buyer and agent share the same on-screen quote worksheet as tools add matched rows. A human-verified, pay-ready quote is filed only after explicit buyer consent. Chrome's native WebMCP API confirms Shopify's built-ins and Packrift tools coexist with zero collisions. Agent Quote Desk turns a live packaging storefront into an agent-native procurement workspace. Try it first Open https://packrift.com/pages/agent-desk?demo=1 and click ▶ Watch a demo agent work this desk . In about 60 seconds, the page runs the actual workflow in your tab: product matching, freight, comparison rows, and savings. No login or special browser flag is needed. If you are testing in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with its WebMCP testing flag enabled, skip ?demo=1 and ask: "Beat this supplier quote on this page." Why I built this At Packrift, customers do not buy packaging by keyword. They buy by dimensions, material strength, pack counts, and landed cost. Freight alone can be 30–100% of the product cost. A buyer may have a supplier quote with inconsistent product names and simply want to know: do these alternatives fit, and what will I actually save? Answering that usually means spreadsheets, product tabs, freight math, and email. I built Agent Quote Desk so the buyer and agent can do that work in one shared, visible workspace. What the agent can actually do Paste a competitor quote from Uline, Amazon, or another supplier in any format. The agent reads the worksheet, matches each line to Packrift's catalog, adds the comparison rows on screen, calculates live freight, and totals the savings. Ask a product-page question such as "Will an 11 × 8 × 3.5 inch stack fit in this box?" The check_fit_in_this_product tool answers from live page context with no network request. For parcel-size orders, use Shopify's built-in update_cart and proceed_to_checkout tools in the same tab. For freight-class orders, use file_pay_ready_quote_from_worksheet . It requires explicit buyer consent and sends the result to Packrift's human-verified quote workflow. Nothing is auto-charged. The buyer sees every tool call mirrored in the Agent Desk panel. The agent is not working behind a curtain. Why this is a WebMCP use case Shopify's built-in tools are useful, but they are the same on every store. They do not know Packrift's box specs, freight rules, quote workflow, or what makes one product a safe substitute for another. WebMCP lets the merchant give an agent that missing domain knowledge inside the page where the buyer is already working. The result is not just easier navigation. It is a procurement workflow that ordinary browser clicking cannot reliably complete. webmcp.json: the giveaway inside the giveaway I also built and deployed webmcp.json , a declarative manifest for agent tools. The idea is simple: what robots.txt did for crawlers, webmcp.json can do for agent capabilities. A merchant lists tools in one JSON file, including static answers, MCP bridges, or HTTPS APIs with page-level scoping. The kit compiles them into live WebMCP tools at page load and refuses unsafe endpoints at compile time. Packrift's get_agent_guide tool ships this way, so an arriving agent can learn the store's workflows before it acts. Anonymous aggregate telemetry records only the tool and page type, never PII, and is public at https://packrift-webmcp-telemetry.packrift-co.workers.dev/stats . How I built it webmcp-merchant-kit is an open-source, zero-dependency layer that registers merchant tools alongside platform tools. It waits for document.modelContext , detects name collisions, scopes tools to pages, validates required input, shapes outputs for agents, and emits register/call/result/error events for the visible UI. The project provides 15 merchant tools across three scopes: six global tools, two product-page tools, and six desk-page tools, plus one tool compiled from webmcp.json . The same production registry serves three transports: in-page WebMCP, remote MCP over Streamable HTTP at https://mcp.packrift.com , and Shopify UCP at https://packrift.com/.well-known/ucp . The live theme integration is about 40 lines of Liquid and one 17 KB script. A bundled polyfill harness makes the complete flow reproducible in any browser. The hard parts and what I learned The first challenge was coexistence. A merchant kit cannot break Shopify's built-in tools or quietly shadow their names, so registration fails safely on collisions and page-scoped tools unregister cleanly. The native API also exposed two details that changed the implementation. executeTool expects the RegisteredTool object rather than a name, and the browser does not enforce inputSchema for the tool. The kit now handles both correctly and validates required fields itself. The final challenge was trust. Maximum autonomy is not always the right goal. A small parcel can go to checkout, but a freight quote should pause for buyer consent and human verification. The workflow makes that boundary explicit. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the challenge window, beginning Aug. 25, 2026: the kit, all 14 coded tools, webmcp.json , the Agent Quote Desk page, the visible event panel, the test harness, and the theme integration. The existing Packrift store and its remote MCP and quote backend are pre-existing and outside the judging scope. Proof it works The one-click demo completes a real catalog and freight comparison and shows $42.90 saved, or 12.1% , on the sample quote. Native Chrome verification is reproducible with node scripts/verify-native.mjs . On the live desk page, 23 native tools coexist with zero collisions: Shopify's 10 built-ins plus 13 Packrift tools available in that scope. The repository includes 10 automated tests plus a browser demo verifier. Real stakes Packrift is a working packaging distributor with 13,000 SKUs, five US warehouses, live freight rates, and real customers. This is not a mock storefront. Agent Quote Desk writes into the same human-verified pipeline that produces pay-ready quotes today. The project is a working demonstration of a bigger idea: merchants should be able to teach agents how their business actually works, while buyers remain in control and can see every step. title: Ariba Integrator Agent
pitch: Supplier onboarding: 120 days → 14. AI agents handle EDI mapping, CIG testing & integration guides via WebMCP. Humans own sign-off. Everyone moves faster.
about_excerpt:
Supplier onboarding: 120 days → 14. AI agents handle EDI mapping, CIG testing & integration guides via WebMCP. Humans own sign-off. Everyone moves faster.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Enterprise supplier onboarding on SAP Ariba is broken. Every new supplier requires 100+ manual 
touchpoints, takes 30–120 days, and bottlenecks at 5–10 concurrent onboardings. The root cause 
isn't complexity — it's that every step is coordination overhead: emails, status checks, EDI 
validation, connectivity tests, guide generation. The work is structured. The bottleneck is human 
bandwidth. WebMCP finally gives agents a browser-native way to take that load off. 

 What it does 

 AribaFlow is a WebMCP-powered procurement integration portal where AI agents and procurement teams 
work side by side to onboard suppliers in 7–14 days instead of 120. 

 Agents handle the 80% that's repetitive: 

 
 EDI document validation — schema checks, ANID mismatch detection, field mapping verification 
 CIG connectivity testing — AS2/VAN/HTTPS endpoint verification, certificate status 
 Integration guide generation — auto-draft from test results, ready for human review 
 Onboarding checklist orchestration — tracks 13-step SI/SIFL workflow, surfaces blockers 
 Supplier readiness scoring — ranked queue so integration teams prioritise the right suppliers 
 

 Humans handle the 20% that matters: governance, sign-off, and exceptions. 

 All agent interactions happen through WebMCP tools registered on the portal — no backend API keys 
exposed, no separate agent infrastructure, just a website that agents can actually use. 

 How we built it 

 The stack: Next.js 14 (App Router) on Vercel , WebMCP Imperative API for tool registration, 
 React frontend with a live onboarding dashboard, and a mock Ariba/CIG backend that mirrors 
real document flows (PO 850/OrderRequest, ASN 856, Invoice 810). 

 WebMCP tools are registered at page load via navigator.tools.register() . Each tool maps 1:1 to 
a procurement workflow action — structured inputs, structured JSON output, designed so an LLM 
can chain them without ambiguity. 

 The domain model comes from real Ariba integration experience: CIG adapter patterns, AS2 
connectivity, cXML/X12 document types, and the SI/SIFL/NEL role separation that governs every 
enterprise onboarding project. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP origin isolation — any document.domain usage breaks the tools API. Had to audit 
every third-party embed and iframe to enforce origin isolation across the portal. 
 Tool schema design — JSON Schema for EDI validation inputs is non-trivial. Too loose and 
agents hallucinate field values. Too strict and valid documents fail. Iterated with the 
WebMCP Inspector extension until tool calls were reliable. 
 Demo vs. reality — real Ariba systems require corporate VPN and supplier ANIDs. Built a 
faithful mock layer that exercises the same error paths (ANID_MISMATCH, MAP_FIELD_MISSING, 
CERT_EXPIRED) so the demo reflects genuine failure modes, not happy-path theatre. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's browser-native model is genuinely different from server-side MCP. The agent and the 
human share the same page state — which means the portal UI and the agent's tool responses have 
to be in sync. That constraint forced better product design: every tool response updates visible 
UI state, so the human always knows exactly what the agent did and why. 

 What's next 

 
 Live Ariba Network API integration (with OAuth, not mock) 
 Declarative WebMCP annotations on the supplier self-service forms 
 Multi-buyer tenancy so integration service providers can run parallel onboarding waves

title: BayShift
pitch: A shared container yard where humans and browser agents plan, act, conflict, and recover safely through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A shared container yard where humans and browser agents plan, act, conflict, and recover safely through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates BayShift Inspiration Container yards look orderly from a distance, but every retrieval is a live coordination problem. The container needed next may be buried under other cargo, destinations may become unavailable, and an operator can change the physical plan while an agent is still reasoning. A stale instruction is not just inconvenient in this setting; it can be unsafe. We built BayShift to explore what an agent-native operational website should feel like when a person and an AI must share control without silently overwriting each other. What it does BayShift is a live container-yard relocation workbench. A human operator and a browser agent act on the same five-stack yard through one deterministic logistics engine. The operator can select targets, move containers, lock stacks, trigger disruptions, inspect the action trail, and rewind work. Through WebMCP, the agent can: inspect the live yard and priority target locate containers and analyze physical blockers validate a proposed move against yard rules simulate ranked minimum-move relocation plans without mutation execute one authoritative relocation retrieve an exposed target inspect everything that changed after a known version rewind a real yard action Every action is reflected on the same visual canvas and recorded as HUMAN, AGENT, or SYSTEM provenance. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Ordinary browser automation sees pixels and clicks controls. BayShift exposes the meaning of the operation: blockers, constraints, legal destinations, versions, dry runs, mutations, and recovery. The key mechanism is optimistic concurrency for human-agent collaboration. Every destructive tool requires the exact expectedStateVersion the agent inspected before planning. If the operator changes the yard first, BayShift rejects the old command with STALE_STATE , returns the expected and current versions, and asks the agent to inspect and replan. Nothing partially mutates. This makes the website better for both sides. The person keeps visible control of the physical operation; the agent gets precise capabilities rather than guessing from the interface; and conflicts become explicit, recoverable events instead of hidden mistakes. What people and agents can do together A person can introduce real operational judgment while an agent handles structured inspection and constrained planning. In the demo, the agent inspects a buried priority container, identifies its blockers, simulates legal moves, and begins execution. The shared state changes during the workflow, so the agent re-inspects and continues from the current yard rather than blindly following an obsolete plan. The result is not “AI controlling a dashboard.” It is a shared workspace where both participants can act, observe each other, recover from conflict, and leave one auditable history. How we built it BayShift is a client-side React and TypeScript application deployed on Vercel. Native tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with strict JSON schemas and read/write annotations. Both the human interface and all nine WebMCP tools call the same domain functions. The engine enforces LIFO movement, maximum stack height, stack and container locks, crane-lane outages, weight ordering, reserved-destination compatibility, urgency metadata, and exposed-target retrieval. Planning is deterministic and non-mutating. Accepted mutations increment stateVersion ; rejected commands never partially change state. The UI includes a responsive 2.5D yard, a priority queue, plan previews, agent tool traces, metrics, disruptions, and a before/after action ledger. Vitest covers the domain and WebMCP contracts with 18 tests, including stale-state rejection, identical human/agent transitions, retrieval, and rewind. Challenges The hardest part was not exposing buttons as tools. It was designing a semantic tool surface that gives an agent enough operational context while keeping every mutation bounded, versioned, and visible to the person. We also had to ensure the visual yard, tool results, and audit history were projections of one state rather than loosely synchronized copies. Accomplishments Nine native WebMCP tools with deliberate read and write boundaries One authoritative engine for human and agent actions Structured stale-state rejection and recovery Deterministic, non-mutating relocation simulation Actor-attributed audit history and physical rewind A complete deployed experience rather than a tool-only proof of concept 18 automated domain and contract tests What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a website exposes domain intent, not DOM mechanics. The strongest agent experience came from designing conflict, reversibility, and provenance as first-class product behavior. We also learned that sharing a state safely is more important than giving an agent broad autonomy. What's next A production version would connect the same tool contracts to a persistent yard event store, authenticated operator roles, live crane and truck telemetry, and approval policies for higher-risk moves. The challenge build intentionally keeps state local and the planner bounded so judges can inspect the complete interaction reliably. title: CommerceGov: Governed AI Commerce via WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority. Like Comment Story Updates AI agent can inspect, but cannot change production. Inspiration (Why you built it) Capability is not authority. Shopify agencies want AI to draft catalog changes. They cannot afford AI that publishes them. One bad catalog change can hit a live store, paid traffic, and brand trust. That is a control problem, not a model-quality problem. WebMCP makes websites directly usable by agents through structured tools. But as agent capabilities expand, applications need a hard boundary between “prepare a change” and “write production.” CommerceGov focuses on that boundary. The agent gets enough capability to discover, inspect, and propose changes, but it does not get authority to change production state — it cannot approve or apply without human review. What it does (The core solution) CommerceGov puts a ChatGPT agent inside the same governed commerce workflow used by human operators — while keeping production authority outside the agent. The agent searches the shop, reads policy and governance state, proposes a change, and creates a Review proposal. Authorized operators review, approve, and apply according to CommerceGov’s workflow and role boundaries. Only then may CommerceGov’s worker write to Shopify. The agent cannot approve, apply, or mutate Shopify production. Those capabilities are not exposed through WebMCP. For Shopify agencies, this means AI can assist with daily catalog operations without receiving direct production authority. Agencies keep control over clearances, review, approval, and the history of governed changes. Live path: ChatGPT selects openai-webmcp-hackathon.myshopify.com , finds The Complete Snowboard , proposes changing the title to The Complete Snowboard — WebMCP Proof , creates a Review proposal, and retrieves its status and audit evidence. Production stays unchanged. How we built it (The technical stack) The backend is Python FastAPI. The operator UI is server-rendered, and Shopify writes go through a CommerceGov worker rather than the agent or browser. The application is hosted on Render at app.commercegov.io . We implemented WebMCP as a bounded tool surface, not a wrapper around the full CommerceGov API. The page's modelContext exposes five tools: search_products get_governance_context propose_change get_change_status get_audit_evidence We deliberately omit approve, apply, and Shopify production-write tools. The agent therefore has no WebMCP handle to invoke them. Each tool is bound to the authenticated shop and target. Proposal status and audit retrieval resolve to the exact proposal the agent created rather than silently switching to a newer object. Production-mutating tools are absent, not merely permission-gated after the fact. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was identity and authority: keeping tenant, shop, product, and proposal bound across tool calls while ensuring that a request for status or audit evidence cannot silently jump to a newer object. We addressed this by keeping the WebMCP surface deliberately small, excluding production-authority tools entirely, and resolving status and audit evidence against the exact proposal created by the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can perform useful catalog work while people retain risk, approval, and production control. The result is one collaboration workflow: agent discovers → agent proposes → human authority → governed apply → Shopify The WebMCP interaction ends before production authority begins. What's next for CommerceGov Next are richer policy explanations, stronger proposal diffs, and more governed mutation classes — under the same rule. WebMCP may add capability. It may not add production authority. title: PunchPilot — field review, drawn on the sheet
pitch: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance. Like Comment Story Updates PunchPilot: field review drawn on the sheet, with ChatGPT beside the reviewer through six WebMCP Site tools. Six WebMCP Site tools registered by every project screen. Three read, two write, one drafts. None verifies, completes, or issues. ChatGPT reads the live context through the read tools, then asks before calling the write tool. The draft pin sits where it was asked for, 62% across and 49% down on sheet A2.02. Verification stays with the person on site. One word of confirmation. The page announces the save with a WebMCP notice and ChatGPT reports exactly what was written. The visit briefing assembled from live data. Nothing issued, nothing published. Inspiration Construction field reviews are done standing on a slab with a tablet, a set of PDF drawings, and last visit's open items. The record that comes out of that walk is a professional document. A generic assistant can summarise notes, but it cannot safely touch the same numbered record the reviewer is looking at. WebMCP is the first thing that lets the page itself hand the agent a small, typed set of actions bound to the project already open, under the reviewer's own identity. What it does PunchPilot is a full field-review workspace on Cloudflare Workers: projects with disciplines and a filed drawing set, numbered reviews per discipline, findings pinned as page-aware percentages on the PDF, photos, status history, per-review checklists, and a frozen issued report for each visit. Every project screen registers six WebMCP Site tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_field_review_context reads the open project, discipline, latest review, and unresolved carry-forward findings. list_open_findings reads the work list. start_or_resume_field_review resumes the active review or opens the next numbered one for a valid floor, discipline, and drawing. create_draft_finding saves a draft pin at a coordinate on the active sheet and selects it on screen. update_or_verify_finding updates a finding; verification is refused unless the item is already corrected, a human confirms it on site, and a note is given. prepare_field_review_briefing assembles a live-data briefing of raised, revisited, and carried findings and issues nothing. There is deliberately no tool that verifies on the agent's word, completes a review, or issues a report. Why WebMCP is the right fit The value is in the binding, not the chat. The tools are registered by the page that already knows which project, discipline, review, and sheet are open, so ChatGPT never has to guess an identifier or scrape a screenshot. Each tool calls the same authenticated API route the buttons call, with the same validation, the same audit trail, and the same identity the worker resolved at the edge. The drawing, the finding log, and the history update in front of the reviewer as the agent works, so every action is visible and checkable on the spot. That is the kind of trust a professional record needs, and it is exactly what a page-registered tool gives that an external API integration would not. How WebMCP makes the experience better Without it, the reviewer types findings on a keyboard while holding a tablet, re-reads last visit's list to know what to revisit, and rebuilds the briefing by hand at the truck. With it, they say "draft a finding at 62 across, 49 down, fire-rated door closer missing at corridor 205, warning, assign the site super" and the pin lands on the sheet with a number. They ask "what is still open on Level 2 electrical" and get the real list. They ask for the briefing and get raised, revisited, and carried counts from live data. Fewer taps in gloves, no retyping, and nothing invented, because every answer comes from the record. What people and agents accomplish together The agent does retrieval, consistent numbering, structured drafts, and the briefing. The human does what only a person on site can: decide what is physically there, whether a correction is acceptable, and whether the record is ready to issue. The tool schemas encode that split. Verification requires humanConfirmedOnSite , a corrected status, and a note. Completion and issuance are buttons, not tools. The briefing is marked draft and carries externalAction: false . How we built it React 19 on vinext (Next-style App Router compiled to one Cloudflare Worker with Vite), plain CSS design tokens, Lucide icons. Cloudflare D1 with Drizzle ORM (eleven migrations), Cloudflare R2 for drawings and photos, pdf.js with a real worker for the drawing canvas. Identity is resolved once in worker/index.ts and re-stamped as internal headers after stripping every client-sent copy. The public contest Site runs a shared Guest Reviewer so judges need no account; a private deployment uses the verified Sites or Cloudflare Access identity instead, with one build flag deciding which. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level page with an AbortController , MCP-shaped results ( content , structuredContent , isError ), readOnlyHint on reads, and additionalProperties: false on every input schema. 123 source-level and behavioural tests run against the production build before every change ships. Challenges Coordinates had to survive zoom, resize, and re-uploaded sheets, so pins are stored as page-aware percentages rather than pixels. D1 caps a statement at 100 bound variables, so every bulk checklist insert is chunked. The hardest design call was what not to expose: there is no tool that completes a review or issues a report, and a test fails if one is ever added, because a report an agent can issue is a report nobody should trust. What's next Photo capture through a tool, voice-first capture on site, and per-member identity on the public Site once WebMCP supports signed-in flows for shared deployments. Try it (judges) Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop app so it loads in the built-in browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open Meridian Commons — Building B . The header shows a Site tools badge once the tools are registered. Start a new ChatGPT thread in that workspace and ask, for example: "Use the PunchPilot Site tools on the open review. Create a draft finding on the current sheet at 62% across and 49% down: Fire-rated door closer missing — corridor 205, warning severity, assigned to the site super. Do not verify or issue anything." ChatGPT reads the context with the read tools, then asks you to confirm before it calls the write tool. Say yes. Watch the pin land, read the finding number in the receipt, and see the "WebMCP · Draft pin saved" notice on the page. Then ask for the briefing. Everything on the Site is fictional and shared. The project, drawings, findings, and the Guest Reviewer are demonstration data. Video guide (2:30) Time What to watch 0:12 The six Site tools by name: three read, two write, one drafts. No tool verifies, completes, or issues. 0:49 The live Site inside ChatGPT's browser, tools bound to the open project, discipline, and review. 1:03 The reviewer asks for a draft finding in plain words. 1:17 ChatGPT reads context through the read tools, then asks before it writes anything. 1:28 "Yes, save it." The count goes 5 to 6, the WebMCP notice fires, and the receipt reads: D-010, pinned, assigned, not verified, no report issued. 1:52 The pin on the drawing at 62 across, 49 down. Still a draft. 2:05 The briefing from live data: recorded, raised, revisited, carried. Nothing issued. title: HABITAT/NULL
pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together.
